title: The English Opening
description: One of the "Big 3" chess openings is now on Chessly. The English is one of Levy's favorites, and an opening you can play for your entire chess career. Best suited for intermediate and advanced players, but of course anyone can try!

lessons.title: The Main Lines (5...0-0 and 5...d6)
lessons.chapter: The Reverse Sicilian (1. c4 e5) Part 1

r1b1r1k1/1p2np1p/1b1p1p2/pPp1p3/2PP4/P3P.text:
If Black tries to break with ...c5 now...

We'll trade on e5.

r1b1r1k1/1p2np1p/1b3p2/pPp1p3/2P3P1/P3PN.text:
And we have ideas of Nd2-e4 and Rg1 and g5.

White is better because of the extra space and the bishop on b2, which is deceptively active.

Black can't capture on g4, because we'd win the bishop after Rg1.

r1b1r1k1/1pp1np1p/1b1p1p2/pP2p3/2P5/P3PN.text:
The knight has to retreat.

We'll gain space in the center by playing d4!

r1b1r1k1/1pp2p1p/1bnp1p2/p3p3/1PP5/P3PN2.text:
Black often challenges our b-pawn.

We'll just push the pawn forward.

We don't want to trade and split our queenside pawns. Neither do we want to open up their rook.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2p1p/1bnp1p2/4p3/1PP5/P3PN2/.text:
The bishop goes back...

And we'll fianchetto our bishop. It aims across the diagonal towards the king. Hence, our position is quite strong because Black is seriously discouraged from moving the e5- and f6-pawns, which would only activate our bishop further.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2p1p/2np1p2/2b1p3/2P5/P3PN2/.text:
The bishop goes to c5.

We'll attack the c5-bishop with b4, and prepare Bb2.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2p1p/2np1p2/4p3/1bP5/4PN2/PP.text:
Black recaptures.

Let's kick the bishop away from b4.

This will accelerate our expansion and development because we're going to get tempi until we reach Bb2.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2ppp/2np1q2/4pQ2/1bP5/4PN2/P.text:
If the queen chooses to take, then they'll simply trade down into a worse endgame after we exchange on f6. 

Structure is very important, and doubled pawns aren't ideal in many situations.

r1b1rbk1/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3qp2Q/8/P2PPN2/1P.text:
We'll cover more squares in the position and we'll get ready to castle kingside.

Moves like Be2 and 0-0 are next, and White is better because of the pawn structure.

r1b2rk1/1pppqp1p/2n3p1/p1b1p3/2P1N3/P3P3.text:
So Black stops that idea.

We'll settle for b3, preparing to fianchetto.

r1b2rk1/bpp1qp1p/2np2p1/p3p3/2P1N2P/PP2P.text:
And we can continue with plans of a kingside attack and castling queenside!

Like we'll find in other variations, ...f5 isn't good because our knight may reroute to a better square like d5.

r1b2rk1/bpp1qp1p/2np2p1/p3p3/2P1N3/PP2P3.text: d6 is logical, to activate the light-squared bishop.

r1b2rk1/bpppqp1p/2n3p1/p3p3/2P1N3/PP2P3/.text:
Black chooses to hold on to the bishop.

And we'll fianchetto.

Notice that the move g6 weakened the diagonal our bishop now sits on.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qp1p/1bnp2p1/4p3/1PP1N3/P3P3.text:
Our bishop sits on the weakened diagonal.

We can also go for an attack here with h4 and h5 and 0-0-0.

Notice how the knight here is quite tricky. Natural moves like ...f5 to kick it out just send it where it wants to go.
And as the queen goes back...

r1b2rk1/ppp2p1p/1bnp1qp1/4p1N1/1PP5/P3P3.text:
The queen recaptures. 

Our knight jumps to the middle, attacking the queen and blocking the e-pawn. 

This prevents any discoveries with a future ...e4.

r1b2rk1/ppp2p1p/2np1qp1/b3p1N1/2P4P/4P3/.text:
And our ideas include stuff like Ne4, and a3 to get the b4 pawn push.

At any moment, if it is useful, Ne4 is a tempo gain that we should hold in reserve.

As you can see, the lack of space is something we'll use to our advantage: the knight on g5. cannot be easily evicted with moves like ...h6 since every pawn move made in front of a king is a weakness and the knight wants to go to e4 anyway.

r1b2rk1/pppp1p1p/2n2qp1/2b1p1N1/2P5/4P3/.text:
The queen takes.

And we move the knight back, with an attack on queen and bishop.

r1b2rk1/ppppqp1p/2n3p1/2b1p3/2P1N3/4P3/P.text:
The queen defends c5.

We'll try to get in b4, expanding on the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/2p5/3nN3/1bB5/4P3/PPQP.text:
Hence, a move like c6 is normal, after which an idea can be:

Capturing on d5 to double the pawns!

r1bq1rk1/pp1p1ppp/8/3p4/1b6/4PN2/PPQP1PP.text:
And lets bring the knight back, to cover the d4 square.

Black won't get rid of their doubled d-pawns easily!

Expect to go 0-0 soon, but keep an eye out for Qb3, which would be an attack on the bishop and on the d5-pawn.

So if Black tries 11...Qf6,for instance, 12.Qb3 is strong.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2p1p/1bnp1np1/3Np1N1/1PP5/P3.text:
Black blocks the diagonal.

We'll exchange on f6, and argue that we've weakened the dark squares around the black king.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2p1p/2np1np1/b2Np1N1/2P5/4P3.text:
Black has to block the diagonal.

We'll trade on f6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/3Np3/1PP5/P3PN2.text:
The bishop falls back.

We'll use an idea we've already seen, and play Ng5, targeting h7.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2bNp3/2P5/P3PN2/.text:
Black retreats...

And now we go b4 for free.

We don't always want to push our pawns out of the opening, but in this case the center is closed and we can fianchetto without any danger.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/3Np3/1bP5/4PN2/P.text:
...d6 is a developing move that seems natural.

Its popularity is close to ...Nxd5 with 17%, according to the database.

We'll prepare queenside expansion with a3.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/b2Np3/2P5/4PN2/P.text:
Black castles.

And now Ng5 is a neat idea! 

We put pressure on h7 and threaten Nxf6+ followed by checkmate on h7.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1p1p/2n2np1/2bNp1N1/2P5/4P3.text:
Cutting out the attack on h7.

We'll exchange on f6, with a knight fork to follow.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2bNp3/2P5/4PN2/P.text:
This bishop retreat is the most popular, but it's not particularly any good.

In the database, it's played 25% of the time.

We'll play Ng5, with significant pressure on h7. Black must block the diagonal.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/1bP5/2N1PN2/.text:
Castling kingside by Black is the most popular move at this point, so we'll go through it first.

This traditional and principled move is played about 45% of the time.

I suggest going for the knight jump with Nd5: if Black trades, the c6 
-knight will be dislodged.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n5/3np3/1bP5/4PN2/PPQ.text:
This trade isn't a blunder at this point since the king is castled.

Although it might seem counterintuitive to bring White's pawn to d5, this move is the second most popular, being played 18% of the time!

Naturally, we will recapture.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/5n2/4N3/1bB5/4P3/PPQP1.text:
For example, if this retreat is innocently played...

Capturing on f7 enables us to win material.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/8/3nN3/1b6/4P3/PPQP1PP.text: And after this capture, we can develop our bishop with a tempo, and set up ideas on f7.

r1bq1rk1/ppppnppp/8/3Pp3/1b6/4PN2/PPQP1P.text:
The knight goes to e7.

Now the e5-pawn is unprotected. We'll take it.

r1bq2k1/ppp2p1p/2np1p1Q/2b5/2P5/P3PP2/1P.text:
The king recaptures...

We'll threaten a crushing check on h7.

r1bq2k1/ppp2p1p/2np3Q/2b2p2/2P5/P2BPP2/1.text:
The diagonal is blocked...

But we'll play b4 to bring our dark-squared bishop into the attack...

r1bq2k1/ppp2p1p/3p3Q/2b1np2/1PP5/P2BPP2/.text:
Black may think they can centralize the knight and go for this intermezzo...

But we've got a cool double bishop sacrifice with Bb2!

r1bq2k1/ppp2p1p/3p3Q/2b2p2/1PP5/P2nPP2/1.text:
We just move up and clear the way for the rook! 

Black is lost!

r1bq2k1/pppp1rpp/5n2/8/1bB5/4P3/PPQP1PPP.text:
The rook recaptures.

And we'll take it with check.

r1bq2rk/ppp2p1p/2np1p1Q/2b5/2P5/P3PP2/1P.text:
The rook guards the mate threat...

We'll trade, removing a defender of the king.

r1bq4/pppp1kpp/5n2/8/1bQ5/4P3/PP1P1PPP/R.text: We've got a fork, winning the bishop and emerging the exchange up.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/2np1n2/p1bNp3/2P5/P3PN2/.text: That's why Black covers the b4 square.

r1bqk2r/1pp2ppp/2np1n2/p1bNp3/2P5/PP2PN2.text:
And now we'll develop the dark-squared bishop, with ideas of b4 or d4 pawn pushes in the future.

Definitely expect to see moves like 8...Be6 (in which case 9. Nc3 is good), or 8...0-0. after which 9. Bb2 is great, with a quick d4 to come.

r1bqk2r/ppp1nppp/3p4/3Pp3/Qb6/4PN2/PP1P1.text: We've got a double attack, winning the bishop!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2bNp3/2P5/4PN2/PP.text:
...Bc5 is one of the options Black has.

It's definitely a solid approach, keeping the bishop safe.

Black players choose this move about 20% of the time.

To this we respond a3, with a possible idea of b4 if Black allows it.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/1bP5/2N1PN2/P.text:
...d6, defending e5, is played 25% of the time in the database.

The idea here remains the same: plant the knight in the center and challenge Black's setup!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/b2Np3/2P5/4PN2/PP.text:
...Ba5 is another option for Black.

It's only played about 10% of the time, so you might not see it a lot, but it definitely comes in handy to know how to play against it!

Be2 is a sound response, preparing to castle.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np4/3np3/1bP5/4PN2/PPQP.text:
This move looks natural, and so your opponents could fall for it.

Believe it or not, it's the most popular move in this position. Black plays it 41% of the time!

And it's a losing blunder. We recapture, attacking the knight on c6.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/1bP5/2N1PN2/P.text:
And now ...Bb4 is a popular way for Black to continue, aiming to undermine our central control. 

Black players play this move 28% of the time.

We'll continue with Qc2, supporting the c3-knight.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2P5/2N2N2/PP.text:
And now, following sound opening principles, both sides have developed their knights.

We'll play e3, preparing the d4 pawn push.

r1bqr1k1/ppp1nppp/3p4/3Pp1NQ/1b6/4P3/PP1.text: We're attacking two pawns and the black king is in trouble.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3p3Q/1bP1p3/4PN2/.text:
Again, d5 with the idea of Bf8 to defend.

We'll encourage the bishop to retreat.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3pp2Q/1bP5/4PN2/P.text:
d5 attacks the center and also intends to bring the bishop back to a defensive role.

We'll chase it back with a3.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2p1p/2np1p2/4pQ2/1bP5/4PN2/P.text:
This move is possible.

It's actually the best recapture if Black plays their cards right.

We'll get the queen to safety and also keep it on the kingside by playing Qh5.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2p1p/2np1p2/7Q/1bP1p3/4PN2/P.text:
Black has to be aggressive!

But we can respond with some aggression as well! We offer a knight by playing Rg1, aiming for open lines against the black king.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2p1p/2np1p2/7Q/1bP5/4Pp2/PP1.text:
This is exactly what we want!

We'll capture, and suddenly the rook comes to life on the g-file!

r1bqr1k1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/3NpQ2/1bP5/4PN2/.text:
d6, attacking the queen, is the most popular move.

We'll play an intermezzo with Nxf6+.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2ppp/2np4/3PpQ2/1b6/4PN2/PP1.text:
Just as an example of what can go wrong...

The c6 knight is still under attack, and our queen has been pushed to a better square.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p1Q2/1bP5/4PN2/PP1.text: Black opens up an attack on the queen!

r1bqr1k1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/1bP5/3QPN2/PP1P.text:
The queen may look awkward on this square, but we're defending against d4 somewhat.

We're going to castle next and boast that we're a pawn up. Be2 and 0-0 and it's up to Black to try to get an initiative.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/3Np3/1bP5/4PN2/P.text:
Black's best move, objectively, but not the most popular.

Same as ...Be7, it's played about 12% of the time.

We'll activate our queen and bring it out to f5.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/2n5/3npQ2/1bP5/4PN2/PP.text:
If Black trades, they can get in trouble quickly.

We'll recapture...

8...Ne7 would drop a pawn.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/5n2/4NQ2/1bP5/4P3/PP1P.text:
Black recaptures.

...d6, winning a piece, is a threat, so we retreat the knight.

r1bqr1k1/ppppbppp/2n2n2/3NpQ2/2P5/4PN2/P.text:
The bishop simply goes back. 

This line is a gambit by Black, because we can take the pawn on e5.

r1bqr1k1/ppppbppp/5n2/3NNQ2/1nP5/4P3/PP1.text:
And now Black's idea is to take advantage of our lack of development.

Let's just trade on b4.

r1bqr2k/ppp2p1p/2np1p2/2b4Q/2P5/P3PP2/1P.text:
The bishop goes to c5...

We'll threaten checkmate with Qh6.

r1bqr2k/ppp2p1p/2np1p2/7Q/1bP5/4PP2/PP1P.text:
The king hides.

We'll prepare b4 to put our bishop on the same diagonal as the black king.

r1bqrbk1/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3p3Q/2P1p3/P3PN2/.text:
It goes back..

And with d4 we claim a central square for our pawn. 

Black has to capture en passant if they want to challenge us, but that would bring our bishop to d3, hitting h7.

r1bqrbk1/ppp2p1p/2n2p2/3pp2Q/2P5/P3PN2/1.text:
It goes back...

We'll exchange pawns in the center.

r2qrbk1/ppp1np1p/4bp2/3p3Q/2PPp2N/P3P3/1.text:
The knight goes to e7. 

This is normal looking: bringing more defenders.

r2qrbk1/ppp1np1p/4bp2/3p3Q/2PPpP1N/P3P3/.text:
The problem is we can bring more attackers and create serious problems for Black.

Our plan is simply g4 and while we do have some strong g5 ideas, g4 mostly supports the computer suggested Nf5 for Nh6+ followed by f5.

r2qrbk1/ppp2p1p/2n1bp2/3p3Q/2PPp3/P3PN2/.text:
The bishop defends d5 and f7.

And now we've got Nh4, transferring attackers to the kingside.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2P5/2N5/PP1PPP.text:
Black develops their knight.

And we'll develop our other knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
One way they may counter our setup is by bringing their pawn out to e5. 

This controls the center directly, and borrows from the positional concepts of the closed Sicilian. Just that in this case, of course, the plans are reversed.

We'll bring our knight out, controlling the center further.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to chapter 1 of the English Opening, which begins with 1.c4. 

Black's most popular response is the Reverse Sicilian, 1...e5. 

In this study, you'll be introduced to the Four Knights line with Bb4, and we'll continue exploring this opening in the next study.

lessons.title: The Sidelines (5...Bxc3 and 5...d5)
lessons.chapter: The Reverse Sicilian (1. c4 e5) Part 1

2kr1b1r/pppb1ppp/2nq4/1B1n2N1/3P4/2N5/PP.text:
It's quite unpleasant to deal with this knight move.

Just look at White's pieces, much more active than Black's!

2kr1b1r/pppq1ppp/2n5/1B6/8/2P1PQ2/P2P2PP.text: And we'll have pressure along the f and b-files!

r1b1k2r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B4q1/3Pp3/2P1P3/P2.text:
Black attacks the bishop and the pawn.

We'll retreat, defending g2.

r1b1k2r/ppp3pp/2nb4/5pq1/3Pp3/1QP1P3/P2N.text:
And our queen comes out, preventing castling. 

Ba3, to trade off Black's powerful dark-squared bishop, is also possible.

r1b1kb1r/ppp2ppp/2nq4/1B1np3/8/2N1PN2/PP.text:
Black could try holding on to the center with Qd6.

They'll try this peculiar move only 2% of the time on average, but it's definitely an interesting line.

Black is going for long castling.

In which case, we'll castle.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qppp/1bnp1n2/8/2PP4/P1N1BN2/.text:
And we castle queenside, supporting the d4-pawn.

We have a plan of attacking on the kingside with h3 and g4!

r1bq1rk1/p1p3pp/2p2p2/8/3P4/4PN2/P2Q1PPP.text:
Black recaptures...

We'll castle, intending Rfc1.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1nppp/3p4/3P4/1b1P4/3B1N2/PP.text:
The knight goes back...

And Qa4 traps the bishop!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B6/3P4/4PN2/P4PPP.text:
And Black gets to safety.

We can castle as well.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/8/1bPP4/2NB1N2/P.text:
This move, opening up the bishop, is popular.

We'll play the knight jump Nd5 and win material by force!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/3p4/3n4/Qb1P4/3B1N2/PP3.text:
Nxd5 defends the bishop for one move...

But it's still trapped! We attack it again with a3.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B6/3P4/4PN2/P2Q1P.text:
And Black castles.

We'll break up their pawn structure by capturing on c6.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bPP4/2NB1N2/P.text:
Black doesn't want to be stuck in the center, so they castle.

We'll castle as well, and after eight moves, only White has pawns in the center!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/8/2PP4/P1N2N2/1P.text:
That's why Black should cover the c5 square.

Now we'll play Qe2+.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B2p3/8/2P1PN2/P2P1.text:
Bd6, developing, is the most popular move.

Let's break in the center with d4!

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B6/3Pp3/2P1PN2/P4P.text:
If Black attempts this push...

We can retreat and attack e4.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2nb4/1B6/3p4/2P1PN2/P4PP.text:
Black usually trades here.

We'll recapture towards the center.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B6/1b1P4/4PN2/P4PP.text:
Bb4+ is a move some players may try. The idea is to gain a tempo towards castling. 

We'll block the check.

r1bqk2r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B6/3P4/4PN2/P2b1PP.text:
Black trades.

Our queen will recapture.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/1bn2n2/8/2PP4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
This retreat, played 16% of the time, is a natural move. 

I suppose Black players under 2000 like the more aggressive route.

We're going to cover the b4 square with a3.

So a simple threat will be c5 and b4, winning a piece.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b1p3/2P5/2N1PN2/.text:
4...Bc5 develops the bishop and comes third in terms of popularity, being chosen 17% of the time.

But we can just gain a tempo on the bishop with d4!

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/2b5/2Pp4/2N1PN2/P.text:
This capture is by far the most natural and most popular.

But we can just recapture and we are left with a strong central pawn duo.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
Black moves the bishop and creates a pin.

Black will probably play this move more than half of the time, so be ready for it!

In the database, it's 57%.

We'll go for rapid development with Bd3!

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/3pp3/2P5/2N1PN2/P.text:
The most popular alternative to 4...Bb4 is 4...d5! It's nearly 25% of games. 

But we can have an advantage by taking. The idea is that we have an extra tempo. 

Usually, in the Sicilian Reversed, it's useful for Black to play with Closed Sicilian motifs. Going for an "open" Sicilian can backfire.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B2p3/8/2n1PN2/PP1P.text:
This trade is by far the most popular move.

Black players love to relieve some central tension and capture on c3, allowing themselves to develop easily.

This capture is played a whopping 64% of the time!

We'll capture towards the center.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/1B6/4p3/2P1PN2/P2P1.text:
e4 gains a tempo on the knight.

The beauty of Ne5 is that it covers the d7 square, so if Bd7 we can just take.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2n5/3np3/8/2N1PN2/PP1P1.text:
The knight recaptures.

And now we'll develop and pin the c6 knight, threatening to double the pawns and ready to castle!

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B1np3/8/2N1PN2/PP.text:
...f6 defends the e5-pawn.

It's the second most popular move, but it's only played 10% of the time!

That goes to show how popular ...Nxc3 is.

The d4 pawn break, once again, is good in these variations.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B2p3/3P4/2n1PN2/P.text:
The knight is traded...

And we recapture.

r1bqkb1r/ppp3pp/2n2p2/1B6/3p4/2P1PN2/P4P.text:
Black trades further...

Again, we recapture.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2P5/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black defends.

With e3, we prepare the d4 pawn break.

Black takes back with the knight.

We'll trade again...

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/4b3/8/PP1PPPPP/R1.text: And it looks like Black is up a piece.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3P4/Q3b3/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
However, there's a check on a4 which Black hasn't counted on!

The bishop is forked and we'll get back the piece, have a material advantage and a winning position!

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/2b1p3/2P5/2N5/PP1PPP.text:
A move that's played 12% of the time is 2...Bc5.

It looks like a logical and natural square for the bishop.

However, we'll prove the bishop on c5 is misplaced once we get our pawns rolling down the board!

As we saw in the previous chapters, our typical strategy is to slowly gain control of the center with the e3-d4 advances. 

We'll follow our plan and now d4 is threatened with tempo.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p2N1/2P1p3/2N5/PP1.text:
The most popular move is actually ...d5, played a whopping 34% of the time.

However, it's a mistake!

Black is going to be over-extended.

We'll take on d5 and undermine the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2P5/2N5/PP1PPP.text:
The most common move in this position is 2...Nf6, activating the knight.

It is the most natural move, after all.
It's played 36% of the time, which is almost 10 million games!

We have a choice here, to go g3-Bg2 or not? In the English White  can choose to fianchetto and develop slowly or develop more quickly and fight for the center. 

We are doing the latter with Nf3.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2P1p3/2N2N2/PP1P.text:
An aggressive move for Black, although played only 8% of the time. 3...d6 4.g3 would be a transposition to our King's Indian Chapter.

The e4-pawn might have a very good chance of being over-extended, however.

We'll move the knight forward and attack the pawn on e4!

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
As in the previous two chapters, Black goes for the Reverse Sicilian.

The most critical response.

We'll build behind the pawn and activate the knight to c3.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to Chapter 3 of our English course!

In this chapter, we'll analyze the most important second move sidelines that Black can throw our way in the Reverse Sicilian.

In online games, you might face a variety of lines, so it's crucial to come prepared!

Let's begin,with 1.c4, The English.

r1bq1k1r/pppp1pb1/2n2Npp/6B1/2P4Q/8/PP2P.text: If they try to chase us out...

r1bq1k1r/pppp1pbN/2n3pp/6B1/2P4Q/8/PP2PP.text:
We've got Nh7+!

We check the king with a discovered attack on Black's queen on d8.

We are going to be up a queen.

We can't really ask for more.

r1bq1k1r/pppp1pbp/2n2Np1/6B1/2PQ4/8/PP2P.text:
They move the king to f8 instead.

Now our knight and queen are under pressure, so it's important to know the next move as well.

We'll sidestep to h4 to keep defending the knight on f6.

Black is out of options here.

r1bq1k1r/ppppbp1p/2n2Np1/6B1/2PQ4/8/PP2P.text: If they slide to f8, which is the alternative...

r1bq1k1r/ppppbp1p/2n2NpB/8/2PQ4/8/PP2PPP.text:
We have checkmate with the bishop!

An 8 move checkmate that only goes to show how dangerous 3...exd4 is for Black.

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/1p1p1n2/1P2p3/Q1P5/4PN2/.text:
It's time to develop ourselves.

Positionally speaking, White is better here, with prospects of d4.

However, an interesting chess game remains to be played!

r1bqk2r/pp2nppp/1p1p1n2/1P2p3/Q1P5/5N2/P.text:
The only safe square is e7.

Having disrupted Black's pawn structure, captured their bishop and pushed their knight back...

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/1pnp1n2/4p3/QPP5/5N2/P2PP.text:
Black has to recapture with the c-pawn.

Let's take advantage of our approach to grab even more space.

We'll attack the c6-knight and chase it away from the center.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/1bnp1n2/3Np3/QPP5/5N2/P2.text:
Black retreats to b6.

Our plan was to trade for the bishop all along.

Here, we gain the bishop pair and damage Black's pawn structure.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/2bNp3/Q1P5/5N2/PP.text:
So they retreat to c5.

But they aren't out of the woods yet.

Let's continue chasing the bishop with b4!

In the process of targeting the bishop, we are also gaining space and improving some pieces.

r1bqk2r/ppp2ppp/2np1n2/4p3/QbP5/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black has to block with the knight in order to defend the bishop.

Having great control of the d5-square, we'll utilize our setup to jump there and put more pressure on the bishop.

Black can't capture on d5 because after cxd5 the pinned knight on c6 would be under attack.

r1bqk2r/pppp1pbp/2n2np1/3N2B1/2PQ4/8/PP2.text:
They could try to counter attack our queen, but we are quicker.

Let's capture with check first, simply winning a piece.

If Black recaptures, we'll simply play Qxf6.

r1bqk2r/ppppbp1p/2n2np1/3N2B1/2PQ4/8/PP2.text:
Black can't do anything but develop and attack our queen.

However, we'll capture with check.

If Black takes back, we'll simply be up a piece.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2np4/5p2/2P5/2NQ2P1/PP2P.text:
We'll just calmly continue with g3 and Bg2, having placed our queen on d3.

No need to hurry - we've got a comfortable position.

r1bqkbnr/ppp3pp/2np4/5p2/2P5/2NQ4/PP2PPP.text:
However, in online games, specially Blitz, you might see ...d6 frequently.

The direct downside is that it blocks the dark-squared bishop.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/5p2/2P5/2NQ4/PP2PPP.text:
We can slide to d3 with an attack on the f5-pawn!

It's actually not that comfortable for Black to defend this pawn.

They could play ...Nge7 or ...g6, but both those moves have negative consequences.

The computer suggests ...Nf6 here, allowing us to capture on f5.

r1bqkbnr/pppp2pp/2n5/5p2/2PQ4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Yes, Black can develop the knight with tempo, but we don't have to retreat all the way.

We can slide to d3 with an attack on the f5-pawn! It's actually not that comfortable for Black to defend this pawn.

They could play ...Nge7 or ...g6, but both those moves have negative consequences.

The computer suggests ...Nf6 here, allowing us to capture on f5.

rnb1qrk1/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/4pp2/1PP5/2N2NP1.text:
An idea is ...Qe8, going to h5.

Black also wants to push ...f4 in the future if possible.

However, we are still not worried.

With d3, we'll establish our pawn chain in the center and remain solid.

rnb2rk1/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/4pp1q/1PP5/2NP1NP.text: Black goes for the queen activation...

rnb2rk1/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/4pp1q/1PP5/2NPPNP.text:
And we'll play e3 to control the f4-square.

Going into the middlegame, our bishop is extremely strong on g2, and once the knight moves, the queens might get exchanged.

Our play should be focused on the queenside where we've got the advantage and can keep pushing.

All in all, there's chess to be played!

rnbk1bnr/ppp3pp/8/4pp2/2P5/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Black has to lose castling rights now.

And with the king on d8, we can develop with tempo!

We are the ones controlling the game.

rnbk2nr/ppp1b1pp/8/4ppB1/2P5/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
It's long castling with check!

This line is basically forced after 3...d6, and we've developed a minor piece and castled with tempo, while Black is still struggling to get their pieces out.

We are better here and will often go on to win the game from this position.
Once Black blocks with the bishop, do you see another move we can throw in?

rnbq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/4pp2/2P5/2N2NP1/.text:
And so does Black.

What plan do we continue with from here?

An interesting idea is b4!

We advance on the queenside where we've got more space with the c-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1p1p/6p1/4b3/2P5/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
Black is forced to recapture with the bishop.

How should we continue now?

We can activate the knight with tempo!

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/4p3/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
It's logical to continue the fianchetto, but now we will win tempi for our development!

3...Bg7 is played 45% of the time.

We'll take on e5.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/8/2P5/2N2NP1/PP2PP.text:
And we'll play a fianchetto of our own.

We are the only player with some control in the center and are better developed.

Our bishop will stand strong on g2, and we'll be able to get the dark-squared bishop out as well.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/1bP5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
As people are taught to get the knights out before the bishops, 2...Bb4 is played only 6% of the time.

However, it's a reasonable developing move that threatens to disrupt our pawn structure.

Although unusual to move the queen on move 3, we'll do it here.

3.Nd5 was a  tempting alternative, but 3.Qc2 could be a shortcut for us to get back into Chapter 1.

rnbqk2r/ppp1b1pp/3p1n2/4pp2/2P5/2N2NP1/P.text:
And so does Black.

This is more of a positional line with both sides activating pieces before going to battle.

We'll castle short...

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/1bP5/2N2N2/PPQ.text:
Black could defend the e5-pawn with ...d6, which is the second most popular move here, played 29% of the time.

An interesting idea for us is to give a check on a4!

This move might seem surprising since we are moving the queen for the second time in five moves.

However, it works very well because Black's bishop is vulnerable.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2P1P3/2P2N2/P1.text:
And we'll continue with e4, supported by the queen.

We are planning a similar assault as in Chapter 1, with d3, g3 and Bg2.

Later on, we could play for f4.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/4p3/2P5/2P2N2/P1QP.text:
Black has to deal with the e5-pawn now, so they do with ...d6.

Now the light-squared bishop is open.

rnbqk2r/pppp1pbp/5np1/6B1/2PQ4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
The more logical ...Bg7 is played 95% of the time.

However, it doesn't save Black in the slightest.

We'll continue putting pressure on the pinned piece by playing Nd5.

Black is out of options here; they only have two defenders and we are attacking the knight with three pieces!

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/1bP5/2N5/PPQPPP.text:
Black continues by developing the knight, ready to castle.

We'll do the same.

As you can see, we have a similar position as some Chapter 1 positions, with minor differences.

Here, 4...Nc6 is the most common move, when 5.e3 sends us back to Chapter 1.

Let's explore some alternatives for Black.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2P5/2b2N2/PPQPP.text:
4...Bxc3 is the third most popular move here, played 17% of the time.

Black trades our knight off.

It might seem like we played 3.Qc2 to recapture with the queen, but...

We'll take back with the b-pawn, towards the center!

This helps us build a strong pawn formation like we encountered in Chapter 1.

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/5n2/5p2/2PPpB1P/2N1P3/P.text:
We'll go for the immediate h4!

We want to push the h-pawn before developing the knight to h3, and leave ourselves with potential attacking opportunities in the future.

Our bishop can develop to e2.

White is slightly better already!

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/5n2/5p2/2PPpB2/2N1P3/PP.text: Once Black develops the bishop and prepares to castle, there's an interesting idea for us.

rnbqk2r/ppppbp1p/5np1/6B1/2PQ4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
Black can unpin with ...Be7, and they do so 3% of the time.

However, it's pretty straightforward why that's a bad move.

The knight on f6 is still pinned to the rook on h8!

That means we can still continue piling pressure on the knight with Nd5.

It can't move.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/3p1n2/4pp2/2P5/2N2NP1/PP.text:
Black develops the knight naturally.

We'll prepare castling...

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5np1/8/2PQ4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
However, ...Nf6 loses the game on the spot!

And the best thing is, the moves play themselves.

Let's pin the knight immediately with Bg5.

Black has two options to defend, and both lose.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/5n2/5p2/2PPpB2/2N5/PP2P.text:
Now they finally get a minor piece out.

Having activated the dark-squared bishop, we can now push e3 and start thinking about the kingside activation.

On the queenside and in the center, we've reached our desired setup.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/3p4/4p3/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
2...d6 is the fourth most popular move, played 10% of the time.

It's a solid approach, defending the center but blocking the bishop on f8.

We'll continue with Nf3 anyway.

It's the best square for the knight to develop to.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/3p4/4pp2/2P5/2N2N2/PP1PP.text:
Definitely an active approach from Black.

They let us place a pawn on c4, but they want to occupy the d4 and the e4-squares!

We'll prepare the fianchetto of our bishop. It's often the best way for us to develop.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/3p4/4pp2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
According to the database, 3...d6 is only played 5% of the time here.

Let's take on e5.

rnbqkbnr/ppp3pp/8/4pp2/2P5/2N5/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Black recaptures, naturally, and now the queens face each other.

We'll trade, as it leads us to an advantage.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/6p1/4p3/2P5/2N5/PP1PPP.text:
Black prepares a kingside fianchetto only 1% of the time.

However, that's still around 250,000 games!

Let's unleash a powerful idea.

We'll strike in the center, with d4, before Black starts developing.

Black has to be careful now.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1p1p/6p1/8/2Pp4/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
Capturing in the center is already on the verge of losing for Black, and it's played 42% of the time!

The position is already extremely dangerous because our queen gets to the center, attacking the rook and preventing Black playing ...Bg7!

The best move for Black is ...Qf6, but even then will we get some tempi and an advantage.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/8/4p3/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
As in the previous two chapters, Black goes for the reverse Sicilian with 1...e5.

The e-pawn takes the center and discourages 2.d4 from us.

We'll continue by activating the queenside knight.

On the second move, Black has got a lot of options.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/4pp2/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
2...f5 is fifth in popularity and Black players opt for it 10% of the time.

It's an aggressive option that resembles the "Grand Prix" attack that White uses against the Sicilian (with e4 and f4).

We'll fight against it by going for the immediate d4!

The idea is to split Black's e-and f-pawns and try to counter-attack quickly.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/5p2/2PPp3/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
Black could gain more space and decline the trade by pushing.

3...e4 is the most popular move in this position, played over half of the time with 51%.

It gives us the f4-square for our dark-squared bishop, however.

We've already activated two pieces against Black's none.

rnbqkbnr/pppp2pp/8/5p2/2Pp4/2N5/PP2PPPP/.text:
Capturing on d4 only gives us what we want, which is dominance in the center.

This move is played 27% of the time.

We'll recapture with the queen.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Study 2 of Chapter 3, we'll take a look at slightly rarer responses by Black after 2.Nc3.

Without further ado, let's go!

We begin with 1.c4.

2rq1rk1/pb1n1ppp/1ppbn3/3pp1PP/2P4N/1PN1.text:
Black got the knight to e6...

But as soon as he added a defender into the position, he had to face another attacking piece!

The bishop on d6 was under fire.

2rq1rk1/pb1nbppp/1pp1n3/3ppNPP/2P5/1PN1P.text:
And after O-O-O, the game continued.

However, White had the clear advantage.

Black's pieces were all tangled up, and White had the active bishop on b2 and prospects of pushing g6 to continue the attack.

That's the Bayonet Slav.

2rq1rk1/pbnn1ppp/1ppb4/3pp1PP/2P5/1PN1PN.text:
Black should maybe have played e4; however, he played the slow ...Nc7 with the idea of ...Ne6.

According to the computer, Oparin should have gone Bd3 here and allowed the fork on e4!

After 14.Bd3 e4 15.Nxe4 dxe4 16.Bxe4 White is winning with the two bishops and kingside aggression.

Oparin wanted to get another piece into the attack, so he jumped to h4 with the idea of Nf5.

2rqnrk1/pb1n1ppp/1ppb4/3pp1P1/2P4P/1PN1P.text:
It was like Kevlishvili was ignoring the kingside attack by playing on the queenside.

His position wasn't losing yet, but White already had some advantage.

And the moves played themselves.

With two pawns on the fifth rank, it was probably time for Black to start reacting.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2nq1n2/3pp3/P7/1P2PN2/1B1.text:
And our idea here is a4, going for Ba3!

This is one way to gain control of the light squares, another one being 10.Bb5.

r1b2rk1/p2n1ppp/2pq4/3p4/3Pp3/1P2P3/PB2B.text: Capturing with the pawn establishes a nice pawn chain.

r1b2rk1/p2n1ppp/2pq4/3p4/3Pp3/1PB1P3/P3B.text:
And here's a nice idea.

We'll go Bc3, with the idea of Qd2 to gain control of the queenside dark squares.

If we achieve that, we'll have threats like Bb4 to skewer the queen or Ba5 to improve the bishop.

We'll also take advantage of the semi-open c-file by placing a rook on c1.

It's important to play against Black's c6-weakness.

r1b2rk1/pp1n1ppp/2nq4/3pN3/3Pp3/1P2P3/PB.text:
In order to remove our most active piece, they'll have to go ...Nd7 to add more pressure to it.

And in all fairness, this does force us to trade.

I recommend trading on c6 to leave Black's pieces tied up on the back ranks.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2nq1n2/3p4/3Pp3/1P2PN2/PB.text:
So they push ...e4.

But the d4-pawn also serves as support to our knight.

Which we can now place in the center!

Black can't play ...Nxe5 because of the fork on e5.

r1b2rk1/pp3ppp/2nq1n2/3pp3/8/1P2PN2/PB1P.text:
Now, instead of going for the previous a4-idea, I suggest a different approach.

Let's challenge the center!

Black taking on d4 would only give us extra activity...

r1bq1rk1/p2n1ppp/1ppbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
Once again, Black can opt for ...b6.

However, as mentioned, this is a slow setup that definitely gives us the green light to start attacking.

Let's go for the usual Rg1 idea.

You know what we are aiming for.

r1bq1rk1/p2nbppp/1pp1pn2/3p4/2PP4/1PN1PN.text:
And most often, they'll try to do that with ...b6.

The bishop is coming to b7.

Having decided against the aggressive g4, I suggest we go for the queen-bishop battery with Bd3.

The f6-knight is the only defender of h7 at the moment!

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/2P5/1PN1PN.text:
If Black goes for ...e5 here, you probably already know what to do.

We'll take on d5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pb4/3np3/8/1PN1PN2/PB.text:
Important to note: it's also possible for Black to recapture in the center with the knight.

This shouldn't prevent our plan, though.

Black just gave up control of the e4-square, so we'll put the knight there! This unleashes our bishop on b2 as well.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
If Black plays this precise move order (which they do more than half of the time), then we will have "wasted" a tempo on Be2 in conjunction with our kingside attack.

Of course we can just go for d4 and O-O and play positionally as well, but let's keep the Bayonet option alive by placing our queen actively on c2, keeping an eye on the kingside.

At this point, let's cover some options for Black.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/3b1n2/3pp3/8/1PN1PN2/P.text:
Once the pawn recaptures...

There's Nb5, attacking the bishop, as per usual.

r1bq1rk1/pp1nbppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
If Black goes for ...Ndb7 to activate the queenside knight...

Now I would be very tempted to go for the aggressive g4 or Rg1 plan. 

In practice White has scored tremendously, but the engine disapproves! 

We'll keep things simple and safe with d4.

Black has to untangle their pieces somehow.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/1N1pp3/8/1P2PN2/P.text:
If Black decides to play without taking any risks, that's okay.

We'll just capture.

r1bq1rk1/pp4pp/2n1pn2/1N1p4/4p3/1P2P3/PB.text:
But once we retreat, we are indeed the only ones with a dark-squared bishop.

And a very active one at that.

r1bq1rk1/pp4pp/2n1pn2/1N1pB3/4p3/1P2P3/P.text: True, Black can develop with tempo here...

r1bq1rk1/ppbn1ppp/2p5/3np3/4N1P1/1P2PN2/.text:
Let's go for the standard attacking idea with g4!

We've got the active queen and bishop and will support the g-pawn with the rook.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/1N1pp3/8/1P2PN2/PB.text:
There's really no point in Black retreating now.

We'll take.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/2P5/1PN1PN.text:
Finally, Black pushes ...e5.

Do you know what to play here?

Well, nothing new.

We'll just capture in the center with the idea of Nb5 if Black recaptures with the pawn. Compare the 8...e5 line.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1ppp/2pb4/3np3/8/1PN1PN1P/P.text:
It comes in handy to cover what to do if Black chooses to play ...Nxd5.

We've got the e4-square available for our knight now.

Black's bishop must move! If 11...Bc7 what do you think we should play? 

12.g4, of course!

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
Black's most common move is ...Re8, possibly supporting ...e5.

Let's go with h3. I propose this subtle idea as we want to push g4 (similar to Rg1) without completely burning our bridges (we can still castle!)

9...b6 is similar to our 8...b6 line. 
We would respond with 10.g4!

r1bqrbk1/pp1n1ppp/2p5/3np3/4N3/1P2PN1P/P.text: If Black chooses to retreat to f8, there's another defender of the king now.

r1bqrbk1/pp1n1ppp/2p5/3np3/4N3/PP2PN1P/1.text:
We'll go for a3.

A useful positional move to take
control of b4. 

We can decide whether to castle next with a quieter positional struggle or go for the aggressive g4-lunge which has been in the spirit of our study!

r2q1rk1/pb1n1ppp/1ppb1n2/3pp3/2P3P1/1PN1.text:
In chess, it's often a good idea to counter your opponent's attack on the side of the board by creating complications in the center.

This is what Black tried here with ...e5.

However, that didn't stop the g-pawn from attacking the f6-knight.

r2q1rk1/pb1n1ppp/1ppbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
Just to illustrate how the game could go on, let's look at a real game played between G. Oparin and R. Kevlishvili in Columbia in 2019.

Black activated the bishop to b7 here.

And, as one should, Oparin started attacking! The next goal was g5.

r2q1rk1/pb1nbpp1/1pp1pn1p/3p4/2PP4/1PNBP.text:
The last move of this line is Rad1, centralizing one of the rooks.

Having positioned a lot of pieces to control the e4-square, we are planning to centralize the other rook with Re1 and play for the e4-break!

White is slightly better with a comfortable position.

The prophylactic ...h6 is on the board.

Black doesn't want to constantly worry about h7 and takes away the g5-square.

r2q1rk1/pb1nbppp/1pp1pn2/3p4/2PP4/1PNBPN.text:
Black doesn't have anything to worry about for the moment, though.

But neither do we.

Let's castle, safe and sound.

The positional approach works as well.

r2qnrk1/pb1n1ppp/1ppb4/3pp1P1/2P5/1PN1PN.text:
The only square it could really jump to was e8.

Did Black's advance in the center mean that White should slow down?

Absolutely not!

The h-pawn followed right in the g-pawn's tracks.

Suddenly, two dangerous pawns found themselves near Black's king.

rbbq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/5n2/1N1pp3/8/1P2PN2/PB.text:
But we can force the issue with Rc1!

Our idea is Nc7. 

Getting Black's dark-squared bishop is of highest priority!
This time it's got the b8-square...

rn1q1rk1/pb3ppp/1ppbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
We'll get the rook off the diagonal and prepare g4!

This signals the beginning of our attack.

rnbq1rk1/1p2bppp/p4n2/1N1p4/3Np3/1P2P3/P.text: Black can kick our knight away...

rnbq1rk1/1p2bppp/p4n2/3p4/3Np3/1PN1P3/PB.text:
But we've got other ideas.

After jumping back to c3, a great idea would be to reroute to the more active c5-square and try to provoke Black to trade that dark-squared bishop after all.

On the kingside, we could try to solve our problems by undermining Black's structure with f3 after castling.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/1ppbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
At multiple branches in this study will we see Black being able to play ...b6.

This type of development usually invites our Bayonet idea.

We'll activate the queen to a nice light-squared diagonal.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
The king castles short.

We'll activate the queen.

As always, it's eyeing the kingside, ready to join a potential future attack.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/5n2/1N1p4/3Np3/1P2P3/PB.text:
Black could try to preserve the bishop in a more passive manner by retreating to e7.

However, this gives us additional chances to keep activating pieces.

With Rc1, we are threatening Nc7 to trap the rook.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
Black could also try to go ...e5 here.

We will deploy a similar idea to the one we saw on the branch on move 6.

Let's take in the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
The most popular option here is ...O-O, played 58% of the time.

Black has developed the kingside and simply castles.

We'll do the same, developing in a calm manner.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3b1n2/1N1p4/4p3/1P2PN2/P.text:
A more aggressive option for Black is to push ...e4.

This does open up our b2-bishop, though.

And gives us the nice central d4-square for the knight.

However, Black's point is to save the dark-squared bishop.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/3b1n2/3pp3/8/1PN1PN2/PB1.text:
Once Black recaptures...

There's Nb5 again.

We'll harass the bishop.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/5n2/1N1pb3/3Np3/1P2P3/PB.text:
Which they can with ...Be5, for example.

It would be great if we were the only player with a dark-squared bishop.

Do you see a direct way to achieve that?

With Ne6, we sacrifice the knight by forking the queen and the rook.

Black is forced to capture.

rnbq1rk1/pp4pp/4pn2/1N1pb3/4p3/1P2P3/PB1.text:
Once they do...

We can get their dark-squared bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp2bppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
Black players choose 5...Be7 the most often!

This move has been played nearly a third of the time, 33%.

Black goes for solid and traditional development and wants to castle quickly.

Let's activate our dark-squared bishop, as we had intended to do anyway.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
6...e5 is not the best way to play, and its popularity being only 3% confirms that.

Now, we'll introduce a repetitive pattern throughout this study.

Since Black has weakened the d5-pawn, let's take it.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P2.text:
From a theoretical point of view,
this is the most precise move.

The good news for us is that this is only played 23% of the time, making it second in popularity.

Black logically develops the bishop to an active square and prepares
castling.

We'll continue as planned and activate the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/3b1n2/3pp3/8/1PN1PN2/PB1P.text:
The pawn recaptures.

And here's a move we most often play in these types of positions.

Let's go Nb5, with an attack on the bishop.

That bishop is one of Black's strongest pieces in this opening and conveniently defends the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2P5/4PN2/PP1P.text:
Black activates the kingside knight as well.

Our queen's knight comes out!

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP.text:
Black goes for the Semi-Slav.

We'll go straight for development with Bb2.

This bishop often becomes very active in the middlegame.

Now, let's go over some popular options for Black on move 5.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black goes for ...c6.

Let's develop the kingside knight first.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2P5/5N2/PP1PPPP.text:
The Slav Defense.

Once again, we'll support the c4-pawn with the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Welcome to Chapter 4!

In this chapter, we are going to analyze the Bayonet Slav.

In multiple openings in chess, the Bayonet Attack is introduced usually when White pushes either g4 or b4 to start an attack, sometimes supported by a rook.

This way of playing is unorthodox and aggressive, and might catch your opponents off guard!

We begin with the English, 1.c4.

1b1q1rk1/rb1n1ppp/p4n2/1p1Np1N1/8/1P2P3/.text:
Of course, Black won't capture on d5 and get checkmated in one move.

Instead, they activate the bishop, actually threatening to capture our knight this time.

But we'll be the ones to capture first, on f6.

1b1q1rk1/rb3ppp/p4n2/1p2p1N1/8/1P1BP3/PB.text:
After Bd3, the position is unclear but equal according to the computer.

Still, even with best play, the onus is on Black to prove compensation for the missing pawn!

1b1q1rk1/rb3ppp/p4n2/1p2p1N1/8/1P2P3/PBQ.text: The other knight recaptures, still keeping an eye on the h7-pawn.

1bbq1rk1/r1Nn1ppp/p4n2/1p1pp1N1/8/1P2P3/.text:
Black's best bet is ...b5, putting pressure on our knight.

And we can implement our Nxd5 idea!

1bbq1rk1/rpNn1ppp/p4n2/3pp3/8/1P2PN2/PBQ.text:
The bizarre resource that the computer relies on is ...Ra7.

Black simply slides the rook out of the way. The idea is ...b5 to attack our knight.

We'll jump to g5 with pressure on the h7-pawn.

There are ideas of Nce6 to fork the queen and the rook, as well as Nxd5 to deflect Black's only defender away from f6!

r1b1k2r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/qPN1PN2/.text:
After the queen recaptures...

There's no reason not to castle kingside.

r1b1k2r/pp1nqppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/bPN1PN2/.text:
Black goes for the aforementioned idea.

Let's capture and lure their queen to a weird square.

r1b1k2r/pp1nqppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
Another idea  is ...Qe7, going for ...Ba3.

Black wants to trade dark-squared bishops.

In this case, this does significantly weaken our chances of getting a successful attack with Rg1 and g4.

Let's just stick to solid and traditional development. We can get an advantage that way too.

r1b1r1k1/1pRn1ppp/p4n2/3pp3/6P1/1P2PN2/P.text:
Guess what; we can go for g4 even without the queens on the board!

This advancement is positionally strong as well.

We've got more active pieces with prospects of attacking as well as playing in the center.

r1b1r1k1/1pRn1ppp/p4n2/3pp3/8/1P2PN2/PB1.text: Once the rook activates to e8...

r1b2rk1/pp1n1p1p/2p1p1p1/3p2Pn/2P5/qPN1P.text:
As we were threatening to move our knight and trap Black's, they defend with ...g6.

Their idea is to free up the g7-square.

All in all, we should always continue with our pawn storm at some point. We push h4!

r1b2rk1/pp1n1pnp/2p1p1p1/3p2P1/2PP3P/qPN.text:
We can finally play d4, with a concrete idea in mind.

Playing ...g6 has severely weakened the dark squares around Black's king, which means we can reroute our knight to h6 or f6!

This can be done via Nh2 and Ng4.

Also, h5 is on the cards.

r1b2rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1p3/3p2Pn/2P5/qPN1PN2.text:
The best move is to jump to the edge of the board with ...Nh5.

Let's continue targeting the knight.

r1b2rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P3P1/qPN1PN.text:
The queen arrives at a3, far away from the kingside...

Where we'll attack with g5!

r1b2rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/qPN1PN2/.text: Black castles as well, and the crucial aspect of the game that remains is...

r1b2rk1/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2PP4/qPN1PN2.text:
Central control!

We've finally pushed d4 and have two powerful pawns in the center.

Meanwhile, Black's bishop on c8 is completely blocked in and hopeless at the moment.

White is slightly better here.

r1b2rk1/pp1nqppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P3P1/bPN1PN.text:
Black goes for the trade.

Let's accept.

r1b2rk1/pp1nqppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
The ...Qe7 idea is that Black wants to render our attack useless by trading one of our most important attackers, the dark-squared bishop.

This shouldn't stop us now, having already played Rg1.

We're "up a tempo" relative to the 7...Qe7 variation.

r1bq1rk1/1pbn1ppp/p4n2/3pp3/8/1P2PN2/PBQ.text:
If Black takes on c7, that's great for us.

We get Black's dark-squared bishop, even at the cost of trading queens.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/2P5/1PN1PN.text:
Meeting flank attacks with central expansion is usually a good idea.

That's what Black does in this instance.

Let's take in the center, as we usually do.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pb4/3np3/8/1PN1PN2/PB.text:
Recapturing in the center doesn't surprise us at all.

There's another way to attack the bishop on d6, as we've shown.

And it's centralizing the knight on e4.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
The most popular move at this point is ...O-O.

However, White scores well after this move, mostly because of the Bayonet with Rg1 and g4!

The g-pawn is coming.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/3b1n2/3pp3/8/1PN1PN2/P.text:
Once Black takes back, we reach a familiar position.

Let's target the bishop on d6.

r1bq1rk1/ppbn1p1p/2p3p1/3np1N1/2B4P/1P2P.text:
We'll go h4!

The h-pawn supports the knight and we are planning to push h5 in the near future.

Meanwhile, the two bishops and the queen are extremely active along the respective diagonals.

Keep in mind that if Black plays ...h6, the Ne6 sacrifice is winning immediately with the queen attacking g6.

r1bq1rk1/ppbn1p1p/2p3p1/3np1N1/2B5/1P2PN.text:
Black blocks with ...g6, which was basically the only move.

However, another idea comes to mind now.

r1bq1rk1/ppbn1ppp/2p5/3np3/2B1N3/1P2PN2/.text:
Black castles instead, which is a mistake!

This move reignites our chances of attacking.

We can immediately put pressure on the h7-pawn with the queen and the knight.

r1bq1rk1/ppbn1ppp/2p5/3np3/4N1P1/1P2PN2/.text:
We'll start the attack with g4!

Of course, the h-pawn will join it soon, as well as the bishop on d3, together with the queen.

As a defensive countermeasure, we can play a3 to prevent ...Nb4.

All in all, extremely pleasant for White.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pb1n2/3pp3/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
If at any point Black pushes ...e5, we've got a concrete counter attack.

Let's capture in the center.

Black can recapture both with the pawn and the knight.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pb4/3np3/8/1PN1PN2/PBQ.text:
If the knight recaptures...

We'll use the e4-square to attack the bishop on d6.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
Finally, Black activates the bishop to d6.

There was no reason to choose the more passive ...Be7 route now.

We'll activate the queen. We continue mobilizing and hold back d4 for a more opportune moment.

However, we also have the powerful Bayonet strategy which is our real idea!

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/3b1n2/3pp3/8/1PN1PN2/PB.text:
If the pawn recaptures...

We'll jump to b5 with the standard idea of hitting the bishop on d6.

r1bqk2r/ppbn1ppp/2p5/3np3/4N3/1P2PN2/PBQ.text:
Once it moves back to c7, Black's position might be a bit too solid to rush with g4.

Let's activate the bishop instead.

The difference is we can get it to c4 now, having traded the c4-pawn.

If Black goes for ...b5 instantly, we don't even mind trading on d5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
This move is a bit inflexible for Black because the knight can no longer go to c6 in case of a cxd5 trade.

Players commit to ...Nbd7 18% of the time, rendering it the third most popular move.

Let's get our bishop to b2, as planned.

r1bqr1k1/pp1n1ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
The more passive ...Re8 puts us in the driver's seat.

Let's initiate a pawn armada.

r1bqrnk1/pp1n1ppp/2pbp3/3p2P1/2P4P/1PN1P.text:
We'll support the g-pawn with h4.

The attack rages on and White's got an edge here.

r1bqrnk1/pp1n1ppp/2pbp3/3p2P1/2P5/1PN1PN.text: Once it jumps away, the next move is very logical.

r1bqrnk1/pp3ppp/2pbpn2/3p4/2P3P1/1PN1PN2.text:
If Black abstains from ...e5, which is the best move and opts for the more passive ...Nf8, all the more fun for us.

Let's kick the knight away from f6.

rbbq1rk1/1p1n1ppp/p4n2/1N1pp3/8/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black can try to prevent our plan with ...a6, attacking the knight.

In this instance, we'll jump to c7 anyway.

rbbq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/5n2/1N1pp3/8/1P2PN2/PB.text:
The most common retreating square is b8.

Black is under a lot of pressure as we'll be able to invade via c7 and obtain the dark square bishop, when our bishop on b2 will be completely dominant. 

Practically this looks really tough for Black, but there is a miracle computer resource to avoid the worst (that your opponents will never find!)

rbbqk2r/pp1n1ppp/5n2/1N1pp3/8/1P2PN2/PBQ.text: Once it retreats, there's a very interesting move to claim advantage.

rbbqk2r/pp1n1ppp/5n2/1N1pp3/8/BP2PN2/P1Q.text:
We take control of the dark squares with Ba3!

Black can't castle now, and we are threatening moves like Rc1 and Nc7+ or Nd6+ to trade off Black's dark-squared bishop.

A more convincing position for White in any case.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/1bP5/1PN1PN2/.text:
Black castles.

Let's go for our usual idea.

We'll activate the queen.

Black hasn't achieved anything particular with ...Bb4 and our ideas remain the same.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/1bP5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
5...Bb4 is actually the fourth most popular move, played 15% of the time.

Black goes after our knight on c3 and it will be hanging if we play d4.

This doesn't disturb our plan, however.

Our bishop from b2 now supports the knight as well.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2P5/4PN2/PP1P.text:
Black activates the kingside knight as well.

We'll develop our queenside knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP.text:
Black goes for the Semi-Slav.

Do you remember our approach?

We'll go straight for development with Bb2.

It is at this point that Black can choose between ...Bb4 and Nbd7.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black goes for ...c6.

Let's develop the kingside knight first.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2P5/5N2/PP1PPPP.text:
The Slav defense.

Once again, we'll support the c4-pawn with the bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
For this second study, I want us to analyze other ways Black may have to develop that don't involve Be7 or Bd6 early.
 
I'm talking about 5...Bb4 and 5...Nbd7. Both of these moves stray from the norm but there are some games played and that's why it's useful to be prepared.

We'll begin with 1.c4.

lessons.title: Black Moves The Light-Squared Bishop Early

2rq1rk1/3b1ppp/Q3pn2/2bp4/8/1P2PN2/PB1P1.text:
And we'll activate the scary dark-squared bishop.

Next, we'll bring the queen back to d3, get the bishop to e2 and castle our king to safety.

White is winning comfortably here.

2rq1rk1/pp2bp1p/2n1pnp1/3p4/3P1P2/2NBP2Q.text: Black could play something like ...g6 to prevent f5.

2rq1rk1/pp2bp1p/2n1pnp1/3p4/3P1PP1/2NBP2.text:
And we are all in!

Creating a pawn storm on the kingside, we use our queen's early development to start an attack.

This line follows the game played between Ferenc Berkes and Ivan Salgado Lopez in 2011, which White won.

2rq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P4/2NBP2Q/PP.text:
In this case, Black is going to be the one to capture the c-file first.

Instead of e4, there is another aggressive idea we could go for.

It's f4, grabbing more space on the kingside.

And there's more to come.

2rqk2r/Q2b1ppp/4pn2/2bp4/8/1P2PN2/P2P1PP.text:
Even if Black attacks our queen, it's nowhere near trapped.

We'll just slide to a6 and have got the whole diagonal to escape to if needed.

2rqkb1r/Q2b1ppp/4pn2/3p4/8/4PN2/PP1P1PPP.text:
Which they try with ...e6.

We'll do the same with b3.

We've got nothing to worry about.

2rqkb1r/nQ1bpppp/5n2/3p4/8/4PN2/PP1P1PPP.text:
So, Black takes on a7.

Let's recapture.

Having lost two pawns on the queenside with little compensation, Black needs to develop quickly.

2rqkb1r/pQ1bpppp/2n2n2/1N1p4/8/4PN2/PP1P.text:
Now Black is forced to defend with ...Rc8.

And lose another pawn on a7.

Even ...Rc7 doesn't work here because of the simple Nxc6, with a counter attack on the queen.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P4/1QN1PN2/P.text:
If Black develops to c6, let's unleash an interesting idea that takes advantage of their tempo losses.

The most aggressive approach as we go for a central Stonewall formation!
 
Black should be punished for their slow opening play. Developing with 8.Bd3 and O-O followed by the e4 pawn break was another logical plan.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3pN3/3P1P2/1QN1P3.text:
And we'll grab more space with the Stonewall.

Next, our bishop will fill the light squares and we'll castle short.

It's fascinating how much space you can get and how much you can transform a position if the other side plays carelessly for just one move!

r2q1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPQ2/PP.text:
Black does the same.

How should we continue the game now?

We are at a crossroads of ideas
and Qh3 is the more aggressive option.

A good alternative was also Rac1 to
prepare play on the queenside.

Our position is flexible enough to allow either option and a serious idea is a timely e3-e4 push to open up our bishops.

r2qk2r/pp2bppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPQ2/PP1.text:
Black activates the bishop to e7, preparing castling.

Let's castle ourselves.

r2qkb1r/p2npppp/1p3n2/1B1N1b2/8/1Q2PN2/P.text: We are simply winning, a pawn up.

r2qkb1r/p2npppp/1p3n2/1B1p1b2/8/1QN1PN2/.text:
So, they have to settle for ...Nbd7.

Do you see a hanging pawn now?

r2qkb1r/pQ1bpppp/2n2n2/3p4/8/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
Black defends with ...Bd7.

Their idea is probably ...Rb8.

However, they haven't accounted for Nb5, threatening Nc7+!

We continue crushing Black's queenside and grabbing pawns.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p1b2/8/1QN1PN2/PP.text:
Black might think they're smart and play ...Nc6, offering the b7-pawn.

This move's popularity is only 6% so you probably won't face it too often.

In many openings an early capture of the b2/b7-pawns is not advised as it is a "poisoned" pawn but here it will not the case due to a precise follow-up.

After capturing on b7, we will be attacking the knight.

r2qkb1r/pp2pppp/2n2n2/3p4/3P4/2N1PQ2/PP3.text:
As the c6-square is free, Black develops the knight there.

This is a refreshing alternative to the usual ...Nbd7.

Let's develop our dark-squared bishop.

A nice aggressive alternative
I like here is 8. g4!? intending to gain space on the kingside.

Following with g5 and h4 would be natural.

r2qkb1r/pp3ppp/2n1pn2/3p4/3P4/2N1PQ2/PP1.text:
After Black creates a pawn chain in the center...

We can calmly continue development with the advantage of the powerful light-squared bishop.

rn1qkb1r/p3pppp/1p3n2/3p1b2/8/1QN1PN2/PP.text:
Another big mistake Black players pick 16% of the time.

There's a forced winning line that's useful to remember.

After our move of Bb5+, Black can't block with ...Nc6 anymore!

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3P4/8/2N1Pb2/PP1P.text:
Black's most solid response is to quickly trade the bishop off and utilize the pawns to control the light squares. 

They are also trying to deflect our
queen away from the b3 square.

We'll recapture with the queen so as not to double our f-pawns.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p1b2/2P5/2N1PN2/.text:
The third most popular move is getting the bishop out to f5, which you will probably face around 15% of the time.

A tempting move but Black must always be wary of developing the bishop early in light of Qb3 ideas, as mentioned.

We'll capture in the center first.

It's important to weaken the d5-pawn so our Qb3 idea gains strength.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2P3b1/2N1PN2/.text:
However, the most popular move, ...Bg4, which is played 38% of the time, definitely is!

Black pins our knight immediately.

Black's early development of
the c8-bishop is often premature due to the weakness on the queenside.

Instead of going for the immediate Qb3, we'll capture in the center first, sticking with the formula we'll use against ...Bf5 as well.

5. Qb3 is a logical idea but Black can play 5...Qb6 to safeguard the queenside for the moment.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3n1b2/8/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
We're happy to see this
recapture as we get a strong center for free.

We'll continue with the logical d4.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/2p5/3n4/6b1/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
Recapturing with the knight is definitely not the best move for Black.

The reason being that there is no pawn on d5 to prevent e4!

We'll play d4 first.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p1b2/8/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
The more logical recapture is ...cxd5.

And we finally put our Qb3 plan into motion.

The queen hits both b7 and d5 and it's not easy for Black to defend.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/6b1/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
Black could recapture in the center with the pawn.

That invites our common Qb3 idea.

In this case, the queen attacks both the pawn on d5 and the pawn on b7.

That means it's not convenient for Black to move the queen away from the defense of d5.

rn1qkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/8/2N1PQ2/PP1P1P.text:
Now Black recaptures with the pawn, covering the e4-square.

The most natural move probably comes to mind, as we shouldn't let Black play ...e5.

We'll expand in the center ourselves, with d4!

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3n1b2/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text: Black opens up the dark-squared bishop...

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3n1b2/3P4/2NBPN2/P.text:
And we'll get our own bishop out.

The game is far from over but we have the edge due to free flowing development and greater central control.

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/3n4/3P2b1/2N1PN2/P.text:
If Black tries to strengthen the knight in the center...

We can actually kick it out with e4!

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/3PP1b1/2P2N2/P4P.text:
And we'll recapture with a massive center.

Having both pawns on e4 and d4 is always beneficial!

rn1qkb1r/pp3ppp/2p1p3/8/3PP1b1/2n2N2/PP3.text: Black's best choice is to take on c3.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/3N1b2/8/1Q2PN2/PP1.text: Black simply hangs the pawn on d5. If ...Qxb3, we'll capture on f6 with check, and then recapture the queen.

rn2kb1r/pp2pppp/1q3n2/3p1b2/8/1QN1PN2/PP.text:
The most popular move in this position is 6...Qb6, which is a mistake!

Believe it or not, you'll face this move almost a quarter of the time.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2P5/4PN2/PP1P.text:
Black plays the most flexible and popular 3...Nf6, occurring around 47% of times.

We'll do the same.

Just to mention, the second most popular move in this position, 4...e6, leads to Semi-Slav, which is not the topic of this chapter.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/3P4/1QN1PN2/PP3.text:
We'll continue by playing in the center.

This variation transposes to the ...Bf5 line.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/5n2/3p4/8/1QN1PN2/PP1P1.text:
This sad retreat is Black's best way to defend the queenside.

Let's strike in the center, as we're allowed to.

We're not winning by force but our opponents going ...Bf5-...Bc8 in the opening can only be in our favor!

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
At this point, we are already familiar with what Black wants after 1...c6.

Instead of placing two pawns in the center right away, we'll play the flexible Nf3.

This move can lead to multiple different lines, as you'll see.

We'll allow ...d5 by Black and let them make a decision in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2P5/5N2/PP1PPPP.text:
Black expands in the center...

And we'll open up our light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In the last chapter covering the Slav Defense, we'll take a look at the Slav Sidelines!

These are the variations you might not see as often as the main lines, but could absolutely catch you off guard if not prepared!

Let's go, starting with 1.c4.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPN2/P.text:
At last, all our minor pieces are developed and our king is castled.

Black has got a passive knight on d7 and a "dead" bishop on c8.

A direct positional idea to start the middlegame would be Rc1, getting the rook to the open c-file.
But Black follows us right away.

r1bqk2r/pp1n1ppp/3bpn2/3p4/3P4/2NBPN2/PP.text:
Black does the same and gets ready to castle.

We'll castle first.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p1p2n2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN1P.text:
As 5...g6, 5...Nbd7 is similar to 4...Nbd7.

It comes in handy not to get confused if Black players go for different move-orders, and they'll choose this one only 4% of the time.

The core ideas usually stay the same for us.

Let's take in the center.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p4n2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN1P/P.text:
Of course, d4.

Here, we don't have to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and it's perfectly fine to get it out to d2 in our setup.

r1bqkb1r/1p1npppp/p4n2/3p4/8/2N1PN1P/PP1.text: After Black recaptures, how will we gain space?

r1bqkb1r/pp1n1ppp/4pn2/3p4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
But they have to keep developing, so they do so with ...e6.

We'll get the light-squared bishop out to d3, as there is no reason to develop it to e2.

Black can't really play ...Bg4 with their bishop being stuck on c8.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/2p2n2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/P.text:
This move is pretty rare (only 4%) but tricky as Black wants to push ...e5. 

If we play the natural d4 then Black tricks us with ...e6 and a Semi-Slav!

The simplest answer against this rare idea is to take on d5, with a slightly better symmetrical position. 

5. Qc2 is also in line with our
repertoire when Black has the unique idea of a rapid 5...e5 6. cxd5 Nxd5! with an interesting reverse Sicilian type game.

r1bqkb1r/pp1npppp/5n2/3p4/8/2N1PN2/PP1P1.text:
Black takes back in the center.

Our next move should be very logical to you.

We'll play d4, leaving the black minor pieces somewhat cramped.

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/3p4/2P3b1/1PN1PN.text:
Black will most probably activate the knight to d7 here, with the idea of ...e5.

What's the simplest way of stopping that?

r2q1rk1/pp1nppbp/2p2np1/3p4/2PP2b1/1PN1P.text:
You probably guessed it: d4.

Admittedly Black is very solid, but so are we. 

The difference is that we have a bit more space on a crowded board so we effectively have a free slight advantage and a full game of chess lies ahead.

We could try to get the rooks to the center and play for e4.

rn1q1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/2P3b1/1PN1PN.text:
Now our knight isn't even pinned once Black goes for ...Bg4.

We'll simply get the king to safety.

rn1qkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/3p1b2/2P5/2N1PN1.text:
A move that's played a whopping 47% of the time is ...Bf5, settling with the f5-square since ...Bg4 is impossible.

We've got an interesting idea to uncork here.

Let's play g4 immediately!

We don't mind weakening our kingside that much, as we'll place a bishop on g2 anyway.

rn1qkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2nb1/3p4/2P3P1/2N1PN.text:
Black retreats to g6, which is the most logical move.

We'll bring our queen out and attack the soft spot on b7.

rn1qkb1r/4pppp/p1p2nb1/1p1p4/2P3P1/1QN1P.text:
Once Black defends with ...b5, it should be clear which pawn we want to capture.

The one in the center.

After all, in chess, the center must be contested at some point!

rn1qkb1r/4pppp/p1p3b1/1p1n4/6P1/1QN1PN1P.text: Black is basically forced to take back with the knight here.

rn1qkb1r/4pppp/p1p3b1/1p1nN3/6P1/1QN1P2P.text:
And as the last move of this line, we'll centralize the knight and attack the bishop on g6.

Of course, Bg2 is in the cards to unleash the strong bishop.

An enjoyable position for White.

rn1qkb1r/4pppp/p4nb1/1p1p2P1/8/1QN1PN1P/.text:
We can play g5 now and dislodge the knight on f6!

That will destabilize Black's center and we'll be able to take the pawn on d5.

rn1qkb1r/4pppp/p4nb1/1p1p4/6P1/1QN1PN1P/.text: Recapturing with the pawn is a mistake, and here's another reason we played g4.

rn2kb1r/1pq1pppp/p1p2nb1/3p4/2P3P1/1QN1P.text:
The best move here is actually ...Qc7.

This move only works with sufficient engine preparation, however.

On the surface it seems like Black hangs the d5-pawn...

Let's capture it!

rn2kb1r/1pq1pppp/p1p3b1/3n4/6P1/1QN1PN1P.text: If Black recaptures with the knight, it's actually not the best for White to capture and win the pawn on d5.

rn2kb1r/1pq1pppp/p1p3b1/3n4/6PN/1QN1P2P/.text:
Instead, we'll go for the bishop on g6.

If we get the active bishop, we'll easily expand in the center with d4 and strengthen our kingside with Bg2.

All in all, White's got a more comfortable position again.

rnbq1rk1/1p3ppp/p1pbpn2/3p4/2PP4/1PNBPN1.text:
We'll get the bishop out to d3.

We'll play Bb2 and eventually try to achieve what Black couldn't: play e4!

This push would give us the central space we need to reach an advantageous position.

Still, White is slightly better even so.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
Having developed the kingside, Black quickly castles.

Very solid indeed.

We'll develop the light-squared bishop now as well.

As Black probably wants to play ...Bg4 anyway, it's best to get it out to e2.

rnbqk2r/1p3ppp/p1pbpn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN1P/.text:
Black develops the bishop to the most active square, d6.

If allowed, they'd love to play ...e5.

Therefore we'll play d4.

We can't go for our Bayonet approach here since Black is threatening to quickly push ..e5 and the a6-pawn prevents our Nb5 jumps.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2p2np1/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
Black activates the bishop...

And so do we.

There's a lot of tension on the a1-h8 diagonal now!

rnbqkb1r/1p2pp1p/p1p2np1/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN1.text:
Once again, we'll go for b3.

6. d4 is also very strong and logical. 

We are basically in the 4...g6 Slav variation where the inclusion of ...a6 and h3 doesn't change the character of the position.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pp1p/p1p2np1/3p4/2P5/2N1PN1P.text:
Instead of playing it on move 4, Black can go for ...g6 here.

Players choose this move-order 6% of the time.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/P.text:
4...a6 is only played 4% of the time in the Lichess database, but is very instructive. Also, that's still over 10,000 games.

It is called the Chameleon or the
Chebanenko Slav. 

4..a6 is a generally useful move to control the b5-square and Black is also waiting for some intel on our setup before deciding further development.

We also adopt a waiting strategy! 

With h3, we make it harder for Black to develop the bishop from c8. Having placed the ball back in Black's court, they've got a lot of options here.

rnbqkb1r/1p2pppp/p1p2n2/8/2p5/2N1PN1P/PP.text:
Taking on c4 gives us exactly what we want.

You should also face this move only about 4% of the time.

Let's recapture with the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1p1pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN1P/.text:
The third most popular move is ...e6, played 13% of the time.

This move does solidify the center.

However, I don't think Black would be too excited to block the light-squared bishop after playing 4...a6.

As per usual, we'll go for the dark-squared bishop fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/p1p2n2/1p1p4/2P5/2N1PN1P/.text:
The immediate ...b5 is actually the second most popular move here, being chosen 16% of the time.

Our c4-pawn is under a lot of pressure and we need to make a decision.

Capturing on b5 would give Black the center, so we'll take the other pawn!

However, 6. b3 was very logical and easy to play but I also have a interesting idea to suggest.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/p1p2n2/1p6/2B5/2N1PN1P/PP.text:
This does walk right into ...b5, but that's okay.

We'll keep our bishop on the strong and active diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/p1p2n2/1p6/8/1BN1PN1P/PP1.text:
After Bb3, we've got a direct plan in the center: go for both d4 and e4!

This position is similar to a Queen's Gambit Declined position where we will quickly put our pawns in the center.

Our approach is extremely active.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/p4n2/1p1p4/1P6/2N1PN1P/P2.text:
We'll go for b4!

This move stops Black's advances on the queenside and freezes their a- and b-pawns.

Very soon, we'll play a4 and take advantage of them over-extending.

rnbqkb1r/4pppp/p4n2/1p1p4/8/2N1PN1P/PP1P.text: After Black recaptures on d5, here's our plan.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/P.text:
4...g6, aiming to fianchetto, is a solid system for Black which is a cross between a Grunfeld and a Slav.

It's played about one tenth of the time, however.

To be honest there is nothing wrong with 5. d4, transposing to mainline theory, and objectively it is even the best move. 

However if we want to keep things a bit more offbeat in our English flavor, the queenside fianchetto is a good option as well!

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/3p4/2P5/4PN2/PP1P.text:
Black plays the most popular move here, which is ...Nf6.

Black players opt for it almost half the time, with 48%.

There's definitely nothing wrong with this traditional developing move that supports the center.

We'll continue in the same manner with Nc3.

From here on, Black has multiple approaches to the position.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2B5/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
We'll just take back and activate the bishop.

Next, we'll go d4 and O-O, unbothered.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pppp/2p2n2/8/2p5/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
Capturing on c4 isn't the way to go and is only played 3% of the time.

We are allowed quick development and an extra pawn in the center.

rnbqkbnr/pp1ppppp/2p5/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black "almost mirrors" our first move.

Let's get the knight out and prepare to meet ...d5 with e3.

rnbqkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2P5/5N2/PP1PPPP.text:
Black strikes in the center.

We'll play our 3. e3 move to be consistent with our repertoire, and support the c4-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In the second study of Chapter 5, we'll cover the Chameleon Slav and other systems in the 3...Nf6 variation by Black.

Without further ado, let's dive in with 1.c4!

r1b2r1k/pp4pp/2n5/3p1p2/3p4/NP2PN2/P4PPP.text:
Pushing it forward would only allow Ne5. Instead, Black trades.

We'll take back with the knight, as this trade suits us as well.

r1b2r1k/pp4pp/2n5/3ppp2/8/NP2PN2/P2P1PPP.text:
Having allowed Black to grab central space, it's time to fight back now.

We'll claim space with d4, attacking the e5-pawn.

r1b2r1k/pp4pp/8/3p1p2/3P4/NP6/P4PPP/R4RK.text:
At the end of the day, we've traded Black's most important pieces and successfully fought against their center control.

Next, we'll get the rooks to the open files and try to reroute the knight to either f3 or d3.

It's extremely important that we have a clamp on the e5-square and it allows us to potentially play for an advantage.

r3kbnr/1p1b1ppp/1pn1p3/3pN3/8/1PN1P3/P2P.text:
Black offers a trade of knights now.

If we capture on c6, we'll give them a chance to undouble their b-pawns!

Therefore, instead of retreating, we'll take on d7.

r4bnr/1p1k1ppp/1pn1p3/3p4/8/1PN1P3/P2P1P.text:
Although we traded our active knight for Black's passive bishop, we've made them lose castling rights.

Now we'll attack the weak b6-pawn, threatening a fork as well.

r4bnr/1pk2ppp/1pn1p3/3p4/N7/1P2P3/P2P1PP.text: So, basically the only move Black has to defend is ...Kc7.

r4bnr/1pk2ppp/1pn1p3/3p4/N7/1P2P3/PB1P1P.text:
And finally, we get the bishop out to b2.

Who would you rather have in this position, White or Black?

rn1qkbnr/pp2pppp/2p5/3p4/2P3b1/4PN2/PP1P.text:
A common amateur mistake Black can make in these setups is a premature development of the bishop to either f5 or g4.

This move, although an inaccuracy, is played 15% of the time by players rating from 1000-2000 ELO.

Our reply of Qb3 is an important move to remember, unpinning and attacking b7.

rn2kbnr/1p1b1ppp/1p2p3/3pN3/8/2N1P3/PP1P.text:
After ...e6, Black's bishop is stuck!

Let's plan the fianchetto of our c1-bishop, with b3.

It's more logical to develop it this way, having played e3.

rn2kbnr/1p1bpppp/1p6/3pN3/8/4P3/PP1P1PPP.text:
To keep the bishop safe, they retreat to b7.

How should we continue development?

The most straightforward move is Nc3, attacking the d5-pawn.

rn2kbnr/1p2pppp/1p6/3p4/6b1/4PN2/PP1P1PP.text:
These two trades have allowed us to isolate Black's doubled pawns on the b-file, which is an enormous positional advantage for us.

Now, with Ne5, we get an improving move with tempo as well.

Black never got to capture our knight!

rn2kbnr/1p2pppp/1p6/3p4/8/1P2PP2/P2P1P1P.text:
I recommend b3 here.

The idea is to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop, activate the knight and castle long.

We've got a position that's easy to play now.

rn2kbnr/1p2pppp/1p6/3p4/8/4PP2/PP1P1P1P/.text: But not isolated like Black's b-pawns.

rn2kbnr/1p2pppp/1pp5/3P4/8/4Pb2/PP1P1PPP.text:
Capturing on f3 is possible here for Black and played 40% of the time, so it's important to cover.

We'll take back, of course. Our f-pawns are doubled...

rn2kbnr/1p2pppp/1pp5/3p4/2P3b1/4PN2/PP1P.text:
Black recaptures on b6.

Now we'll take in the center as well.

rn2kbnr/pp2pppp/1qp5/3p4/2P3b1/1Q2PN2/PP.text:
...Qb6, offering a trade of queens, is played here 29% of the time. ...Bxf3, a common alternative, fails to the simple Qxb7. 

Here, capturing allows us to maintain an advantage.

rn2kbnr/ppq1pppp/2p5/3p4/2P3b1/1Q2PN2/PP.text:
Another move to defend the b7-pawn is ...Qc7.

It's also convenient for Black to place the queen on the c-file and target the bishop on c1.

Therefore we'll get our knight out to c3 quickly. Now we are definitely threatening to capture in the center.

rn2kbnr/ppq2ppp/2p1p1b1/3pN3/2P3P1/1QN1P.text:
Black retreats to g6...

And we'll capture on d5, finally.

rn2kbnr/ppq2ppp/2p1p3/3p4/2P3b1/1QN1PN2/.text:
And Black is forced to defend with ...e6, still not capturing our knight on f3.

We offer the knight on e5, but Black mustn't capture it because of the attack on b7.

rn2kbnr/ppq2ppp/2p1p3/3pNb2/2P5/1QN1P3/P.text:
So, they'll probably retreat to f5.

Let's continue attacking the bishop and prove why the early ...Bg4 wasn't optimal for Black.

We'll take the opportunity to play g4 with tempo.

rn2kbnr/ppq2ppp/2p3b1/3pN3/6P1/1QN1P3/PP.text: We captured now because after ...exd5 Black can't retreat the bishop on the c8-h3 diagonal anymore.

rn2kbnr/ppq2ppp/2p3b1/3pN3/6PP/1QN1P3/PP.text:
And we can continue hunting it with h4.

The idea is, of course, h5.

We've got a lot of space and activity here with a slight advantage.

rnb1k2r/pp2q1pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2P5/NP2PN2/.text:
Black's queen develops with tempo.

We'll guard the knight with our queen.

rnb1k2r/pp2q1pp/2p2n2/3ppp2/2P5/NP2PN2/P.text:
