r1bqr1k1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/2n5/2PNP3/2N1B1P.text:
Black invades the c5-square.

Our queen goes to c2 to support the e4-pawn and to connect the rooks.

r1bqr1k1/ppp1ppbp/1nn3p1/8/7P/2NPB1P1/PP.text:
Black develops the knight instead.

We'll keep attacking!

r1bqr1k1/ppp1ppbp/1nn3p1/8/8/2NPBNP1/PP1.text:
Black could centralize the rook.

We'll try to trade off Black's strong kingside defender.

r1bqr1kb/ppp1pp1p/1nn3pB/8/8/2NP1NP1/PP1.text:
Black keeps the bishop, but our bishop on h6 is dangerous.

Let's attack on the kingside with h4.

r2q1r2/p1p1ppkp/1n4p1/2p3N1/8/2NP2P1/PP1.text:
In return, Black attacks our rook.

Rg1 is the only way to save it. 

We have lost the rights to castle kingside, but that doesn't bother us!

r2q1r2/p1p1ppkp/1n4p1/2p5/8/2NP1NPb/PP1Q.text:
Black could try to prevent our king from castling kingside.

We'll attack the bishop right away.

r2q1r2/pbp1ppkp/1n4p1/2p3N1/8/2NP2P1/PP1.text:
Black retreats back to b7.

We'll play our queen to e3, where it is more active and attacks the c5-pawn.

r2q1r2/pbp1ppkp/1n4p1/2p5/8/2NP1NP1/PP1Q.text:
Black fianchettoes and pins our knight.

We'll improve the queen and attack the c5-pawn.

r2q1r2/pbp1ppkp/1n4p1/6N1/2p5/2NPQ1P1/PP.text:
We'll castle queenside! 

The rook is dangerously lined up with Black's queen, and our knight on g5 is very active.
Black advances the c-pawn so as to not lose it.

r2q1r2/pbp1ppkp/1n4p1/8/2p5/2NPQNP1/PP2P.text:
And we'll castle queenside.

White has better piece placement, the rooks are connected and the pawn structure is also better than Black's.

r2q1rk1/pBpn1pb1/1n4p1/4p2p/6bP/2NPB3/PP.text:
Even though our light squares may seem weak, they aren't.

We'll take.

r2qr1k1/pBpnppb1/1n4p1/7p/6bP/2NPB3/PP1Q.text:
Black develops the knight.

Let's win the material.

r2qr1k1/ppp1ppbp/1nn3b1/8/8/2NPB1P1/PP1Q.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop.

Once again, we're going for the dark-squared bishops trade to weaken the dark squares.

r2qr1k1/ppp1ppbp/1nn3p1/5b1P/8/2NPB1P1/P.text:
Black defends g6 with their bishop.

We'll trade in order to open up the h-file.

r2qr1kb/ppp1pp1p/1nn3bB/8/8/2NP2P1/PP1QP.text:
Black doesn't want to trade.

Let's develop the knight and prepare to jump to h4!

r2qr1kb/ppp1pp1p/1nn3pB/7P/6b1/2NP1NP1/P.text:
We'll push anyway! 

The h-file will open up, and another idea is to reroute the knight to e4.

r2qr1kb/ppp1pp1p/1nn3pB/8/6bP/2NP1NP1/PP.text: Black tries to control the h5-square.

r2qr1kb/ppp2p1p/1nn1p1bB/8/7N/2NP2P1/PP1.text: As planned, the knight is amazing on h4 and Black's king doesn't feel safe.

r2qr1kb/ppp2p1p/1nn1p1bB/8/8/2NP1NP1/PP1.text: Black opens up lines for their queen.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2pb1/1n4p1/4p2p/6bP/2NPB3/PP.text:
This exchange sacrifice isn't good. ...e5 has added nothing for Black.

We'll simply take on b7.

rn1qr1k1/ppp1ppb1/1n4p1/7p/6bP/2NPB3/PP1.text:
If Black captures on g4 with the bishop...

...we'll get the b7-pawn with the rook falling next.

rnb2rk1/pp2pp1p/1np3pQ/8/3q4/2NP2P1/PP2P.text:
Black's idea is to defend the dark-squares with ...Qg7.

We'll go for expansion on the kingside.

rnb2rk1/pp2ppqp/1np3p1/8/7P/2NPQ1P1/PP2P.text:
Trading the queens would help Black. 

We'll retreat the queen and try to make use of our superior development and space on the kingside.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/1np3p1/8/8/2NPB1P1/PP1Q.text:
Black blocks the diagonal.

We'll use our classic plan here — trade off the dark-squared bishops.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2pp1np1/8/2PPP3/2N3P1/P.text:
Black gets their king into safety.

We'll prepare to castle as well. 

We have a very imposing center and it seems like Black isn't able to generate sufficient pressure against it. 

Let's look at one typical variation where both sides follow logical development.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2PPP3/2N3P1/.text:
Black attacks the center in King's Indian fashion.

We'll get our king into safety.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/8/8/2NPB1P1/PP2P.text:
Black gets their king out of the center.

We'll create a queen-bishop battery and aim it at Black's kingside.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pb1/1n4p1/4p2p/7P/2NPB1P1/P.text:
Black stops it.

But we persist in our plan of expanding!

10...hxg4 11.h5 allows us to open up lines. Black is in a lot of trouble if they capture our pawns!

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/1n4p1/4p3/8/2NPB1P1/PP1.text:
Black expands in the center.

We'll follow up with a common plan here — kingside expansion.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/2p2np1/8/2P1P3/2N3P1/PP.text:
But we'll gain central space in return!

Black can't really go into a Grunfeld now and should go for a more King's Indian approach. 

We examined a similar case after 3...c6.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/2p2np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1P.text: Black tries to restrict the activity of our light-squared bishop.

rnbqk2r/pp2ppbp/2pp1np1/8/2PPP3/2N3P1/PP.text:
Black fianchettoes the bishop.

We do as well.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/8/8/2NP2P1/PP2PPB.text:
Black fianchettoes as well.

We'll bring the bishop to e3. 

It will help to launch a kingside attack with h4 and h5 coming.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
Black continues in more of a King's Indian style.

This happens a mindblowing 90% of the time!

We'll quickly fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/2p2np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1.text:
Not a very common move order, but it could transpose to a main line (and very solid) "Fianchetto Grunfeld" which we are interested in avoiding with our repertoire.

We'll try to make the ...d5-push more difficult.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2p2np1/3p4/2P1P3/2N3P1/.text:
Black goes for central activity. 

You won't encounter this very often, with about 16% of games, but it should be covered anyway.

We'll trade once.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/2pp1np1/8/2P1P3/2N3P1/P.text:
This is an unusual move order that leads to more of a King's Indian position. 

Nevertheless, it happens 35% of the time. 

We are a bit "tricked" out of
our usual setups, but Black is playing pretty passively.

Let's grab space in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5Pp1/8/8/2p3P1/PP1P1P1P.text:
Black regains the material.

We'll recapture with the b-pawn, so d4 can be pushed next.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/3p4/4P3/2N3P1/PP1P.text:
Black recaptures.

And we'll gain space in the center, which also comes with an attack on the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/5np1/4P3/3p4/2N3P1/PP1P.text:
Black doesn't move the knight, but instead counter-attacks our knight.

We'll capture on f6 to double up the f-pawns.

rnbqkb1r/pp2pp1p/6p1/3pP3/4n3/2N3P1/PP1P.text:
Black saves their knight instead.

We'll add pressure to it by fianchettoing the bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pp3p1p/5pp1/8/3P4/2P3P1/P4P1P/R.text:
White expands in the center.

We have the better center, our dark-squared bishop nicely aims at the kingside, and the light-squared bishop will control the h1-a8 diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/1n4p1/8/8/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
Black retreats the knight.

Our next move of d3 is a very important move for our Anti-Grunfeld! 

The pawn on d3 is very solid and
Black will not have an easy way to counterattack the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/5np1/3p4/2P5/2N3P1/PP1.text:
Last chapter we examined Black going for the central thrust a move earlier but some players stick to the standard...Nf6/...g6/...d5.

We'll trade the flank c-pawn for Black's central d-pawn, and lure out their knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp1pp1p/6p1/3n4/8/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll fianchetto with tempo.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
And Black goes for 2...g6 which happens 36% of the time, looking to bring the bishop to g7.

We'll respond in a similar manner, aiming to bring the bishop to g2 and control the d5-square.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black responds by developing the king's knight.

We'll bring our knight out as well.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
For this second study, we'll look at the 5...Nb6 retreat in the Nf6/g6 and d5 setup. 

But we'll also see what could happen if Black chooses to play 3...c6 or 3...Bg7, which transposes back to 3...c6 lines.

We'll start with the English, of course!

rnbqr1k1/ppp1ppb1/1n4p1/7p/7P/2NPB1P1/PP.text:
Black stops our idea.

But we're determined to attack on the kingside and push g4.

10...hxg4 11.h5 allows us to open up lines.

rnbqr1k1/ppp1ppbp/1n4p1/8/8/2NPB1P1/PP1Q.text:
Black centralizes the rook.

We'll go for the attack!

1r1q1rk1/ppp1npb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP2P.text:
11...Rb8 is a slight mistake.

It simply allows us to develop the queen with tempo, hitting the a7-pawn.

Black can't push ...a6.

1r3rk1/1ppqnpb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
Black could also avoid the trade with ...Rab8.

This gives us the a-file right away.

We'll invade and put pressure on b7.

1r3rk1/Rppqnpb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NPb.text:
Black can try to trade bishops.

We'll play e4, which is not the only move but an interesting idea since Black is about to trade light-squared bishops. 

We put our pawns on the light squares in anticipation of the trade.

1r3rk1/Rppqnpbn/3p2pp/1P2p3/2P1P3/1QNP1N.text:
Qb3 is an antidote for that.

A great improving move is to centralize the knight on d5, as well as to push d4 at some point.

We want to open up our bishop on b2.

1r3rk1/Rppqnpbn/3p2pp/1P2p3/2P1P3/2NP1NP.text: The knight retreats to h7 now, possibly preparing ...f5.

1rbq1r1k/1pp1n1b1/3p2pp/1P2pp1n/2P5/1QNP.text:
They slide to b8 instead.

We've captured the a-file now, and we'll place the rook deep into Black's territory with Ra7.

Black's strong suit is the kingside here.

1rbq1r1k/Rpp1n1b1/3p3p/1P2pppn/2P5/1QNP1.text:
And that's where they'll advance, this time gaining space with ...g5.

They'd love to push one of their pawns to continue the attack.

1rbq1r1k/Rpp1n1b1/3p3p/1P2pppn/2P5/1QNP2.text:
But we'll just play Nd2 to prevent them pushing with tempo.

On the queenside, we'd love to double up and play Ra8, while pushing c5 and b6!

It's hard for Black to continue the attack as the pawns are semi-frozen. 

For example ...f4 will surrender the wonderful e4-outpost to our knight.

1rnq1rk1/ppp2pb1/3pbnpp/1P1Np3/Q1P5/3P2P.text:
Meanwhile, our knight can centralize to d5 and grab even more space.

White is better here with a comfortable position.

1rnq1rk1/ppp2pb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/Q1P5/2NP2P.text: Their best defense is ...Nc8, and now their pieces look passive on the back rank.

2q2rk1/Qpp1npb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text: And the queen retreats now, defending the pawn.

2q2rk1/Qpp1npb1/3p1npp/1PP1p3/8/2NP1NP1/.text:
There have been a lot of trades, but c5 is the key move to claim a small advantage.

Our queen is very active, and the rook is coming to c1.

3q2k1/1Bp2pbp/3p2p1/1P6/2br4/5QP1/r3PP1P.text:
Black brings it to a2, attacking our e2-pawn.

But we've got a great countermeasure.

3q2k1/1Bp2pbp/3p2p1/1P6/2br4/5QP1/rB2PP1.text:
We'll block their attack with Bb2!

The bishop also attacks the rook on d4 and the bishop behind it. Black could be in a lot of trouble here.

The computer already suggests it's best for them to sacrifice the exchange with ...Rxb2.

5rk1/1ppqnpb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NPb/1.text:
We can even allow Black to trade light-squared bishops here.

We've got Qa7, targeting the b7-pawn.

5rk1/1ppqnpb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/1.text:
If Black trades, that can only play into our hands.

We'll recapture with the queen, of course.

Now it can infiltrate on the a-file.

5rk1/Qppqnpb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/1.text:
Black takes on g2.

We'll recapture.

r1bq1r1k/1pp1n1b1/3p2pp/1P2pp1n/2P5/1QNP.text:
Pushing ...h6 is always useful for Black to get some breathing room and prevent our knight from jumping to g5.

Also, they might want to push ...g5 at some point to expand on the kingside!

We'll continue playing on the queenside. Let's offer a trade of rooks, seeking to gain control of the open a-file.

r1bq1r1k/1pp1n1bp/3p2p1/1P2pp1n/2P5/1QNP.text:
That's why Black sidesteps with ...Kh8.

Usually, we would develop our bishop to a3.

But since the a-file has opened up it might be safer to activate it to b2 instead.

r1bq1r1k/pp4bp/3p2p1/1P2pn1n/4Np2/BQ1P1N.text:
That's what we'll do with Ne4.

The pawn on d6 is weak and pinned.

There are still ideas of placing a knight on g5 and threatening Nf7+.

White is close to winning here.

r1bq1r1k/pp4bp/3p2p1/1P2pn1n/5p2/BQNP1NP.text:
Black recaptures, and now their d6-pawn is weak.

And the opponents' weak points should be attacked!

r1bq1r1k/ppp1n1bp/3p2p1/1P2p2n/2P2p2/BQN.text:
If Black is aggressive with ...f4, we can actually keep ignoring them!

Let's push c5.

Black's d6-pawn is under pressure, and playing for ideas like Ng5-Nf7+ is possible.

r1bq1r1k/ppp1n1bp/3p2p1/1P2pp1n/2P5/1QNP.text:
Black slides to h8 to evade this threat.

The next piece we should develop is the dark-squared bishop.

We'll activate it where we're the strongest: on the queenside!

On a3, the bishop monitors the c5-square and the d6-pawn. We want to push c5.

r1bq1r1k/ppp3bp/3p2p1/1PP1pn1n/5p2/BQNP1.text:
Black improves their knight...

And we'll take on d6.

r1bq1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/1PPn4/2NP1NP.text:
Black can play ...c6.

Should this stop our plan?

No! We control the b5-square with everything we've got on the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/1pp1n1bp/3p2p1/1P2pp1n/2P5/2NP1.text:
It jumps to e7...

And we've got another active move with the queen.

There could be some fireworks on the diagonal.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pb1/2np1npp/4p3/1pP5/P1NP1N.text:
Black captures...

And we'll take back, naturally.

The a-file is now open, but we're threatening b5.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pb1/2np1npp/p3p3/2P5/P1NP1N.text:
The most popular here is ...h6, controlling the g5-square.

Black often wants to develop the light-squared bishop to e6 and doesn't want our knight attacking it.

We'll proceed with our planned b4.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/2np1np1/p3p3/2P5/2NP1NP.text:
The most popular move for Black here is to directly prevent our b4 idea with ...a5.

However, a lot of people won't play that move, especially in faster time controls.

We'll insist on playing b4, with a3!

This is the most consistent approach.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/2np2p1/p3p2n/2P5/P1NP1N.text:
As on move 8, Black could jump to h5 with a similar idea, i.e. to push the f-pawn.

Let's go for b4 anyway.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/1pPn4/P1NP1N.text:
It's convenient for Black to trade,
as they open up the rook.

We recapture, still intending b5.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p3p3/2Pn4/P1NP1N.text:
In this line, Black logically relocates the knight before the b-file steamroller arrives.

The knight is good on d4.

We'll remain consistent with our plan although Nxd4 and Nd2 were possible alternatives.

r1bq1rk1/1pp3bp/2np2p1/4pp1n/1PP5/2NP1NP.text:
Of course, they'll push ...f5.

But as in the variation on move 8, we should focus on our own queenside attack rather than react to Black's not-so-dangerous one.

Let's attack the knight on c6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1n1bp/3p2p1/1P2pp1n/2P5/2NP1.text:
Once the knight retreats...

The Qb3 idea is useful to remember.

We line up the queen with Black's king and threaten some potential discoveries.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pb1/2np1npp/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
8...h6 is the fourth most popular move in this position.

Black doesn't want our pieces coming to g5.

That's fine, we'll still expand on the queenside!

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
The most popular move in this position is ...Nc6, developing the knight.

It's played 41% of the time, which is around 120 thousand games.

The knight will jump to d4 in some variations and controls the b4-square.

We'll prepare b4 with Rb1.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/4p2n/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
You could also see ...Nh5.

The point is that Black wants the quick ...f5, which is Black's main pawn break in the KID.

We should push b4 without delay.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np2p1/4pp1n/1PP5/2NP1NP.text:
Black pushes forward as well.

But we are quicker with b5!

r1bq2k1/1pp2pbp/2np2p1/8/1PP1r3/5NP1/4PP.text:
Black captures again.

We've got time for b5 now.

r1bq2k1/1pp2pbp/3p2p1/1P6/2Pnr3/5NP1/4PP.text:
The knight is under attack, but it doesn't have to retreat to e7 as usual. It jumps to d4.

We'll trade.

r1bq2k1/1pp2pbp/3p2p1/1P6/2Pr4/6P1/4PPBP.text:
Black recaptures with the rook, hitting our queen.

We'll play the natural Qb3.

r1bq2k1/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/8/1PP1r3/5NP1/P3P.text:
Black takes back.

We've forced some trades, and now we've got time for b5!

r1bq2k1/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/nP6/2P1r3/5NP1/P3P.text:
The knight jumps to a5, attacking the c4-pawn.

We can't really push it.

But we can defend and attack the rook at the same time.

Where should the rook go?

r1bqr1k1/1pp2pbp/2np1np1/4p3/1pP5/P1NP1N.text:
Black trades.

And we'll take back.

r1bqr1k1/1pp2pbp/2np1np1/8/1PP1p3/2NP1NP.text:
Black plays their intended ...e4 push.

We don't mind the trades in the center in these positions. Our queenside potential remains.

r1bqr1k1/1pp2pbp/2np1np1/p3p3/2P5/P1NP1N.text:
You are probably already familiar with this move.

Black activates the rook on the e-file and wants to push ...e4.

It shouldn't distract us from achieving our queenside plans. Let's push forward with b4.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
8...Re8 is only the sixth most popular move in the position.

Black wants to push ...e4 and create trouble in the center and on the diagonal.

We'll play b4 anyway.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2pbp/2np1np1/8/1PP1p3/2NP1NP.text:
Black forces ...e4.

But we'll still be completely fine. We'll capture on e4.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/8/1PP1n3/2N2NP1/.text:
Black recaptures.

Let's trade once again.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/nP6/2P5/6P1/P2NPP.text:
Well, the e8-square seems the safest.

The rook shouldn't wander in the center this early.

r1bqr1k1/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/nP6/Q1P5/6P1/P2NP.text:
Now we can activate the queen, hit the knight and defend the pawn.

Again, our bishop is very active and White is slightly better here.

r1q2r2/ppp1npbk/3p2pp/1P2p3/2P3n1/1QNP2P.text: Black plays the prophylactic ...Kh7 to reintroduce possibilities of ...f5.

r1q2r2/ppp1npbk/3p2pp/1P2p3/2P3n1/BQNP2P.text:
We develop naturally with Ba3, supporting a c5 break.

15...Qf5 looks dangerous, but we will defend with Nd1. 

Queen to f5 also loses contact of the b7 pawn, so we can take it and then fall back to f3 or h1.

r1q2rk1/ppp1npb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP2Pb.text:
The most aggressive approach from Black, going all out at our king. 

We are objectively better but it will take accurate play to beat back Black's ideas while progressing on the queenside.

We'll retain our bishop with Bh1.

r1q2rk1/ppp1npb1/3p2pp/1P2p3/2P3n1/2NP2P.text:
Black jumps forward with the knight, hitting some weak spots in our camp and planning tricks with the ...e4 pawn push.

Now Qb3 comes in handy, defending the knight.

Also, if the f-pawn moves, there could be a discovered check lurking with c5.

r1q2rk1/ppp1npb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP2P1.text:
A better, multipurpose way of defending the b7-pawn is ...Qc8.

Black lines up the bishop with the queen and wants to trade light-squared bishops in the future.

Let's play Re1 and preserve our powerful bishop on g2.

r2q1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/1P2p3/2Pn2b1/2NP1.text:
As per usual, Black can't do much about the queenside.

The KID is mostly Black playing on the kingside!

Let's capture on c6.

r2q1rk1/1pp1npb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP.text:
Black retreats to e7...

And we'll develop the bishop to b2.

Activating it to a3 might generally be better, but when Black has played ...a5 and opened up the a-file, we can't develop it there.

r2q1rk1/1pp2pb1/2npbnpp/4p3/1PP5/2NP1NP1.text:
And ...Be6, the most common approach here from Black, does nothing to stop it.

We'll simply continue with b5.

r2q1rk1/1pp2pbp/p1npbnp1/4p3/1PP5/2NP1NP.text:
Black wants to take control of the b5-square, preventing the immediate b5 by us.

But we can use our a-pawn to help out.

r2q1rk1/5pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2Pn2b1/2NP1NP1/.text:
Black recaptures, and now we've got the b-file.

However, there's some pressure on the knight on f3.

Let's relieve it by trading on d4, unleashing an attack on the c6-pawn.

r2q1rk1/5pbp/2pp1np1/8/2Pp2b1/2NP2P1/4PP.text:
We can't capture it right away though, because our knight is under fire.

Let's centralize it and offer another trade.

r2q1rk1/5pbp/2pp2p1/8/2Ppn1b1/3P2P1/4PPB.text:
Black takes.

We'll take back with an attack on the c6-pawn.

Which bishop would you say is better, ours on e4, having an actual target or Black's on g7, staring at its own pawn?

r2q1rk1/ppp1npb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP.text:
Black retreats to e7.

And we'll jump to d2.

Our bishop is unleashed with an attack on the b7-pawn.

Black's got two real ways of defending it, since c6 weakens d6.

r2q1rk1/ppp2pb1/2npbnpp/4p3/1PP5/2NP1NP1.text:
Black activates the bishop, and Black proves the point of ...h6.

There's no Ng5 now.

But there is still b5!

r2q1rk1/ppp2pbp/2npbnp1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
8...Be6 is fairly popular and natural, but it does absolutely nothing to stop our plans.

With b4, we'll create a strong pawn storm, and we're not faced with any threats.

A good alternative here was also Ng5, to hit the bishop right away.

r2q2k1/1Bp2pbp/3p2p1/1P6/2br4/1Q4P1/4PP1.text:
Black takes on c4, so we don't have time to take the rook on a8.

Let's slide to f3.

The rook is still under attack on a8.

r2q2k1/1pp2pbp/3p2p1/1P3b2/2Pr4/1Q4P1/4P.text:
The best developing square for the bishop is f5, hitting our rook.

But we can give up the exchange with Bb2, counter-attacking the black rook!

Our bishop on b2 is strong.

r2q2k1/1pp2pbp/3p2p1/1P6/2Pr4/1Q4P1/1B2P.text:
We'll just recapture on b1.

We will regain our exchange soon and the powerful light-squared bishop continues to give us small nagging pressure.
Black accepts the rook offer, and we won't even capture on d4 right away.

r2q2k1/1pp2pbp/3pb1p1/1P6/2Pr4/1Q4P1/4PP.text:
If Black absent-mindedly develops the bishop to e6, hitting our c4-pawn...

We can actually give it up to capture on b7!

r4rk1/1ppq1pbp/p1npbnp1/4p1N1/PPP5/2NP2P.text:
We can jump to g5 and hit the bishop first, also controlling the h3-square.

Our bishop is great and there's no problems.

r4rk1/1ppq1pbp/p1npbnp1/4p3/PPP5/2NP1NP1.text:
Black improves the queen, and we don't need to hurry with b5 right away.

There might be threats of ...Bh3.

r4rk1/1ppqnpb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NPb/.text:
Black goes for the trade.

We'll trade rooks instead.

r4rk1/1ppqnpb1/3pbnpp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
Another common idea by Black, creating a battery. Black wants ...Bh3, trading the light-squared bishop.

We'll fight for the a-file with Ra1.

Re1 was also logical to anticipate ...Bh3 but it seems like we can ignore the bishop trade here.

r4rk1/3q1pbp/2p3p1/3p4/2PpB1b1/3P2P1/4PP.text:
Black pushes in the center.

Let's take, naturally.

We want to keep their d-pawns doubled.

r4rk1/3q1pbp/2pp2p1/8/2PpB1b1/3P2P1/4PP1.text:
Black has to defend.

Their main idea here is ...d5.

We'll activate the rook, since there isn't too much we can do to prevent  it.

r4rk1/3q1pbp/6p1/3p4/3p4/3P1PP1/5P1P/1RB.text:
And we'll recapture, of course.

After all is said and done, the position is simplified but our king will be very safe. 

Black's doubled pawns are more vulnerable than ours, and we have the better minor piece.

r4rk1/3q1pbp/6p1/3p4/3pB1b1/3P2P1/4PP1P/.text:
Black recaptures, still with tempo.

I suggest we offer a trade here, as Black has restricted our light-squared bishop anyway.

r5k1/1ppqnpb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/1QNP1NP1/.text:
We'll recapture.

We're going to trade off the rooks and then try to invade down the a-file with our queen.

Black doesn't have much control of the light squares so we have ideas such as Nd5 and Nd2-e4.

We can also push e4 first to support Nd5. Another plan to look out for is to push for b6 or c5 (or d4) if it can open up the position favorably.
Black finally chops off the bishop.

r5k1/1ppqnpb1/3p1npp/1P2p3/2P5/2NP1NPb/1.text:
Once Black recaptures...

We've got Qb3.

The point is to free up the rook to slide to a1.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2P5/2NP2P1/PP.text:
Black opens up the light-squared bishop.

It's natural to prepare the ...e5-push.

We'll develop the knight and prepare to castle, awaiting ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
And Black plays it.

We'll castle.

Although we are playing "less ambitiously" with a d3 setup instead of d4, we have a couple of advantages to our setup.

We have great light square control with our bishop on g2, while our plan is very simple and
straightforward with a queenside pawn storm.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PP.text:
In the KID, Black's first 4 moves almost always look like this.

The king is safely castled.
 
We'll play d3 and reinforce our light-square control.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
And both bishops get developed.

Our bishop stands strong on g2.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
Black prepares the fianchetto.

We have similar ideas, going for a fianchetto of our own.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black goes for ...Nf6.

They want the King's Indian setup with ...g6 and ...Bg7.

Having moved the c-pawn, we'll develop behind it with Nc3.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In Chapter 8, we will prepare against the King's Indian. 

In this first study, we'll take a look at Black's traditional approach in the King's Indian Defense, the Classical setup.

Black will place the two knights on f6 and c6, and play to control the center from afar.

Let's learn how to deal with this setup. As always, we'll open with the English.

B4r1k/p2q2bp/6p1/2P1pbNn/3n4/1Q1P2P1/PP3.text: Before recapturing, Black has an improving move in the center to hit our queen.

B4r1k/p2q2bp/6p1/2PQpbNn/3n4/3P2P1/PP3P1.text:
And we'll offer a trade in the center.

Black will probably get the bishop on a8.

Nevertheless, our position is much better because of the material advantage and the passed c-pawn.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/pPn1p3/2P5/2NP1N.text:
Black's point was that we give up the c5-square, so they can jump there with the knight.

But we are the ones with the space on the queenside.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/pPn1p3/2P5/2NP2P.text:
And we'll try to get rid of their strong piece with Nd2 and Nb3.

Our bishop is extremely active now as well.

r1bq1rk1/1ppn1pbp/3p1np1/p3p3/1PP5/2NP1N.text:
Black going for ...a5 now doesn't really do anything.

We wanted to push b5 anyway.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2pbp/2np2p1/4p2n/2P1P3/2NP1N.text:
A better move for Black than 8...f5 is activating the knight to c6.

This is more solid for Black, but doesn't threaten anything.

We can just continue developing with Bg5, provoking f6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np1pp1/4p1Bn/2P1P3/2NP1.text:
Once they play it...

We'll just retreat to the next best square, e3.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np2p1/4pp1n/2P1P3/2NPBN.text:
And Black advances to f5 now, having grabbed a tempo themselves.

Nothing to be afraid of. We'll capture.

r1bq1rk1/pppn1p1p/3p2p1/8/1PP1N3/5NP1/P3.text:
Black has won a rook for a piece, but we've got a trick.

Let's go for Bg5, attacking the bishop and the queen at the same time.

Black blocking ...Bf6 doesn't help their cause as we capture with the knight and continue applying pressure, for example with Qd4.

r1bq1rk1/pppn1pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
7...Nbd7 is played 11% of the time and seems natural just like 7...Nc6, but is actually a bit passive.

Black does little to delay our queenside expansion and might have different plans, namely in the center.

We'll expand immediately on the queenside with b4.

r1bq1rk1/pppn1pbp/3p1np1/8/1PP1p3/2NP1NP.text:
If Black tries to hit us in the center, we're ready.

Let's take.

r1bq1rk1/pppn1pbp/3p2p1/8/1PP1n3/2N2NP1/.text:
Black recaptures with the knight.

Our knight on c3 is pinned and attacked twice.

We'll sacrifice the exchange!

r1bq1rk1/pppn3p/3p1pp1/6B1/1PP1N3/5NP1/P.text: So, they block with the pawn, counter-attacking our bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pppn3p/3p1ppB/8/1PP1N3/5NP1/P3P.text:
But now our bishop can slide to h6 and there's no ...Bg7 to block.

Both of Black's rook and bishop are under attack.

We'll be getting some material back with a much better position.

r1bqr1k1/1pp2pbp/2np1np1/p3p3/2P5/P1NP1N.text: Black going for ...Nc6 on move 9 transposes to the main line.

r2q1rk1/ppp3bp/2np1np1/4pb2/2P5/2NPBNPP/.text:
After Qd2, there are a lot of instructive ideas in this position.

On the kingside, we can advance with g4 and push our knight into g5 at some point.

On the queenside, we have ideas of b4 and b5 as usual.

In the center, our rook can come to e1.

r2q1rk1/ppp3bp/2np2p1/4pb1n/2P5/2NPBNP1/.text:
The bishop recaptures.

We'd love to fork Black's pieces with g4, so we'll prepare it with h3!

Black has to move one of the minor pieces.

r4r1k/pB1q2bp/2n3p1/2P1pbNn/8/1Q1P2P1/PP.text:
The best they can do is activate the knight...

And we'll take, acquiring a rook and three pawns for the two minor pieces.

Not the worst of trades!

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/1PP5/2NP1BPP.text:
We'll try to undermine that structure right away with the instructive b4.

Our bishop really is the key piece.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1BPP/.text: Blocking with the pawn makes their position more solid.

rn1q1rk1/pp4bp/2pp2p1/4pbNn/2P5/2NP2P1/P.text:
Black protects against the most urgent threat which was the attack on the b7-pawn.

But we aren't done creating threats. Let's play Qb3, attacking b7 again, and planning a discovery.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2P3b1/2NP1NP.text:
It definitely makes sense to activate the light-squared bishop next, namely to g4.

However, it doesn't grant Black any edge whatsoever.

We'll attack the bishop.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1bPP/.text:
At this point, it only makes sense for Black to capture.

We'll recapture with the bishop and attack the b7-pawn.

Should Black block with the knight or the pawn?

rn1q1rk1/ppp3bp/3p2p1/4pb1n/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
Recapturing with the bishop and activating it makes more sense.

Let's attack with Ng5, a multipurpose move!

The queen sees the knight on h5 and the pawn on b7 is under attack.

rn3r1k/pp1q2bp/6p1/2PBpbNn/8/1Q1P2P1/PP3.text:
The king has to step to h8.

We'll capture on b7 and trap the rook!

rn3rk1/pp1q2bp/2p3p1/2PppbNn/8/1QNP2P1/P.text:
That's why Black pushes ...d5 and blocks, thinking they've solved all their problems.

We break through by sacrificing the knight!

rn3rk1/pp1q2bp/2pp2p1/4pbNn/2P5/1QNP2P1/.text:
If Black defends the b7-pawn...

We've got this discovered check.

Capturing on d6 would be an amazing positional benefit for us.

rn3rk1/pp1q2bp/6p1/2PppbNn/8/1Q1P2P1/PP3.text:
Black has to capture.

We've already regained two pawns for the piece, and we'll capture on b7 as well.

rnbq1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/p3p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
Black going for the setup with ...c6 and ...a5, preventing our b4 idea. This is the most solid approach for them.

We'll play a3, and keep trying for b4.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
7...c6 is the second most popular move in this position, played 16% of the time.

It is logical to build a big center and oppose our bishop on g2.

Let's slide our rook to b1, with our standard idea of advancing on the queenside.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/3p1np1/8/2P5/2NP2P1/PP.text:
Black opens up their light-squared bishop.

They want ...e5, of course.

We'll develop the kingside knight and prepare castling.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
Black strikes in the center.

And we'll castle.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4p2n/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
7...Nh5 is only played 1% of the time, but has an instructive idea behind it.

Black wants to make way for f5-f4.

We'll push in the center with e4, and take control of the f5 right away. We also allow our queen to eye h5.

It blocks our bishop but we can't allow Black's plan to proceed unopposed.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p2p1/4pp1n/2P1P3/2NP1NP.text:
Black could, logically, still try to advance the f-pawn to f5.

But this gives White the advantage.

We played e4 so we could capture on f5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p4/4Np1n/2P5/2NP2P1/PP3.text:
We can sacrifice the knight in the center.

If Black takes we'll regain the piece immediately.

This is a winning position for White.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p4/4pp1n/2P5/2NP1NP1/PP.text:
Black recapturing with the g-pawn is a mistake.

Here's why the queen being on the d1-h5 diagonal is important.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PP.text:
Time for Black to castle.

With d3, we'll connect the pawn chain on the light squares.

Our dark-squared bishop is now ready to come into the game.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
Black develops...

And so will we.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
Black wants to fianchetto.

We'll prepare to do likewise.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black goes for ...Nf6.

We'll activate the knight, aiming for g3 next.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
For this second study of Chapter 8, we'll take a look at how to play against Black's alternatives to the most popular ...Nc6 on move 7.

Some of Black's setups demand different type of play than others, and it's important to recognize when to vary your approach.

Let's begin with 1.c4.

rnbqr1k1/1p3p2/2pp1bpp/p3p3/2P5/P1NP1NP1.text:
The bishop recaptures.

We'll redirect our knight to d2.

Having solved the problem of Black pushing ...d5, we can finally focus on our queenside expansion.

Our d-knight could also jump to e4 at some point.

rnbqr1k1/1p3pb1/2pp1npp/p3p1B1/2P5/P1NP1.text:
Black attacks our bishop.

We take. We don't mind giving up this bishop since the knight was useful for Black's central play.

rnbqr1k1/1p3pb1/2pp2pp/p3p3/2P5/P1NP2P1/.text: The bishop goes back to g7.

And we'll make sure the knight on c3 is well protected and there are no ...e4 tactics. 

The position is roughly balanced but we have great light-square control and a straightforward b4-b5 bulldozer.

rnbqr1k1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/p3p3/2P5/P1NP1NP.text:
Black prepares ...d5 now.

We don't have to go b4 immediately, we can address Black's threats first. Now Bg5 transposes into a line we've already seen.

Black is eager to let us push b4 if they get ...d5 in exchange.

Now the e5-pawn is protected.

Let's pin the knight, which helps support ...d5 and ...e4.

rnbqr1k1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p3p3/2P5/2NP1NP1.text:
Black stops b4 with ...a5 before proceeding with potential center operations.

But we are persistent and play a3!

An alternative to this move was e4 to grab more central control.

rnbqr1k1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p7/2P1p3/P1NP1NP.text:
If Black is aggressive with ...e4, we don't have to capture and let them activate their pieces.

We'll retreat the knight to e1, and encourage Black to exchange in the center.

rnbqr1k1/1pp2pbp/3p1np1/p7/2P5/P1NN2P1/1.text:
And we'll recapture conveniently with the knight.

Our bishop comes to life now.

rnbqr1k1/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2P5/2NP1NP1/.text:
7...Re8 is a challenging approach by Black, played 5% of the time.

Black wants to advance in the center, and prepares it with the rook.

Rb1 makes sense, getting off the long diagonal before it opens up, and also preparing b4.

r1b1k2r/pppnbp1p/5np1/1N2p1B1/2P5/5NP1/P.text:
That gives us a new front of attack, threatening a fork.

Black is probably even lost here.

r1b1k2r/pppnbp1p/5np1/4p1B1/2P5/2N2NP1/P.text: Black moves the king away and unpins, but it doesn't help them a whole lot.

r1b1k2r/ppppqpbp/2n2np1/1N6/2P5/4Q1P1/PP.text:
We've got the potent Nb5 once again.

If Black's queen leaves d8, this move is often strong to threaten a fork on c7.

r1b1kb1r/ppppqp1p/2n2np1/8/2P5/2N1Q1P1/P.text: As Black wants to fianchetto, they'll probably block with the queen.

We don't have to trade ourselves.

Let's take a move to develop and prepare to recapture with the bishop if needed.

r1b4r/ppkn1pbp/2p2np1/4p3/2P5/1PN2NP1/P3.text:
11.b3 is a good move here to claim the advantage.

We'll get the bishop to b2 and jump to g5 with the knight to attack the f7-pawn.

A good idea to keep expanding on the queenside at some point would be b4-b5.

r1bk3r/pp1n1pbp/2p2np1/4p3/2P5/2N2NP1/PP.text:
9...c6 grabs control of some squares in the center.

As previously, we'll pin the knight on d7.

r1bk3r/pppn1pbp/5np1/4p3/2P5/2N2NP1/PP2P.text:
Black defends.

And we've got time to castle.

r1bk3r/pppnbp1p/5np1/4p1B1/2P5/2N2NP1/PP.text:
It's more solid for Black to defend with the knight on d7 than with the knight on c6.

However, you can see that Black's pieces are stuck together on the back ranks.

Let's pin that knight as well with Rd1!

r1bq1rk1/1p1n1pbp/2pp1np1/p3p3/1PP1P3/2N.text:
Black challenging us now is "too late".

Of course, we won't capture on a5 and open up their rook.

We'll push b5 instead, just as we intended.

And Black has done nothing to stop us.

r1bq1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/p1n1p3/2P1P3/2NP.text:
Black's knight hops into the outpost on c5.

It might seem logical to take the knight on c5 and double Black's pawns...

r1bq1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/p1n1p3/2P1PP2/2N.text:
But we have got other ideas!

We'll advance with f4, creating tension in the center.

Of course, we are threatening to capture on e5 and then capture the knight.

White is better here.

r1bq1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/pPn1p3/2P1P3/2NP.text:
Yes, we do give up the c5-square.

But our aggression on the b-file is what's important to us.

r1bq1rk1/1p3pbp/n1pp1np1/p3p3/2P1P3/2NP2.text:
Black is going to build behind their queenside structure now, planning ...Nc5.

They can't stop us on both sides of the board.

Time to get the bishop out with Be3.

r1bq1rk1/pp1n1pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2P1P3/2NP2.text:
If Black just develops lazily and traditionally for one move, we know what to do.

Let's go for the immediate b4, aiming for b5.

r1bqk2r/pppp1pbp/2n2np1/8/2PQ4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
Again, if Black attacks our queen...

We'll just slide to e3, with check.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1p1p/2n2np1/8/2PQ4/2N3P1/PP.text:
One could argue that the most logical move for Black is to develop and attack our queen.

But the check on e3 is a big part of plans to ruin Black's coordination.

r2q1rk1/1p3pbp/2ppbnp1/pPn1p3/2P1P3/2NP2.text: Black activates the bishop, and here's a calm move to demonstrate our plans for the future.

I like h3 here to grab some more control of the g4-square and tuck the king on h2 at some point.

Remember to activate the dark-squared bishop on a3 to x-ray the dark diagonal.

Our rook will become a monster on the b-file.

All in all, White stands slightly better.

r2q1rk1/pp3pbp/2n1bnp1/4p1B1/1PP5/1QN3P1.text:
And as the last move of the line, we'll avoid the queen trade with Qb3.

The queen supports our queenside operations and opens up the d1-square for the rook.

In the center, Nd5 would be great to continue applying the pressure.

rn1q1rk1/5pbp/p1ppbnp1/4p3/PPP1P3/2N3P1/.text: Black can target the c4-pawn immediately...

rn1q1rk1/5pbp/p1ppbnp1/4p3/PPP1P3/2NQ2P1.text:
But we can defend it with the queen.

Although the computer claims equality in this position, I'd argue White's position is much simpler to play.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/2p1bnp1/3pp3/1PP1P3/2NP2.text:
It's the central ...d5-push!

Black creates chaos in the center.

We don't want to let them capture and win material/grab the initiative.

We'll take once.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/2ppbnp1/4p3/2P1P3/2NP2P1.text:
One of the most challenging lines arises after 8...Be6.

Black happily develops the light-squared bishop, controlling the d5-square for later.

They haven't done much to prevent us from achieving our goals on the queenside, however.

Now b4 is the most straightforward choice amongst the other options such as 9. h3 or 9. b3.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/4bnp1/3pp3/1PP5/2NP2P1/P.text:
Black recaptures, and there's still some tension left, with c4 a target.

But instead of dealing with that, I recommend a more venomous move.

We'll pin the knight on f6 and threaten to capture on d5!

Our bishops are extremely strong.

rn1q1rk1/pp3pbp/4bnp1/4p1B1/1Pp5/2NP2P1/.text:
Black takes on c4.

We'll recapture once.

They don't have time to take again because of the hanging b7-pawn.

rnb1k2r/ppppqpbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N1Q1P1/PP2P.text:
Black basically has to block with the queen.

We have a couple of reasonable ways to develop here, but I'll suggest a funny-looking move.

rnb1k2r/ppppqpbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N1Q1PN/PP2P.text:
Let's jump to h3, with the idea of Nf4 and Nfd5, if possible.

Our bishop will activate to g2 and we don't mind a queen trade as we'll recapture with the bishop, of course.

rnbk1b1r/ppp2p1p/5np1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP2P.text:
The king recaptures.

And now the pin on the knight is powerful.

We'd love to play something like Nd5 to keep applying pressure.

rnbk3r/ppp1bp1p/5np1/4p1B1/2P5/2N3P1/PP2.text:
Not when Black unpins immediately, though.

We'll just develop the kingside knight and hit the pawn in the center.

rnbk3r/ppp2pbp/5np1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP2PPB.text:
The king must capture.

In the last line where a similar position happened, I recommended Bg5.

Here, the knight on f6 is already defended, so we'll play differently.

Let's develop the knight with an attack on the e5-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/1p3pbp/2pp1np1/p3p3/2P1P3/2NP2P.text:
Don't be discouraged if Black directly plays against our queenside expansion.

There are still developing and improving moves we can make in the center/on the kingside.

First of all, I suggest taking away the g4-square from Black's bishop.

rnbq1rk1/1p3pbp/p1pp1np1/4p3/2P1P3/2NP2P.text:
Black could try to counter our queenside plan by "mirroring" it, with ...a6, preparing ...b5.

This is an inaccuracy of sorts, however, since we are faster.

Let's bulldoze the queenside with b4.

rnbq1rk1/5pbp/p1pp1np1/1p2p3/1PP1P3/2NP2.text:
Black expands with ...b5, thinking they've grabbed crucial space and stopped our idea.

But we'll put pressure on their queenside. Let's use the b-pawn as a hook with a4!

If the a-file opens up, that would be amazing for us.

rnbq1rk1/5pbp/p1pp1np1/4p3/PPp1P3/2NP2P1.text:
It's likely that Black will capture on c4.

We'll take back, of course, and we've gotten rid of the weak backwards d3-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2p2np1/8/2P5/2NP2P1/PP.text:
It's the peculiar-looking ...c6. This move is played 29% of the time.
Black plays against our bishop and simply wants ...d5 in the center.

We'll take the Botvinnik formation against this move, placing the e-pawn in the center, grabbing more space and preventing ...d5.

It is of bigger importance to restrict Black's central expansion than to keep our bishop active.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2pp1np1/8/2P1P3/2NP2P1/.text:
Black has to settle for ...d6.

They can change their plans here.

Once we activate our knight...

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp1np1/4p3/2P1P3/2NP2P1.text:
Black can go for ...e5 instead of ...d5, which is a flexible approach that keeps the bishop on c8 open for development.

We castle, and arrive at the "Botvinnik Formation." This is a possible setup (g3, Bg2, c4, d3, e4, Nge2) against many of Black's options.

We are aiming to discourage ...d5, while retaining Rb1 and b4 as an option.

rnbq1rk1/pp3pbp/2pp2p1/4p2n/2P1P3/2NP2P1.text:
We might come across ...Nh5 here.

The idea is to free up the f-pawn, trying to play ...f5.

After all, it is the main pawn break for Black in the KID.

We are unconcerned and simply continue with our plan.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp2p1/4pp1n/2P1P3/2NP2P1.text:
Once Black pushes...

We'll take here.

This opens up our bishop on g2 again and prevents Black from acquiring too much space in the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp4/4pp1n/1PP5/2NP2P1/P3.text:
Let's continue with our queenside plan, aiming for b5.

White has an advantage here, but be prepared to face a sharp position with a lot of fireworks.

Often times, Black will look to play ...f4 here, to which we can answer with something like Bf3.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp4/4pp1n/2P5/2NP2P1/PP2.text: Also, their king position is now a touch weakened.

rnbq1rk1/pppp1pbp/5np1/8/2P4Q/2N3P1/PP2P.text:
We can still slide to h4.

If we succeed in playing Bg5, we'll be in great shape.

Our knight will activate to f3 and we'll castle.

rnbq1rk1/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PP.text:
And Black castles.

...d6 transposes to positions we cover elsewhere in more depth, e.g. 5.Nf3 0-0 6.0-0 e5 7.d3 and we're back into known territory.

5.d3 keeps our pawns together. Black's got multiple options here, but we'll cover only one of them in this study.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/3p1np1/4p3/2PP4/2N3P1/PP.text:
Once again, ...d6 here is not the best idea.

Black simply surrenders to an inferior position from the get-go.

Let's capture in the center.

rnbqk2r/ppp2pbp/5np1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP2PP.text:
Black recaptures.

And we'll trade queens.

rnbqk2r/pppp1pbp/5np1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP1P.text:
Black could go for ...e5 here as well, although it's played only 1% of the time.

We'll challenge that pawn immediately.

rnbqk2r/pppp1pbp/5np1/8/2PQ4/2N3P1/PP2PP.text:
If Black develops and threatens a discovery, we can retreat with tempo.

We'll check on e3.

rnbqk2r/pppp1pbp/5np1/8/2Pp4/2N3P1/PP2PP.text:
Black will most likely capture.

And we'll take back.

The difference with the bishop on g7 is that Black can now castle and avoid the uncomfortable check on e3.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/8/2P5/2N3P1/PP1PPP.text:
Black completes the fianchetto 91% of the time, so be prepared to see this move by far the most often.

We'll also fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/3p1np1/4p3/2PP4/2N3P1/P.text:
Supporting the e5-pawn with the d6-pawn is a mistake that leads to a forcing line, in which we get the advantage.

It's played only 12% of the time here.

We'll take on e5.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5np1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP2P.text:
Black has to recapture, and now the queens see each other.

We'll trade them off.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5np1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP1.text:
Black could try to surprise us here and go for the quick ...e5, although it is played extremely rarely in the database, less than 1%.

Still, it's positionally instructive how to play against this.

We'll push d4 and open the position.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5np1/8/2Pp4/2N3P1/PP2P.text:
The most reasonable move is for Black to capture, which they do 71% of the time (173 games).

We'll recapture.

The alternative of pushing ...e4 is a mistake after 5.Bg5 pinning the knight.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
Black prepares the fianchetto.

We'll do the same.

Black won't be the only one with a strong bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black goes for 1...Nf6.

The King's Indian formation includes the fianchetto of the dark-squared bishop, quick castling and often pawns on the dark squares like ...d6 and ...e5.

We'll just continue developing here with Nc3.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
For this final study, we'll analyze the Botvinnik formation, consisting of pawns on the light squares in the center, the bishop on g2 and the g-knight on e2.

As always, we'll open with the English.

1r1q1rk1/1p1bppbp/p1np1np1/2p5/2P5/1PNPP.text:
They'll prepare it with ...Rb8.

But we're okay with them pushing ...b5.

Let's castle and prepare to fight against it.

1r1q1rk1/3bppbp/p1np1np1/1pp5/2P5/1PNPP1.text:
Black pushes on the queenside.

We'll simply centralize the a-rook.

If Black takes, we'll recapture with the d-pawn and have an open d-file for us.

1rq2rk1/3bppbp/p1np1np1/1pp5/2P5/1PNPP1P.text:
They could go for the aforementioned ...Qc8 idea.

But we have more important ideas than dealing with that right away.

I like centralizing the knight here and offering some trades.

1rq2rk1/3bppbp/p1np2p1/1ppn4/2P5/1P1PP1P.text:
If Black takes in the center, we don't have to hurry and capture the bishop.

In fact, we'd like Black to capture us on b2!

We'll recapture in the center first, hitting the knight.

1rqn1r2/3bppkp/p2p2p1/1ppP4/3P4/1P2P1P1/.text:
That's exactly what we'll do.

Black capturing on d4 would most certainly play in our favor.

This line actually follows the game between A.Rakhmanov and J.Sarkar in 2013, which White won.

All in all, White is better here with more activity and the key d4-pawn break.

1rqn1rk1/3bppbp/p2p2p1/1ppP4/8/1P1PP1P1/.text:
They retreat to d8...

And now we can relinquish the bishop tension.

The idea is that we can get rid of our doubled d-pawns by pushing d4.

2kr2nr/pb1q1p1p/1pnp2p1/2pNp3/2P2P2/1P1P.text:
However, he just brought the king to safety, which was the best move.

Magnus activated the knight, preparing castling.

There was more pressure on e5 now, and he was threatening to capture.

2kr2nr/pb1q3p/1pnp1pp1/2pNp3/2P2P2/1P1P1.text: Which provoked ...f6 from Jakovenko, weakening his structure even more.

Magnus castled here, and you can see how appealing White's position is.

He went on to win the game in a pretty convincing fashion.

r1b1k1nr/p2qppbp/1pnp2p1/2p5/2P5/1PNP2P1.text:
Black will do the same, of course.

We'll fianchetto, and the queen protects the bishop.

r1b1k1nr/pp1qppbp/2np2p1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1/.text:
If they do continue copying us, we've got an answer for that as well.

And one of the lines includes a game of none other than Magnus Carlsen.

We'll play b3 and go for our planned setup.

r1bq1rk1/1p1pn1bp/2n2pp1/p1p1p3/2P5/P1NP.text:
We'll simply continue developing.

The knight is coming to e2, and we are going to castle short.

In the future, still trying to play for b4 would be a good idea.

r1bq1rk1/1p1pnpbp/2n3p1/p1p1p1B1/2P5/P1N.text:
If Black doesn't play ...f6 and let's us keep the pin, we aren't just going to keep it in place.

Let's actually capture on e7.

r1bq1rk1/1p1pnpbp/6p1/p1p1p3/2P5/P1NP2P1.text: Black recaptures with the knight to keep some control of the d5-square.

r1bq1rk1/1p1pnpbp/6p1/p1p1p3/2P5/P1NPP1P.text:
And I'd recommend e3 here.

We can still place a knight on d5 in the future, while developing naturally and looking for that b4-break.

White is slightly better here.

r1bq1rk1/p2p1pbp/2p1pnp1/2p5/2P5/1PNP2P1.text:
A natural recapture is ...bxc6, recapturing towards the center, still intending ...d5.

Having traded our light-squared bishop, we play to control the light squares with our pawns, starting with f3!

They will minimize the influence of Black's light-squared bishop.

Also, our dark-squared bishop can roam free between the pawns.

r1bq1rk1/p2pnpbp/2p1p1p1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NP2.text:
Black castles out of the way.

Having achieved what we wanted, we'll just develop.

r1bq1rk1/p3npb1/1pnpp1pp/2p5/2P4P/1PNP1N.text:
It's convenient for Black to prepare a fianchetto here...

But we aren't afraid of a four-bishop fianchetto.

We'll just castle to safety.

r1bq1rk1/p3npbp/2p1p1p1/2pp4/2P1PP2/2NP1.text: We'll just castle and laugh in the bishop's face.

Even if Black plays ...d5, there's no need to capture and open up the position.

That only helps Black's bishop break free.

r1bq1rk1/p4pbp/2p1pnp1/2pp4/2P5/1PNP1PPN.text:
And I suggest we activate the knight to h3.

It can reroute to f2 from where it's controlling the center.

Having doubled Black's c-pawns, it would be a great idea to target the weak c5-pawn with something like Na4.

r1bq1rk1/pp1p1pbp/2n1pnp1/2p5/2P5/1PNP2P.text:
The most challenging is for Black to prepare ...d5 with ...e6.

Let's uncork our anti-e6 idea. We'll actually capture on c6!

The knight is removed from controlling the d4-square.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/2p5/2P5/1PN3P1/.text:
The queenside knight activates to c6.

I suggest we simply continue developing pieces to reach our intended setup.

Black can't do much to stop us.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1/.text:
Black castles.

They can't continue mirroring our moves.

Let's continue with our setup.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npb1/2npp1p1/2p4p/2P4P/1PNP1.text:
We'll develop the knight to f3, when the g5-square can be used as a great improving jump for our knight or any other piece.

In the meantime, we'll castle and play for d4, supported by e3.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npb1/2npp1p1/2p4p/2P4P/1PNP2.text: If Black stops us right away, that's fine.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npb1/2npp1pp/2p5/2P4P/1PNP2P.text:
Black might not commit to ...h5 and play ...h6, with more control of the g5-square.

The idea is that they want to push ...g5 in case we go h5 now.

That stops our plans for the moment, but we'll just carry on developing with Nf3.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2np2p1/2p1p3/1PP5/P1NPP.text:
We've got e3 to open up the e2-square for the knight.

Our bishop on g2 is amazing, as well as our rook on b1.

They might become the key trouble makers for Black soon.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2np2p1/2p1p3/2P5/1PNP2P.text:
The king castles.

And we'll continue with e3, with the knight probably coming to e2.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2npp1p1/2p5/2P5/1PNP2P1.text:
And they'll castle.

We've got a real, non-mirroring middlegame on our hands.

I suggest h4 here, expanding on the kingside and trying to push h5.

Since we haven't castled and Black has, if the h-file opens up we might get a nice attack.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2p1p1p1/2p5/2P1PP2/2NP1.text:
So we'll play it.

Their bishop is still stuck and we've "won" the opening.

However, there's still chess to be played.

r1bq1rk1/pp2npbp/2p1p1p1/2p5/2P2P2/2NP1N.text: Once Black castles, they've done nothing to stop e4.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/2p5/2P5/1PN1P1P.text: They open up their bishop as well.

And let's get our knight to e2, not to block the bishop.

We want to expand with d4 but it's also possible to play more slowly with d3, Qd2, Rd1 and then go for some d4/e4/f4 expansion later depending on Black's moves. 

We will see a similar situation in the main line.

r1bq1rk1/pp2ppbp/2np1np1/2p5/2P5/1PNP2P1.text:
Black castles.

And we'll fianchetto.

There could be some tension on the long diagonal soon!

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/2p1pnp1/2p5/2P5/1PNP2P1/.text:
We'd love to see Black recapture with the d-pawn, as it means they've given up on playing ...d5.

We'll just continue developing, and fianchetto.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/2p2np1/2p1p3/2P5/1PNP2P1.text: Always watch out for ...e5 from Black's side, as it opens up the light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pbp/2p2np1/2p1p3/2P5/1PNP2PP.text:
We'll continue with h3 to prevent ...Bg4, and might even play g4 ourselves.

Not having to worry about ...d5, our knight can develop naturally to f3 and attack the e5-pawn.

r1bqk1nr/1p1p1pb1/2n3pp/p1pNp3/2P5/P2P2P.text:
That's why Black plays ...h6 to take control of the g5-square.

We have other ways to develop, and we'll play e3, securing the d4 square, and with the idea of future expansion.

r1bqk1nr/1p1p1pbp/2n3p1/p1p1p3/2P5/P1NP2.text:
Once Black develops their bishop...

I suggest immediately jumping in with Nd5.

Nothing can challenge our knight for now and if Black goes ...Nf6 we've got Bg5.

r1bqk1nr/p2p1pbp/2p1p1p1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1/.text:
If Black recaptures with the b-pawn...

We'll keep expanding on the dark squares, controlling e5 and preventing expansion by Black.

The light-squared bishop is completely stuck and useless behind its own pawns!

r1bqk1nr/p4pbp/1pp3p1/2p5/2P5/2NPBNP1/PP.text:
And finally, we can make a queen-bishop battery and try to trade the dark-squared bishops, as the center has opened up and Black's bishop is strong.

Castling queenside is a good idea, with an equal but not a peaceful position.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2n1p1p1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1.text:
Just like 5...d6, 5...e6 is played a quarter of the time, aiming for a future ...d5.

As in the 5...Nf6 line, there's an important idea to remember here.

We take on c6! We intend to bury Black's bishop on c8. 

An alternative in our style is 6. h4!?.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2n3p1/2p1p3/2P5/2NP2P1.text:
5...e5 is played only 7% of the time, but it's definitely a move worth considering.

This gives us full control of the d5-square.

Black has blocked their dark-squared bishop for a moment, and  thus we'll try to expand on the queenside.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2n3p1/2p1p3/2P5/P1N3P1.text:
If Black just develops, which they will 82% of the time...

We'll push b4 as planned.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/2n3p1/4p3/1pP5/P1N3P1/.text:
Capturing on b4 actually grants us a winning advantage!

Let's take back and continue to offer the pawn.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/6p1/1N2p3/1nP5/6P1/3PP.text:
I suggest Nb5, with ideas of both Nd6+ and Ba3 to attack the knight.

Black is in some trouble and might not even be able to castle.

r1bqk1nr/pp1p1pbp/6p1/4p3/1nP5/2N3P1/3PP.text: If Black is greedy and takes one more time...

r1bqk1nr/pp1pppbp/2n3p1/2p5/2P5/2N3P1/PP.text:
At this point, you can just expect Black to keep copying you.

4...Nc6 is played 54% of the time.

A natural move is d3, opening up the bishop.

You'll see our idea very soon.

r1bqk1nr/pp2ppbp/2np2p1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1/P.text:
Black will mirror us 25% of the time. 

How do we break this chain of identical moves being played on both sides?

We'll play Qd2!

We want to play b3, fianchetto the bishop on b2 and make sure it's protected by the queen on d2.

r1bqk1nr/pp3p1p/2p3p1/2p1b3/2P5/2NP2P1/P.text:
The bishop recaptures.

Which allows us to develop with tempo, hitting it.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2np2p1/2p1p3/1PP5/P1N3P1.text:
You might see the passive ...d6 here, keeping the structure together but not really doing anything about our push.

We'll support the b-pawn with the rook, also getting it off the dangerous diagonal.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2np2p1/2p1p3/2P5/2NP2P1/.text:
6...e5 is definitely an another interesting idea by Black.

They want to avoid any tension on the dark diagonal and grab more central space, while activating their  light-squared bishop.

We'll continue with our setup no matter what, and play b3.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2npp1p1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1/P.text:
Black going for 6...e6 looks natural, but it blocks the light-squared bishop.

And Black can't go for ...d5 as that would simply lose a pawn.

As planned, we'll continue with our setup, and play b3.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2p1p1p1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1/P.text:
If Black captures with the d-pawn, they won't be playing ...d5, but might want to go for ...e5 to open up the bishop on c8.

That's why it's important to control the e5-square with a pawn.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2p3p1/2p1p3/2P2P2/2NP2P1.text:
If Black goes for it, we are prepared, although they have managed to open up the bishop.

It comes at a certain price, though.

Let's take and force their hand.

r1bqk1nr/pp3pbp/2p3p1/2p5/2P5/2NP1NP1/PP.text:
It slides back to g7, naturally...

And we can continue targeting Black's weaknesses with Be3.

For the cost of them being able to activate their bishop, we are developing with tempo and causing trouble.

r1bqk2r/1p1pn1bp/2n2pp1/p1p1p1B1/2P5/P1N.text:
A sound chance to escape is ...f6, kicking our bishop away.

But it always weakens the king and  blocks the bishop on g7.

Let's just retreat safely to d2.

r1bqk2r/1p1pnpb1/2n3pp/p1pNp3/2P5/P2PP1P.text:
And we'll get our knight to e2.

We'll transfer it to c3 and still be aiming for the b4-break, with Rb1 to support it.

Black has made some severe weaknesses in their position that we'll be able to take advantage of.
Black gets the knight to e7...

r1bqk2r/1p1pnpbp/2n3p1/p1p1p3/2P5/P1NP2P.text:
That's why ...a5 is a good idea, designed to prevent b4.

Remember the d5-square we are controlling? Well, the knight on e7 is the only piece Black has that controls that square.

Let's pin it. Black might find themselves tied down here.

r1bqk2r/p2pnpbp/2p1p1p1/2p5/2P2P2/2NP2P1.text:
The best they can do is continue to develop and castle.

Of course, ...d5 is the main pawn break for them.

In the meantime, we've got time for e4 as well!

Now two of our pawns control the d5-square.

r1bqk2r/pp1pnpbp/2n3p1/2p1p3/2P5/P1NP2P1.text:
The knight activates to e7.

And we'll get the rook off the diagonal and prepare b4 once again.

If we put it into motion, we'll gain a lot of space and challenge Black's unstable structure.

r1bqk2r/pp1pppbp/2n2np1/2p5/2P5/2NP2P1/P.text:
5...Nf6 is the most popular move in the Lichess database under 2000 ELO, played 35% of the time.

We'll play Qd2.

We want to play b3 and Bb2, and the queen from d2 will cover the bishop on b2.

r1bqk2r/pp2npbp/2np2p1/2p1p3/1PP5/P1N3P1.text:
