This is the most direct response.

But we'll keep on going with our ideas of provoking weaknesses.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bpp1/2n1p2p/2pn4/7P/1PN1PN2/.text:
9...h6 creates a hook for us to attack.

With g4, we are going to attack the hook and open up lines.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bpp1/2n4p/2p1p3/6PP/1Pn1PN2/.text:
To win the pawn, Black would have to make this trade which activates our bishop. 

This trade is necessary because the queen can't defend the knight and the bishop going to h4 at the same time.

We'll of course recapture.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bpp1/2n4p/2pnp3/6PP/1PN1PN2/.text:
One of the few moves to not lose. Black has to counter in the center.

Our next move of Rg1 both defends g4 and supports the g5-pawn push. Black can get overrun if they don't do anything. 

We are offering the h-pawn, but this isn't a major concern.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n1p3/2pn4/7P/1PN1PN2/P.text:
Black should just develop and not stress excessively.

Our plan of putting pressure on h7 should still be played. 

We avoid the c2-square because of Nb4 jumps.

r1bq1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P4/1PN1PN2/.text:
That's why you'll often see regular development.

We'll just develop, waiting to set up a favorable IQP position.

r1bq1rk1/pp3p1p/2n1pbp1/2pn2N1/7P/1PN1P3.text: 10...g6 defends and blocks our view of h7.

r1bq1rk1/pp3p1p/2n1pbp1/2pn4/4N2P/1PN1P3.text:
Not only are we threatening the pawn, but we're threatening Nxf6+ to remove the defender of the dark squares and control them ourselves with our bishop. 

Black is in trouble.

r1bq1rk1/pp3pp1/2n4p/2p1p3/6Pb/1PB1PN2/P.text:
Black wins a pawn.

But we'll win the bishop pair.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pb2/2pn4/7P/1PN1PN2/P.text: 9...Bf6 seeks to add a defender to the kingside.

Black develops their knight.

With Ng5, we attack the h7-pawn and threaten checkmate.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n1pb2/2pn4/7P/1PNBPN2/P.text: We attack h7, and should Black respond with ...g6 or ...h6, we have attacking ideas either with Ne4 or g2-g4.

r1bq1rk1/pp4p1/2n1pb1p/2pn1p1P/8/1PN1PN2.text:
This is a normal continuation that can serve to illustrate some points about the position. 

Black wants to defend the kingside, and ...Bf6 is a logical way to try and do that.

We'll trade on d5.

r1bq1rk1/pp4p1/2n2b1p/2pp1p1P/8/1P2PN2/P.text:
Black recaptures.

We'll trade on f6.

r1br2k1/p1q1b1pp/1pn1p3/2pn1pN1/2B3PP/1P.text:
And despite the fact that material is equal, White's attack is tough to defend against.

You'll want to play moves like gxf5 and Nb5. The more lines you can open up for your pieces, the better.

r1br2k1/p1q1b1pp/1pn1p3/2pn1pN1/2B4P/1PN.text: Black will obviously bring the rook to the d-file.

r2q1r2/pb2bp1k/1pn1p1p1/1BpN4/7P/1P2P3/P.text:
But before h5 we play Nxd5 to open up our bishop. 

Our attack is pretty strong, and we're playing h5 to great effect.

r2q1rk1/1p3ppp/p1n2n2/2bp4/6b1/1PN1PN2/P.text:
Black creates a retreat square for their bishop.

We get our rook on the open file.

r2q1rk1/bp3ppp/p1n2n2/3p3b/8/1PN1PN1P/PB.text:
We want the bishop to go to h5 so we can force a trade. 

If they capture on f3, this is only good for us because we get the bishop pair.

Now Nh4 is a really strong move. Our knight is coming to f5.

r2q1rk1/bp3ppp/p1n2n2/3p4/6b1/1PN1PN2/PB.text:
Black brings the bishop back.

And we're guaranteed a slight edge after h3.

r2q1rk1/bp3ppp/p1n2n2/3p4/7N/1P2P2P/PB2N.text:
And we recapture with the knight to open up our bishop and control the d4-square. 

We're going to have great control of the dark squares leading to the g7-square, and when our knight hops to f5, it'll also put some kingside pressure.

r2q1rk1/pb2bp1p/1pn1p1p1/1Bpn2N1/7P/1PN1.text:
Black blocks the attack on h7.

But we can sacrifice on h7!

r2q1rk1/pb2bppp/1pn1p3/1Bpn4/7P/1PN1PN2/.text:
This, for example, is an error.

Ng5 begins the attack. 

Note that f5 can't be played because we've drawn the defensive bishop to b7.

r2q1rk1/pb2bppp/1pn2n2/2pp4/3P4/1PNBPN2/.text:
The knight comes out to c6 and places pressure on d4.

Since there's more pressure, taking on c5 is a good idea.

r2q1rk1/pb2bppp/2n2n2/2pp4/8/1PNBPN2/PB3.text:
And now the very natural 12. Rc1 is a move you should look to play in these positions and against the hanging pawns. 

Na4 is a strong maneuver to start putting pressure on the c5-pawn, and we should enjoy a solid middlegame, trying to attack those central pawns however we can.

This is Black's best recapture, avoiding the IQP. 

Volunteering for an isolated pawn isn't in their best interest.

r2q1rk1/pp2bppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P2b1/1PN1PN2.text:
To illustrate the point, let's say Black brings their bishop out to g4.

We can engineer the IQP position by capturing on c5.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2bp4/6b1/1PN1PN2/PB.text:
Black recaptures, and suddenly they're in an IQP position they may not be so ready to handle. 

We have some ideas.

First we castle. Before anything else, king safety is necessary.

rn1q1rk1/pb2bpp1/1p2p2p/2pn4/6PP/1PN1PN1.text:
11. Rh3 was played by Nepo in the 2018 Olympiad and he went on to win with a great attack. 

Rh3 gets the rook out of potential danger. g5 is coming with great effect.

rn1q1rk1/pb2bppp/1p3n2/2pp4/3P4/1PNBPN2/.text:
9...c5 is another common idea.

Castling is good. 

There's no need to do anything about the central tension.

rn1q1rk1/pbp1bppp/1p3n2/3p4/3P4/1PN1PN2/.text:
Black fianchettoes, or else b6 created light-squared weaknesses.

I like the aggressive placement of our bishop with Bd3.

rnbq1rk1/p1p1bppp/1p2pn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2.text:
Many QGD players use this idea. Since the e6-pawn blocks the bishop on c8, many beginners and intermediates are taught that ...b6 to fianchetto is useful.

However, ...b6 doesn't solve all their issues. 

We'll take on d5, now that the bishop has committed itself to b7.

rnbq1rk1/p1p1bppp/1p3n2/3p4/8/1PN1PN2/PB.text:
Black recaptures. 

Black's ...Bb7 idea is countered, in a way.

We should now place a pawn on d4.

rnbq1rk1/p3b1pp/1p2p3/2pn1p2/7P/1PN1PN2/.text:
This move seeks to block the diagonal right away.

Now the trade on d5 is good for us because the knight was a useful and active piece.

rnbq1rk1/p3b1pp/1p6/2pp1p2/7P/1P2PN2/PB1.text:
Black recaptures, but they are lacking a crucial defender of the kingside.

We'll push forward, with the aim of provoking weaknesses.

rnbq1rk1/p3bpp1/1p2p2p/2pn4/7P/1PN1PN2/P.text:
The pawn controls g5, trying to stop our knight jump.

But we can play g4 and target h6!

rnbq1rk1/p3bppp/1p2p3/2pn4/7P/1PN1PN2/PB.text:
8...b6 is another way to develop. 

It works out well because there isn't a cxd5 move anymore.

We'll play 9. Qb1 to start putting pressure on h7.

rnbq1rk1/p5pp/1p3b2/2pp1p1P/8/1P2PN2/PB1.text:
Black may think there's nothing for us here.

But we'll just keep on playing and create weaknesses.

rnbq1rk1/p6p/1p3bpP/2pp1p2/8/1P2PN2/PB1P.text: Supposing Black pushes, now we can improve our queen.

rnbq1rk1/p6p/1p3bpP/2pp1p2/8/1P2PN2/PBQP.text:
And with d4 coming up next, we'll open things up favorably for us. 

We'll play moves like Rd1 and Be2, and we of course don't mind a trade of dark-squared bishops because Black will have dark square weaknesses around the king.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4p3/2pn4/8/1PN1PN2/PB1P.text:
This option doesn't give us a clear way to the IQP, so we'll have to look for another plan.

h4 is an unconventional approach I've found for you. 

Let's go for the king!

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/4pn2/2pp4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
6...c5 is the most natural continuation.

Against ...c5, we'll take on d5 first.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/5n2/2pp4/8/1PN1PN2/PB1P.text:
This is the most popular option, but we can actually give Black an IQP that they may not be comfortable with.

And they're pretty much guaranteed an IQP unless they find the odd 8...b6, which creates a lot of weaknesses on the light squares. 

The bishop wouldn't be able to cover them all.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pb2/2pn4/7P/1PN1PN2/PB1.text:
This move is not good.

We could contemplate 9. g4, but Qc2 is good enough.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
Black castles.

And we fianchetto, of course. 

Our bishop will aim across the dark squares in the center.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP1.text:
4...Be7 is a standard way to play the QGD. 25% of players go for this. There are 55,000 games in the database from this position. 

Black is saying they're not committing to any more pawn moves yet, and they're just going for quick development.

We'll go for 5.b3 here to fianchetto the bishop and get it on a strong diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1P3/PP1P.text:
Black develops their kingside knight.

And we develop ours.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
Black expands.

And now we push the e-pawn, controlling d4. 

In case you missed it, 3...d4 would not make sense because we can capture and if Black recaptures with the queen, we gain a tempo by playing Nf3.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black begins to see if we'll agree to go into another opening.

We'll develop, controlling d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
The English is a very flexible opening. As such, you can often transpose to other well-known openings in a way that's comfortable for you. 

This is why in this chapter we'll take a look at how to play the Queen's Gambit Declined out of our English Repertoire. We begin with 1.c4.

2rq1rk1/3n1ppp/p1pb4/3p4/5P2/1P1QP2P/PB2.text:
But we'll control e5 and block the bishop's view towards our kingside. 

We'll continue with Ng3 and if 18...Nc5 you can play Qd1 to take the queen to the kingside after Ng3. 

You can check out So(2812)-Nakamura (2785) Paris 2017. So went on to win a nice game.

2rq1rk1/3n1ppp/p1pb4/3p4/8/1P1QPP1P/PB2N.text: Black may try to activate the knight.

2rq1rk1/5ppp/p1pb1n2/3p4/8/1P2PP1P/PB2NP.text:
Black defends c6.

We'll develop our queen to d3, connecting our rooks.

2rq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bbp3b/8/1PN1PN1P/P.text: Our aim isn't to push g4 but to control the g4-square using our h3-pawn.

2rq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bbp4/6b1/1PN1PN2/P.text:
It's possible that Black should try 11...Rc8 to support the knight and enter the open c-file.

We should play the natural move h3 to attack the bishop.

2rq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2bp3b/8/1PN1PN1P/PB.text:
At this point there are many plans. The best ones are those that focus on the d4-square. 

Nb5 is good because it aims to open up the bishop. You'll also want to play Nbd4 to have a knight sitting on d4, blockading.

r1bq1rk1/5ppp/p1p2n2/2bp4/8/1PN1PN2/P4PP.text:
Black castles. 

This is expected. We'll play Bb2.

r1bq1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bbp4/8/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
Black castles, too.

And we're getting everything we want with our fianchetto plan.

If Black allows Bb2, they'll be in big trouble because we'll have the perfect setup against the IQP.

r1bqk2r/5ppp/p1p2n2/2bp4/8/2N1PN2/PP3PPP.text:
Black recaptures.

And we can proceed with our b3 plan.

r1bqk2r/5ppp/p1pb1n2/2pp4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
If Black develops without the capture on d4, we'll now capture to make the bishop move again.

We win a tempo with dxc5.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bbp4/8/2N1PN2/PP3P.text:
Black recaptures but has now moved the bishop twice in the opening.

We'll castle.

r1bqk2r/pp3ppp/2nb1n2/1Bpp4/3P4/2N1PN2/P.text: If Black develops the bishop, we'll take on c5.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n2n2/1Bpp4/3P4/2N1PN2/.text:
This is the most popular move. 

Black seeks to get rid of our pin.

We'll capture on c6.

r1bqkb1r/5ppp/p1p2n2/2pp4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP3.text:
Black gets an open b-file, but we'll get to accomplish everything we want out of the opening.

First we'll castle. 

If 9...cxd4, 10. exd4 helps us control the c6- and d5-pawns with the d4-pawn alone.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/3p4/2N1PN2/P.text:
When this capture is played, we'll want to give Black their IQP and have them defend that position.

The pressure on c6 is secondary;
Black can easily defend. 

Mostly, we want to fight the IQP in the long run.

r1bqkb1r/pp3ppp/2n2n2/2pp4/3P4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
The knight comes out to c6 and puts some pressure on d4.

Let's pin it. 

We generally want to play ideas like b3 and Bb2, and then dxc5 after the bishop on f8 moves.

r2b1rk1/p4ppp/2p5/8/4N3/8/PP3PPP/2R2RK1.text:
And we can start putting pressure on the weakness. 

b3 will be played to keep the pawn safe from any b-file pressure, and we'll probably want to attack the c-pawn while also creating some luft for our king with g3 if there's ever some danger.

r2b1rk1/p4ppp/2p5/8/4N3/8/PP3PPP/R4RK1 w.text: Black has to recapture with the bishop to avoid an even worse structure.

r2q1k1r/p4ppp/2pN4/4b3/8/8/P4PPP/1R1Q1RK.text:
The bishop retreats and attacks the knight.

We'll move away and attack the bishop.

r2q1k1r/p4ppp/2pN4/8/8/8/Pb3PPP/R2Q1RK1.text:
Black has to move their king.

We get on the open b-file.

r2q1k1r/pR3ppp/2p5/8/2Nb4/8/P4PPP/3Q1RK1.text:
But our rook invades the 7th rank. 

This position is equal according to the engine but I like White's practical chances. It's difficult for Black to defend. 

Qb3 is a strong move to start looking at the f7-pawn.

r2q1rk1/1p3ppp/p1n2n2/1Bbp4/6b1/1PN1PN2/.text:
This is a useful waiting move. 

However, it's kind of useful for White, too. We can now change the structure from an IQP to weak hanging pawns.

We take the knight.

r2q1rk1/5ppp/p1p2n2/2bp4/6b1/1PN1PN2/PB3.text:
Black recaptures.

Our strategy against the hanging pawns is to contain them. 

We will do this with our rook on the c-file and our knight moving away from c3.

Black may pin us with the light-squared bishop.

Our reply of Ne2 may seem surprising, but it allows us to control the d4 square, and the engine approves.

r2q1rk1/5ppp/p1p2n2/2bp4/8/1P2PP2/PB2NP1.text:
We recapture. 

Since Black may want to attack h2, the move f4 is good to block a bishop's view of h2 and to control e5. 

Ng3 is also a great move because the f5-square may end up being a strong square for us.

r2q1rk1/5ppp/p1p2n2/2bp4/8/1P2Pb2/PB2NPP.text: This capture isn't bad for White. The doubled pawns aren't weak and the g-file may be useful.

r2q1rk1/5ppp/p1pb1n2/3p3b/8/1PN1PN1P/PB3.text:
The bishop retreats.

Now Ne2 targets control of d4.

This is similar to the 7...a6 line, but the difference is that the rook is on the c-file already.

r2q1rk1/5ppp/p1pb1n2/3p4/6b1/1PN1PN2/PB3.text:
The bishop avoids tactics since the rook x-rayed it.

h3 is a useful move for us. We attack the bishop and remove the h2-target.

r2q1rk1/5ppp/p1pb1n2/3p4/8/1P2Pb1P/PB2NP.text:
This doesn't trouble us.

We'll recapture and can use our rook on the g-file in the future.

r2q1rk1/p4ppp/2p2b2/8/4N3/8/PP3PPP/R2Q1R.text:
Black has the option of castling. 

They may do this to keep the king safe because the position has opened up too much.

The queen trade takes us to a good endgame.

r2q1rk1/p4ppp/2pb4/8/8/2Q5/PP3PPP/R1B2RK.text: But we keep our pawns together and aim at the weak c-pawn for the rest of the game.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2Bb4/3Q4/8/2n5/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
Black trades on c3.

And instead of capturing on c3, we'll retreat the queen, keeping our structure intact.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2bb4/1B1Q4/4n3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
This is the only move that doesn't lose for Black.

We'll trade on c6.

r2q1rk1/pp3ppp/2n2n2/1Bbp4/6b1/1PN1PN2/P.text:
One of the moves that you may see here and that presents the biggest challenge is ...Bg4. 

Our knight, which used to control d4, is pinned.

Continuing to develop is a good idea. 11...d4 isn't possible due to 12. Na4.

r2qk2r/1p1b1ppp/p1nb1n2/3p4/3N4/2N1P3/PP.text:
Black may get ready to castle.

But we can start building pressure against the pawn.

r2qk2r/1p3ppp/p1nbbn2/3p4/3N4/2N1PB2/PP3.text:
Black defends d5. 

Obviously, we don't want to play Nxe6 because that would help Black fix their structure.

r2qk2r/1p3ppp/p1nbbn2/3p4/3N4/4PB2/PP2NP.text:
Instead, we want to go for a regular blockade against the isolated d-pawn by having our knights defend each other. 

We also want to fianchetto our dark-squared bishop, which will strengthen our d4-control.

r2qk2r/p2b1ppp/2pb4/1B1p4/4N3/8/PP3PPP/R.text: We can take a piece and Black cannot capture any of our hanging pieces yet because of the d6-bishop!

r2qk2r/p2b1ppp/2pb4/1B1p4/4n3/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
One could consider this the incorrect capture. 

Black doesn't lose or anything, but we can get a nice edge.

r2qk2r/p2bbppp/2p5/3p4/4N3/3B4/PP3PPP/R1.text:
I like recovering our pawn here. 

We will have equalized materially but we will be better structurally.

r2qk2r/p2bbppp/2p5/8/4B3/8/PP3PPP/R1BQ1R.text:
And we recapture. 

We have, once again, long-term pressure on the c-pawn and we can expect to win it. 

Be3 and Qd3 or Qf3 are great moves, depending on how Black plays this. If the h7-pawn stays a target, you want to play Qd3 with tempo. 

If the h-pawn moves, Qf3 is better.

r2qk2r/p3bppp/2p2n2/6B1/4p3/2N5/PP3PPP/R.text:
Black unpins.

And we go ahead and take the knight, which will allow us to take on e4.

r2qk2r/p4ppp/2p2b2/8/4p3/2N5/PP3PPP/R2Q1.text:
We have a better structure. 

We can now make use of our pieces and start targeting weaknesses. We'll take on e4.

r2qk2r/p4ppp/2p5/8/4N3/8/Pb3PPP/R2Q1RK1.text:
This capture is also feasible. 

Nevertheless, there are many complications and it probably isn't safe for a human to play.

We give a check. This ensures the Black king cannot castle.

r2qk2r/p4ppp/2pb1n2/8/4p3/2N5/PP3PPP/R1B.text:
The c6-pawn is weak.

Bg5 pins the knight, further weakening e4.

r2qk2r/pp1b1ppp/2nb1n2/1B1p4/3N4/2N1P3/P.text:
Black develops their bishop.

The move e4 works well for us here because we're castled and Black's king is in the center.

r2qk2r/pp1b1ppp/2nb1n2/1B6/3Np3/2N5/PP3P.text:
Black can take with the pawn.

Our approach here will be to take on c6 and create a weakness.

r2qk2r/pp1b1ppp/2nb4/1B1p4/3Nn3/2N5/PP3P.text:
Against 10...Nxe4, we'll take on c6 as well.

This opens up some lines favorably for us because we have castled.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2bb1n2/1B6/4p3/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
This move is forced to defend the d6-bishop.

We'll trade again.

r2qk2r/pp3ppp/2bb4/1B1p4/4n3/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
This is the correct recapture.

We'll capture on d5 with the queen.

Tricks like Bxh2+ don't work because the queen is defended by the c3-knight.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p1n2n2/1Bpp4/3P4/2N1PN2.text:
If Black prompts us, we will not capture, as we don't want to help Black activate their bishop.

I find that Be2 present a strategical challenge. 

We're asking Black what they'll do with the d7-bishop.

r2qkb1r/1p1b1ppp/p1n2n2/3p4/3p4/2N1PN2/P.text:
If this trade happens, let's give Black an IQP.

The IQP is a weakness in the endgame.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n2n2/1B1p4/3N4/2N1P3/P.text:
Black defends c6.

And we can castle.

r2qkb1r/pp1b1ppp/2n2n2/1Bpp4/3P4/2N1PN2/.text:
7...Bd7 is very popular as well. 

It aims to simply break the pin.

We should castle kingside.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/2pq4/8/1P2PN2/P2P1PP.text:
7. b3 prepares to attack the queen.

Our bishops are way more powerful with the open lines we have. We should have nice and stable pressure in the middlegame since Black cannot develop both bishops comfortably.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/2pq4/8/4PN2/PP1P1PPP.text:
Black is advised not to play this way. 

The bishop on c8 would still be blocked and the queen is a target.

rnbqk1r1/pp3p1p/8/3pB3/1bp5/4PN2/P2P1PPP.text:
But that's why Be5 is designed to bring the bishop to g3 to neutralize the rook's influence on the g-file.

After 10...Nc6 and 11.Bg3, there's c3 to worry about. It's not a big deal: all we have to do is if 11...c3, 12. a3, forcing Ba5. The bishop on a5 takes away the Qa5 move from Black.

rnbqk1r1/pp3pBp/8/3p4/1bp5/4PN2/P2P1PPP/.text: The rook will have pressure on the g-file.

rnbqk2r/pp3ppp/8/3p4/1bp5/4PN2/PB1P1PPP/.text:
Black may take on b4.

But this lets us capture on g7.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/2pn4/8/2N1PN2/PP1P1P.text:
This move is an option for Black. It is rare, but you may still see it.

If we trade here, Black will be forced to recapture with either a pawn or queen. 

I argue that both options give us a small advantage.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/2P5/2N1PN2/PP1.text:
4...c5 is thematic in the Queen's Gambit Declined: it's a pawn push designed to control d4 and to challenge the d4-pawn. 

It is played 20% of the time, more than 45,000 games.

We should just capture the d-pawn. 

We'll be able to continue our plans afterwards.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/5n2/2pp4/8/2N1PN2/PP1P1P.text:
Black recapturing with the pawn is the most common move. It is played 78% of times. 

The reason for this is that players are taught that recapturing with pawns in the center helps them control more squares with the pawns.

Against pawn duos like this, it's useful to establish a central pawn as well, to stop their advance.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/2pp4/8/4PN2/PP1P1PPP/R.text:
This is the correct recapture. 

There are no tempi on Black's queen, and the pawns control the center.

But we've got the unconventional strike b4! 

We're undermining the c-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/3p4/1Pp5/4PN2/P2P1PPP/.text:
Black may avoid the capture if they want to preserve the c-pawn and its control of the center.

However, this helps us control d4.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/3p4/1p6/4PN2/P2P1PPP/R.text: If Black takes, they're playing into our hand.

rnbqkb1r/pp3ppp/8/3p4/1p6/4PN2/PB1P1PPP/.text:
Without the c5-pawn, we now control d4 completely. Our pressure on the diagonal is significant. 

We'll play around the d4-square and threaten to win the b-pawn back while developing our pieces. It's a very pleasant position for us and Black may be uncomfortable when you blitz out Rc1, Bb5, 0-0 and Nd4 with ease.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1P3/PP1P.text:
Black develops their knight.

And we develop ours.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/8/2P1P3/2N5/PP1P1.text: Our idea in that opening is further d5 control, but more of that will come later.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text: This leads us to the next chapter, which is an opening called the Mikenas-Carls.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
The 2...d5 pawn push puts us in Queen's Gambit Declined territory.

I don't want us to go to direct Queen's Gambit territory with 3. d4. 

Instead, consider 3. e3 as an "Anti-QGD".

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
The possibility of transposing into a Queen's Gambit Opening arises out of 1...e6. 

1...e6 is the precursor to a ...d5 pawn push, which happens in the Queen's Gambit Declined.

Against 1...e6 we'll develop our knight and control d5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
For this second study, I want us to turn our eye to 4...c5. 

Black may want to control the d4-square with the c-pawn. Nevertheless, we'll still get our d4-pawn push on the board. 

Let's begin with 1.c4.

r1b2rk1/1pq1bppp/p1n1pn2/2p5/P1BP4/2N1PN.text:
You may see 10...Qc7, ignoring the pawn for now.

We should therefore aim to place our c1-bishop on the best possible square if there are no central trades.

r1b2rk1/2q1bppp/ppn1pn2/2p5/P1BP4/1PN1PN.text:
Black may attempt to do the same.

And just remember that d5 is a good move if the conditions are favorable.

r1b2rk1/2q1bppp/ppn2n2/2pp4/P1B5/1PN1PN2.text:
Black takes.

We'll recapture with the knight.

r1b2rk1/2q1bppp/ppn5/2pn4/P1B5/1P2PN2/4Q.text:
Black trades knights.

We'll recapture, pinning the knight.

r1b2rk1/2q2ppp/ppn2b2/2pB4/P7/1P2PN2/4QP.text:
The bishop may attack our rook.

But a dark-squared bishop trade is a useful idea for us here, leaving us with the more active minor pieces.

r1b2rk1/2q2ppp/ppn5/2pB4/P7/1P2PN2/1b2QP.text:
A trade is the most logical outcome.

We'll recapture.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/2p5/P1B5/2N1PN2.text:
Black castles. 

Now it's important to show what kind of reactions Black may have to us finally playing d4. They could of course capture the pawn, or do something else.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/8/P1Bp4/2N1PN2/.text:
You could also see this capture because maybe Black isn't interested in the tension in the center.

The reason it's fine to take with the pawn and accept an IQP is because d5 is coming.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p3pn2/3nN3/P1BP4/2NR4/1.text:
But we'll start making use of our IQP by having as an anchor for our attack. 

Our rook will pivot to g3 where it will aim at the king. 

The good thing about this is that g3 and h3 are both good options for the rook, depending on how Black reacts during the attack. We should have a comfortable edge here.

r1bq1rk1/1p2bppp/p3pn2/8/PnBP4/2N2N2/1P2.text:
Black may go for blockading the d5-square.

We'll make use of the e5-square.

r1bqk2r/1p2bppp/p1n1pn2/2p5/P1B5/2N1PN2/.text:
The bishop comes out to e7.

And we'll get the rook to the d-file.

r1bqkb1r/1p3ppp/p1n1pn2/2p5/P1B5/2N1PN2/.text:
Black develops their knight.

Qe2 continues our preparations to pushing d4. Rd1 is coming next.

The rook will help support the pawn up the board.

r2q1rk1/1p1bbppp/p3pn2/4N3/PnBP4/2N5/1P2.text:
Black could attempt to get their bishop into the game, too.

We should be ready to undermine the knight which defends the kingside with Bg5.

r2q1rk1/1p2bppp/p1b1pn2/4N1B1/PnBP4/2N5/.text:
After 13...Bc6, Black is saying they're fine with the trade on c6 because their pawn will help control d5.

We'll take them up on this offer since the c-pawn can be weak, and we are acquiring the bishop pair.

r2q1rk1/4bppp/p1p1pn2/P5B1/1nBP4/2N5/1P2.text:
And I like playing a5 here, to prevent Black from playing a5 themselves and anchoring their knight. 

We'll also have a nice rook lift to start applying pressure on the knight. Moves like g3 are also sound because Black lacks a light-squared bishop and we need to create luft for the king.

r4rk1/1bq2ppp/ppn5/2pB4/P7/1P2PN2/1Q1R1P.text:
We'll double on the d-file and we'll be ready for a bishop trade, since we can't allow the bishop on b7 to aim at f3 and g2. 

If the knight moves, we'll also play Qe5 to trade queens since we have control of the only open file.

rnbq1rk1/p4ppp/1p3n2/2pp4/Nb6/1P2PN2/PB1.text: b6 is the best way to defend the pawn.

And now the calm Be2. 

We're going to castle, place a rook on the c-file and make use of the e5-square for our knight. 

The bishop on b4 only delayed d4, but it's not going to be the most useful piece after we castle.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4p3/2pn4/1b6/1PN1PN2/PB1.text:
This is a bad move: Black isn't recapturing with a pawn, so they're losing control of the center. 

The bishop on c8 is also trapped behind the pawns.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4p3/2pn4/1b6/1PN1PN2/PBQ.text:
You will even get pressure on h7, 0-0-0, and really dynamic chances against Black's kingside. 

Black is down in development and with less central control, despite the fact that we are delaying moving our d-pawn. 

If ...Nxc3 or ...Bxc3, we'll recapture with the d-pawn to open up our rook on d1.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/4pn2/2pp4/1bP5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
6...c5 is a popular move now.

We'll take in the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp3ppp/5n2/2pp4/1b6/1PN1PN2/PB1.text:
Black recaptures. 

And now d4 is not possible because of the pin on the knight.

So we'll go 8.Na4 to threaten a3 and to take on c5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/4pn2/8/2BP4/2N1PN2/PP2.text:
And we'll continue with standard development. 

If ...c5, we'll take and bring our rook to the d-file. We'll also push our e-pawn not only to control central squares, but to develop our dark-squared bishop.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1bP5/1PN1PN2/P.text:
The most common move is for Black to castle.

We'll just fianchetto.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/1PP1PN2/P4.text: And after Black castles, we can already make use of the bishop.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/BPP1PN2/P4.text:
We target the rook and ask Black how they'll defend their dark squares. 

Qc2 and Rd1 are normal developing moves we'll strive for in this middlegame in which we're up the bishop pair and have pressure against the central pawns. With two c-pawns, we'll be able to do much against Black's center.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/4pn2/8/2B5/2N1PN2/PP1P1.text:
Now you'll most likely see 5...Be7. This is the most natural developing move.

We'll simply push in the center with our d-pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/1bP5/2N1PN2/PP1.text:
Black may play this move. 

It occurs in 14% of games in the database, which accounts for more than 31,000 games. 

Black's aim is to undermine the knight and make the d4-pawn push harder to play.

5.b3 helps us stay consistent.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/1Pb1PN2/P2P.text:
Some people think it's a good idea to trade on c3. 

I don't like it since I think they're giving up the bishop pair for nothing.

We'll recapture.

rnbqkb1r/1p3ppp/p3pn2/2p5/P1B5/2N1PN2/1P.text:
But since we went a4, we didn't do anything about the c-pawn push. 

This is nothing to concern ourselves with too much, though.

We'll castle first. 

d4 and d5 is our plan, but it's always good to castle first.

rnbqkb1r/1pp2ppp/p3pn2/8/2B5/2N1PN2/PP1P.text:
Or you may also see 5...a6. This move aims to achieve the ...b5 pawn push and it's a common idea in these Queen's Gambit positions.

6. a4 is a very logical reaction. 

We're preventing an easy b5 and creating a retreat square for our bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P5/2N1P3/PP1P.text:
Black develops their knight.

And we'll develop ours.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/8/2p5/2N1PN2/PP1P1.text:
Finally, 4...dxc4 is played in around 11,000 games, or ony about 5% of games in the database. 

But the reason it's important is because we're being taken to Queen's Gambit Accepted territory, and we need to know what to do.

Recapturing the pawn and developing is a pretty easy option.

rnbqkbnr/ppp2ppp/4p3/3p4/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
Black pushes their d-pawn.

And we'll go for our Anti-QGD controlling d4 and protecting our c-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppp1ppp/4p3/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
And Black will play their standard 1...e6 approach.

We'll develop our knight.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
We know that Black pushing ...c5 is thematic in the Queen's Gambit Declined. 

But Black could also potentially veer things into Queen's Gambit Accepted territory, or they could play a natural looking move to put pressure on our knight (4...Bb4). 

Let's see how to combat these options. We begin with 1.c4.

3rkb1r/2pn1ppp/1pB1p3/p7/P1PP4/2P2P2/5P1.text:
And the bishop occupies the weak queenside light-squares. 

White's position is very comfortable with the bishop pair and the open b and g-files.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q7/1bPP4/3B1N2/P2B1.text:
Black develops.

And we'll put pressure on the b4-bishop.

r1b1k2r/pp3ppp/2n1p3/q7/2PP4/3B1N2/P2Q1P.text:
We'll recapture. 

White is once again doing very well, with the better center and the better development.

r1b1kb1r/pp3pp1/2n1pq1p/8/2Pp4/2PB1N2/P4.text:
Black tries to win a pawn on d4 and weaken our center.

We'll recapture with the pawn.

r1b1kb1r/pp3pp1/4p2p/8/2Pq4/3B4/P4PPP/1R.text:
We save the rook. 

Black's king is still in the center, our bishops have more scope and there are always Bh7+ threats lurking if Black castles and doesn't protect their queen.

r1b1kb1r/pp3pp1/4pq1p/8/2Pn4/3B1N2/P4PPP.text:
Black wins a pawn!

But we'll trade...

r1b2rk1/ppp2pp1/2nb1q1p/4p3/2P1B3/2P2N2/.text: We'll have good play on the semi-open b and e-files, and the bishop on e4 is a very strong piece.

r1b2rk1/ppp2ppp/2nb1q2/4p3/2P1B3/2P2N2/P.text:
Black brings the knight to c6.

With Qc2, the queen and bishop create a battery aimed at Black's kingside.

r3k2r/p1pn1pp1/1p1bp2p/8/2PP1P2/2PB4/P4P.text:
We free up the f3-square for our king in preparation for the endgame. 

We have the bishop pair, open files for our rooks, and more space.

r3k2r/p1pn1pp1/1p1bp2p/8/2PP4/2PB1P2/P4P.text: Black wants to bring the knight into the game.

r3k2r/pbpn1pp1/1p1bpq1p/8/2PP4/2PB4/P2N1.text: We have a simple plan here —improving the pieces, starting with Nd2.

r3kb1r/2pn1ppp/1p2p3/p7/P1PP4/2PB1P2/5P1.text:
Black stops our expansion.

The bishop gets centralized to e4, which also comes with an attack on the rook.

r3kb1r/p1pn1ppp/1p2p3/8/2PP4/2PB1P2/P4P1.text:
Black develops conventionally.

Let's gain some space on the queenside with a4.

rn1qkb1r/ppp2ppp/4b1n1/8/3P4/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
Black recaptures with the bishop to not mess up their pawn structure.

We'll just keep pushing in the center! 

It's all about space here, and our king is fine on e1 since Black is lacking development.

rn2k2r/p1p2pp1/1p1bpq1p/8/2PP4/2PB1b2/P4.text:
Black wants to double up our f-pawns, but they give up the bishop pair.

Our queen recaptures.

rn2k2r/p1p2ppp/1p1bpq2/6B1/2PP4/2PB1b2/P.text:
The only move for Black to not lose immediately.

Now Qd2 is a clever move. We support our bishop on g5, and the black queen is still attacked.

rn2k2r/p1p2ppp/1p2pq2/6B1/2PP1b2/2PB1b2/.text:
This is the only move for Black, otherwise they would lose the queen.

We'll capture the bishop.

rn2k2r/p1p2ppp/1p2pq2/8/2PP1B2/2PB4/P2Q1.text:
Black captures on g2.

We'll save our rook.

rn2k2r/pbp2pp1/1p1bpq1p/8/2PP4/2PB1N2/P4.text:
Black aims the bishop at our kingside.

And we'll centralize the rook to the semi-open e-file.

rn2k2r/pbp2ppp/1p1bpq2/8/2PP4/2PB1N2/P4P.text:
This is a bad move that illustrates why you need to prevent Bg5.

Let's go ahead and attack the queen.

rn2k2r/pbp2ppp/1p2pq2/8/2PP1B2/2PB4/P2Q1.text:
And White castles queenside. 

We've got the bishop pair, and furthermore, our bishop on f4 is very powerful on the kingside dark squares.

rn2kb1r/p1p2ppp/1p2p3/8/2PP4/2PB1q2/P4PP.text:
Black trades the queens.

We recapture.

rn2kb1r/p1p2ppp/1p2pq2/8/2PP4/2PB1b2/P4P.text:
Black trades on f3 immediately, which happens in nearly 15% of games.

We don't mind a queen trade.

White will be doing well in the endgame.

rn2kb1r/pbp2pp1/1p2pq1p/8/2PP4/2PB1N2/P4.text:
Black covers the g5-square.

We'll castle.

rn2kb1r/pbp2ppp/1p2pq2/8/2PP4/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
Black fianchettoes.

d3 is a typical place for the light-squared bishop. 

It occupies the b1-h7 diagonal and fights for the e4-square.

rn2kb1r/ppp2ppp/5q2/4p3/2P1B1b1/2P2N2/P2.text: We'll protect it with the bishop, and threaten the b7-pawn.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/4p3/5qB1/1bPP4/5N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black tries to play actively and take advantage of our uncastled king.

We can just simply retreat the bishop.

rnb1k2r/pp3ppp/4p3/q7/1bPP4/5N2/P2B1PPP/.text:
Black tries to improve their queen.

We'll develop the bishop to d3 and prepare to castle.

rnb1k2r/ppp2ppp/3b1q2/4p3/2P5/2PB1N2/P2P.text:
Black chooses to develop the dark-squared bishop.

We'll get castled.

rnb1kb1r/p1p2ppp/1p2pq2/8/2P5/2P2N2/P2P1.text:
Black prepares to fianchetto their light-squared bishop.

We'll take over the center with d4.

8.c5 is an interesting gambit that you could play, but let's keep things solid.

rnb1kb1r/pp3pp1/4pq1p/2p5/2PP4/2P2N2/P4P.text:
Black stops Bg5 with 8...h6.

We'll bring the other bishop to the d3-square.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4p3/5qB1/2Pp4/2P2N2/P4PP.text:
Black saves the queen.

And now we recapture on d4.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4pq2/2p5/2P5/2P2N2/P2P1P.text:
The most popular move, which happens in 32% of the games, is 7...c5.

Black fights for the d4-square.

But we'll push anyway! 

Let's play actively here.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/4pq2/8/2Pp4/2P2N2/P4PPP/.text:
Black doesn't stop Bg5 and captures on d4 immediately.

So we'll attack the queen.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/4pq2/8/2P5/2P5/P2P1PPP/.text:
Black captures the pawn.

We'll continue by developing the knight.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5q2/4p3/2P5/2P2N2/P2P1P.text:
Black decides to push in the center instead. 

This isn't a very popular move (occurring nearly 10% of times in the database), but should be covered anyway. 

We'll focus on development and bring our bishop to d3.

rnb2rk1/ppp2ppp/3b1q2/4p3/2P5/2PB1N2/P2P.text:
Black does as well.

We'll centralize our bishop on e4, looking to put pressure on the diagonal and also blocking Black's e-pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/1n6/3pP3/3P4/2NBB3/PP3P.text: We are much more active here, and with Nge2 and O-O coming, our position is very comfortable.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/1n6/3pP3/3P4/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
Black re-routes their knight, which was blocking the development of other pieces.

The bishop on e3 will support our central pawns.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p1n1/3P4/3P4/2N5/PP3PP.text:
The knight retreats to g6.

We'll grab the pawn on e6!

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4p3/3Pn3/8/2N5/PP1P1PPP.text:
Black regains the material by capturing on e5.

Let's expand with a tempo by playing d4!

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pP2/8/2P5/2p5/PP1P1PPP.text:
Black captures our piece in return.

We'll recapture on c3, so we'll have d4 later.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/3p4/2P1P3/2N5/PP1P.text:
The best move to counterattack, immediately pressuring our central pawns. 

This is the most common response, with 38% occurrence.

We'll push in the center and attack the knight.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/4pn2/4P3/2Pp4/2N5/PP1P1.text:
Black responds actively and attacks our knight in return.

Let's capture on f6, since moving the knight is too passive.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/6n1/3P4/7P/2N5/PP3PP1/R.text:
And we'll grab even more space by pushing the h-pawn!

White's position is very solid with a slight advantage. 

Black is once again lacking development and has less space.

rnbqkb1r/pppn1ppp/4p3/3pP3/2P5/2N5/PP1P1.text:
Black retreats their knight instead, which is the most popular move here with 54% of the games.

We'll snatch the central pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppn1ppp/8/3pP3/8/2N5/PP1P1PPP/.text:
If Black recaptures on d5 with the pawn...

...we can create a strong center by playing d4.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
Black opens up the dark-squared bishop.

And with e4, we go for the Mikenas-Carls variation! 

It is a very challenging system
for Black to face since we grab a large chunk of the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black responds with the development of their kingside knight.

By developing the b1-knight we add even more control to the center.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Let's study the Mikenas-Carls Variation, where we take early central control. 

In this study, we'll see what happens when Black goes for 3...d5, which is the most popular.

We'll start off with the English, of course!

r1b1k2r/1p1pqnpp/pB2pp2/2P2n2/1Q2N3/8/PP.text:
But a queen trade would only benefit Black, so we push our c-pawn, increasing our control of the dark squares. 

We have more space and our pieces are just beautifully placed.

r1b1k2r/1p1pqnpp/pB2pp2/5n2/1QP1N3/8/PP3.text: Black tries to release the pressure with a queen trade.

r1b1k2r/1pBp1npp/p3pp2/4n3/N1P5/8/PP3PPP.text:
...we have Na4! 

Looking to invade the weak queenside squares.

r1b1k2r/1pBp2pp/p3pp2/4P3/8/2N5/PP1KB1PP.text:
The knight on a1 is lost, and our pieces are much more active. 

With the better pieces and the dark-square control on the queenside, we have the advantage.

r1b1k2r/1pBp2pp/p3pp2/4P3/8/2N5/PPn3PP/R.text:
Black goes for the fork.

We'll move the king and ensure that the knight can't get back out.

r1b1k2r/1pBp2pp/p3pp2/4n3/2n5/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
Black captures on c4, since the knights protect each other.

But with f4, we'll attack one of them!

r1b1k2r/1pBp2pp/p3pp2/4n3/5P2/2N1n3/PP4P.text:
Black intends to fork us on c2, but our pieces will be superior.

Let's grab the knight.

r1b1n2r/1p2k1pp/pB2pp2/2Ppn3/8/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Black is going for activity.

We'll capture en passant.

r1b1n2r/1pBpk1pp/p3pp2/2P1n3/8/2N5/PP3PP.text:
The knight retreats.

We'll retreat our bishop and let it keep an eye on the weak queenside dark-squares.

r1b4r/1p2k1pp/pB1npp2/4n3/8/2N5/PP3PPP/R.text:
Black recaptures.

And let's pin the knight on d6 and just keep adding pressure to it!

r1b4r/1p2knpp/p2npp2/2B5/8/2N5/PP3PPP/R3.text:
Black reinforces d6.

Now our rook joins the attack!

r1b4r/1pBpk1pp/p2npp2/4n3/2P5/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
Black's king defends the knight.

We'll advance the c-pawn and attack it.

r1bBk2r/1p1p2pp/p2npp2/4n3/2P5/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Black takes our queen.

Our bishop retreats and attacks the knight.

r1bqk1nr/1p1p1ppp/p2bp3/4n3/2P5/2N5/PP3P.text:
Black captures, which is practically forced.

Now, our queen gets to a dominant position and takes aim at some weak dark squares while attacking the knight.

r1bqk1nr/1p1p2pp/p2Qpp2/4n3/2P5/2N5/PP3P.text:
Black keeps the knight in the center and protects it.

We'll develop the c1-bishop and continue our dark-square domination!

r1bqk1nr/1p3ppp/p2bp3/2P1n3/8/2N5/PP3PPP.text:
Black captures the knight.

We'll take back with the pawn, which will be a great asset that gives us space and limits Black.

r1bqk2r/1p1p1npp/pB1Qpp2/5n2/2P1N3/8/PP3.text:
Black threatens our queen once more.

We'll retreat to b4, keeping the queen on the dark-squared diagonal, where it protects the b6-bishop.

r1bqk2r/1p1p2pp/pB1Qpp2/4nn2/2P5/2N5/PP3.text:
But Black can counter-attack ours.

Let's go ahead and capture the queen.

r1bqk2r/1p1pn1pp/p2Qpp2/4n3/2P5/2N1B3/PP.text:
Black is going for ...Nf5, to kick out our queen.

But we have Bb6, trapping the black queen!

r1bqk2r/1p1pnnpp/pB1Qpp2/8/2P5/2N5/PP3PP.text:
...Nf7 is a move we would like to see.

We have an opportunity to improve our knight by centralizing it!

r1bqk2r/1p3ppp/p2Ppn2/4n3/8/2N5/PP2BPPP/.text:
And White prepares to castle. 

The d6-pawn is a thorn in Black's side, and the combination of the bishop pair plus more space gives us an advantage.

r1bqkbnr/1p1p1ppp/p3p3/1N2n3/2P5/2N5/PP3.text:
Black could ignore it, and attack our knight instead.

Let's jump into Black's camp with a check!

r1bqkbnr/1p3ppp/p2pp3/1NP1n3/8/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Black attacks our knight in return.

We'll simply take on d6 with check.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/2n1p3/2p1P3/2P5/2N2N2/.text:
Black develops the queen's knight.

And here comes d4! 

We offer a pawn sacrifice to speed up our development.

r1bqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/4n3/2PN4/2N5/PP3PP.text:
As anticipated, Black grabs the e-pawn, otherwise they'll just lose space for nothing.

But our knight moves to b5, eyeing the weakness on d6.

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/3pp3/1N2n3/2P5/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Black's second option is to occupy the d6-square with their pawn.

Let's chip away at the weak d6-pawn and play c5!

r1bqkbnr/pp3ppp/4p3/1Np1n3/8/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
Capturing the pawn would be a big mistake.

Now Bf4 is a very strong move! 

We attack the knight on e5 and eye the weak c7-square.

r1bqkbnr/pp4pp/4p3/1Np1p2Q/8/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
We'll avoid a queen trade and capture on e5 next.

White is completely winning. Black's king is weak, and there are a lot of threats.

r1bqkbnr/pp4pp/4pp2/1Np1n3/5B2/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Black supports the knight so we cannot invade on c7.

We'll get rid of Black's most active piece.

r1bqr1k1/pp1nbppp/3p1n2/2pP4/4PP2/2N2N2/.text:
Black develops.

Let's get the king into safety.

r1bqrbk1/1p1n1ppp/p2p1n2/2pP4/4PP2/2N2N2.text: Black would like to push ...b5 and gain space on the queenside...

r1bqrbk1/1p1n1ppp/p2p1n2/2pP4/P3PP2/2N2N.text:
...so we will stop it! 

We've got a very nice center and more space for our pieces to maneuver!

r1bqrbk1/pp1n1ppp/3p1n2/2pP4/4PP2/2N2N2/.text:
Black attacks our e4-pawn.

We'll simply protect it with the queen.

r1br4/1p2knpp/p2npp2/2B5/8/2N5/PP2BPPP/3.text:
And with Be2, White prepares to castle. 

We'll connect the rooks, and our position is very comfortable with the bishop pair and more active pieces.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/3p1n2/2pp4/2P1PP2/2N2N2.text:
Black trades.

We'll recapture towards the center.

rnbq1rk1/pp2bppp/3ppn2/2p5/2PPPP2/2N2N2/.text:
Black creates some central counterplay.

Let's close down the center with d5! 

We have more space.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1bppp/3ppn2/8/2PPPP2/2N5/PP4.text:
Black castles.

We'll get our kingside development going with Nf3.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1p1p/4p1p1/4P1B1/2P3Q1/2P5/.text:
And we take control over the dark squares! 

Black's passivity and weak dark squares will be fatal.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1p1p/4p1p1/4P3/1bP3Q1/2N2N2.text: And after this simple developing move, White is much better with greater activity and more space.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/4p3/4P3/1bP5/2N5/PP1P1.text:
Retreating immediately would be very passive.

We'll play Qg4 to attack the g7-pawn.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1ppp/4p3/4P3/2P5/2P5/PP3PPP.text:
The only available square for the knight!

We'll move our queen to g4 and attack the g7-pawn.

This is a very common move in these variations.

rnbqk2r/ppp1bppp/3ppn2/8/2PPP3/2N5/PP3PP.text:
Black prepares to castle.

And we'll grab even more space with f4!

Aesthetic but 5. Nf3 was also perfectly normal.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/4p3/4P3/2P1n1Q1/2P5/PP3.text: We fork the knight and the g-pawn, winning material.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/4p3/4P3/2P1n3/2P5/PP3PP.text: Jumping to e4 is a big mistake.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/4P3/2P5/2b5/PP1P1P.text:
Black trades on c3 first.

We'll recapture and open up our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/8/1bP1P3/2N5/PP1P1.text:
Black goes for 3...Bb4. 

This is actually a mistake! Yet, it happens 16% of the time!

We can gain space with e5.

rnbqkb1r/pp1p1ppp/4pn2/2p5/2P1P3/2N5/PP1.text:
Black might try to push ...c5, which doesn't happen very often (9%), but it is tempting for Black to try to take advantage of the weak d4-square.

We'll force Black's knight to retreat all the way back to g8.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/3ppn2/8/2P1P3/2N5/PP1P1.text:
Black might go for a non-commital approach with 3...d6. 

We can see this move in 12% of the games.

Let's grab the center with d4!

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/4pn2/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPP.text:
Black opens up the dark-squared bishop.

And we'll go for the Mikenas-Carls variation! 

It is a very challenging system
for Black to face since we grab a large chunk of the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black responds with the development of their kingside knight.

We'll develop our queen's knight and add even more control to the center.

rnbqkbnr/pp1p1ppp/4p3/2p1P3/2P5/2N5/PP1P.text:
The only available square!

We'll develop our other knight and support the pawn on e5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
If Black does not challenge your center in move 3, they may choose a bishop move or another, less confrontational pawn move. 

Let's see how to deal with them in this second study. We'll start with 1.c4, of course!

rnbqr1k1/pp2bppp/3p1n2/2pP4/4PP2/2N2N2/P.text:
Black centralizes their rook.

We'll continue to develop, and prepare to castle.

r1b1qrk1/pp1np1bp/2pp1np1/5p2/1PPP4/2N1P.text:
A move like ...c6 now is sober. 

It controls the center and admits that Black is simply going to be playing with less space.

r1b1qrk1/pp1np1bp/2pp1np1/5p2/PPPP4/2N1P.text:
We're going to have a much better position moving forward. 

We will employ our ideas of queenside play due to having more space on that side of the board, striving for moves like Qb3, a5 and b5 to open up lines.

r1b1qrk1/pppn2bp/3p1np1/1N2pp2/1PPP4/4PN.text:
Thanks to our bishop on b2, we have this tactic. 

Black cannot defend c7 without losing a central pawn. 

10...e4 may seem like something to consider, but 11.Ng5 or 11.Nxc7 work in our favor, being +3 according to Stockfish. 

11.Ng5 is simpler, because in the Nxc7 line we'll have to find ways to free our knight from a8.

r1b1qrk1/pppn2bp/3p1np1/4pp2/1PPP4/2N1PN.text: The timing on this isn't good at all, especially once the queen has gone to e8.

r1b1qrk1/pppnp1bp/3p1np1/5p2/1PPP4/4PN2/.text:
Black continues preparing their pawn push.

But we can continue developing with Nc3, since we have more space and ...e5 doesn't solve their problems.

r1b2r1k/2pnq1bp/1p1ppnp1/p1P2p2/PP1P4/1Q.text:
Once we open the position up, we'll have great piece play because of our pieces. 

We've got easy moves to find to apply pressure at the right moments. 

Ba3 to attack the queen on the dark diagonal, Nb5 to attack the c7-pawn. Black won't be able to hold on for long.

r1b2r1k/2pnq1bp/1p1ppnp1/p4p2/PPPP4/1QN1.text: If Black tries stopping us, we've got more pawn breaks to open up the position.

r1b2r1k/p1pnq1bp/1p1ppnp1/5p2/1PPP4/1QN1.text:
The knight goes to d7 where it helps prepare a pawn break.

Unfortunately for Black, we have a significant space advantage. We have some time to start pushing things on the queenside.

rn3r1k/pbp1q1bp/1p1p1np1/2PPpp2/1P6/1QN1.text:
Our queen on b3 and knight on c3 guard the powerful d5-pawn, so 13.c5 is possible. 

We're threatening 14.c6. It's a move we'll likely play in conjunction with a4 and a5 to open up the queenside. White is doing well.

rn3r1k/pbp1q1bp/1p1p1np1/3Ppp2/1PP5/1QN1.text: In case Black chooses to keep the position closed, we'll insist.

rn3r1k/pbp1q1bp/1p1ppnp1/5p2/1PPP4/1QN1P.text:
Black may fianchetto.

We'll push d5, blocking the bishop. We would love to open up the c-file for our rook.

rnb1qrk1/pp2p1bp/2pp1np1/5p2/1PPP4/2N1PN.text:
The queen goes to e8 to support e5. 

If 8...a5, 9.b5 is good because our b5-pawn has enough support.

We'll continue with our plan of expanding on the queenside.

rnb1qrk1/pp4bp/2p2np1/4pp2/PPP5/2N1PN2/1.text:
And we castle. 

If ...e4, we've got Nd4. 

We're going to play Qb3 and Rd1, pushing our queenside pawns up the board to create strong counterplay in reply to Black's expansion. We have a small advantage.

rnb1qrk1/pp4bp/2pp1np1/4pp2/PPPP4/2N1PN2.text:
Let's say that Black attempts this pawn break without ...Nbd7.

If 9...Nbd7, we'll castle and we've got a similar position to 7...Qe8 in our hands.

We can capture and clarify the situation in the center because the situation on the queenside favors us.

rnb1qrk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/1PPP4/4PN2/.text:
Placing a queen on e8 isn't that odd in Dutch positions. 

The problem for Black here is that they lack space and the queen cannot even go to the kingside yet because the g6-pawn is in the way.

We should therefore just castle.

rnb2r1k/p1p1q1bp/1p1ppnp1/5p2/1PPP4/1QN1.text:
Going for another fianchetto is a sound choice for Black. 

It's trying to find solutions for their lack of space.

But since we are the ones with space, we can start getting ready to open up lines after Rfc1.

rnb2r1k/ppp1q1bp/3p1np1/4pp2/1PPP4/1QN1P.text:
Black pushes the e-pawn forward. 

This is a standard pawn break that you should be aware of. Black is trying to gain space and free their position.

The problem with the pawn break is that we have developed our pieces harmoniously and Black still has many underdeveloped forces.

We take on e5.

rnb2r1k/ppp1q1bp/3ppnp1/5p2/1PPP4/2N1PN2.text:
...Kh8 is a move you'll see in many Dutch lines because the king wants to get off the light square diagonal.

b3 is one of the best squares for our queen.

It supports the queenside pawns.

rnb2r1k/ppp1q1bp/5np1/4pp2/1PP5/1QN1PN2/.text:
Black recaptures.

And this knight centralization is good. 

We'll likely get a pawn wedge on d5.

rnb2r1k/ppp1q1bp/6p1/3Ppp2/1P6/1Q2PN2/PB.text:
And we recapture. 

Our queen is already in an optimal position. We'll centralize rooks with Rfd1. 

Rac1 is an option, but so is a4 for b5. In particular, if Black gives us a hook on the queenside to attack, a move like a6 or c6, we'll be wanting to play b5.

rnb2rk1/ppp1q1bp/3p1np1/4pp2/1PPP4/2N1PN.text:
This would be a premature pawn push. 

Yes, our b4-pawn is loose, but the central dynamics are more important.

Therefore we will just take.

rnb2rk1/ppp1q1bp/3ppnp1/5p2/1PPP4/4PN2/P.text:
The e7-square is great for the queen because it will help support pawn breaks and keep the queen relevant.

Our knight has the great c3-square.

rnb2rk1/ppp1q1bp/5np1/4pp2/1PP5/2N1PN2/P.text:
Black recaptures. 

But now with Nd5 we can land a knight in the center with great effect.

rnb2rk1/ppp1q1bp/6p1/3Ppp2/1P6/4PN2/PB2B.text:
And we can just take with the pawn because although b4 hangs, so does e5. 

If a logical move like Rd8, Qb3 is good. We'll be defending everything and centralizing our rooks soon with Rfd1.

rnbq1rk1/pp2p1bp/2pp1np1/5p2/1PPP4/4PN2/.text:
Black can attempt 7...c6 to try and prevent us from controlling the d5-square.

Since this may end up similar to the 7...Qe8 line, our plans stay the same, and we'll play Nc3.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/1PPP4/4PN2/.text:
Black plays 6...d6. The plan of Black's opening is to go ...e5 at some point if possible.

We should now clear the way for castling.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3ppnp1/5p2/1PPP4/4PN2/PB.text:
Black may realize they'll just need to play with less space. This is probably a sober realization.

We should castle.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/4PN2/PP3P.text:
Black fianchettoes, as expected in this line.

And now b4! We accelerate our queenside play and create a square for our bishop to come out to.

In the future a4 will be useful to completely take the queenside over, but for now we content ourselves.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2P5/5N2/PP1PPP.text:
Black develops their knight to control e4.

We'll play d4.

Having this central pawn duo is something we'll be using against the Dutch.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
This is the Leningrad Dutch. 

From this move order, it has been played 20% of the time in around 37,000 games. 

Black's aim is to fianchetto and develop quickly.

We'll play the solid e3. Black may think we're going for a b3-setup. But we're actually planning something different.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black can play the Dutch Setup and choose what type of Dutch they'll go for in the coming moves.

We'll continue with normal development. 

It's important to get the knight out to control the e5-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
Against any opening that's not 1.e4, Black can play the Dutch Setup: they can play 1...f5 and then develop their pieces in many ways. 

Those who own the Dutch course have seen a couple of these variations: the Stonewall, the Gotham Dutch and the Leningrad. In this study, we'll focus on the Leningrad which features a g7 fianchetto from Black.

We'll start off with 1.c4.

r1b2rk1/pp1n2pp/2pqp3/3p1p2/2PPn3/2NBPN2.text:
11.Rab1 prepares queenside expansion. With little happening on the kingside for Black, it seems we're the only ones that will be having fun on the queenside. 

The goal of Rab1 is to push the b-pawn and attack the hook on c6. Eventually, we may end up having an open file for the rook and Black will struggle with developing the light-squared bishop.

r1b2rk1/pp1n2pp/2pqpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2NBPN2.text:
Black cannot play 10...e5 because their f-pawn would hang.

Therefore, we should just castle and wait to see Black's hand.

r1b2rk1/ppp1b1pp/2nppn2/5p1q/1PPP4/2N2NP.text:
This is a bad square for the knight because it encourages us to gain more space, which is what we want.

We'll simply advance on the queenside.

r1b2rk1/ppp1bn1p/3ppn2/1P3ppq/P1PP4/B1N2.text:
You should expect a kingside attack of some sort. 

But just keep the rule of +2 in mind. If Black doesn't have +2 attackers, you should be perfectly able to fend off their attack.

r1b2rk1/ppp1bn1p/3ppn2/1PP2ppq/P2P4/B1N2.text:
Therefore, we can just keep on pushing on the queenside. 

After 13...dxc5 and 14.dxc5, we can even consider pushing c6 to get even more space. Depending on what Black does, there are some knight maneuvers we'd like to make - ideas like Ne1 for Nd3, for example.

r1b2rk1/ppp1bnpp/3ppn2/1P3p1q/P1PP4/2N2N.text:
This would be the only logical maneuver for that knight, but I hope it shows how you can take over the center of the board to limit Black's choices.

Now Ba3 makes the e5-pawn break impossible to play due to the pin on the d6-pawn.

r1b2rk1/pppnb1pp/3p1n2/1NP1pp1q/1P1P4/5N.text:
We're winning on the queenside. 

Black will at least lose a pawn in this transaction. The engine gives us a +2 advantage.

r1b2rk1/pppnb1pp/3p1n2/2P1pp1q/1P1P4/2N2.text:
Black isn't as quick as us, even though they'd like to be. 

The move 10...e5 illustrates this point. This is their desired pawn break, but they simply aren't ready for it.

r1b2rk1/pppnb1pp/3ppn2/5p1q/1PPP4/2N2NP1.text:
You should expect the knight to come out at this point. 

Black really wants to try and attack.

However, we'll play c5. Our space advantage is significant, and our attack seems to be getting places a lot quicker.

r1bn1rk1/ppp1b1pp/3ppn2/1P3p1q/2PP4/2N2N.text:
The knight falls back to d8.

We can gain more space by playing  a4.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PPn3/5NP1/PP.text:
But we should be perfectly fine. 

Nc3 and e3 are coming right up. We'll have a solid center and connected rooks. The position is about equal.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP.text:
Black could castle now.

We'll castle as well.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/1bPP4/5NP1/PP.text:
This check is also feasible to get quicker development.

We'll block with the bishop as we don't mind a trade of dark-squared bishops. 

After all, it is Black who has chosen to weaken their dark squares with ...f5 and ...e6.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PPQ.text:
After this trade, we'll recapture with the queen.

The c3-square remains a good square for our knight. 

Ne4 isn't a problem because we can just move away to c2.

rnb1k2r/pp4pp/2pqpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/4PN2/PPQ.text:
Black will recapture.

And after developing, we still have a strong position because we control the e5-square and having fewer weak squares in the long term.

rnb1qrk1/ppp1b1pp/3ppn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
And this is the common Dutch idea that you're bound to see. 

Black knows that they can attack in the Dutch, and Qe8 to h5 is a classic maneuver for that purpose.

We have a strong bishop on g2 that will help defend our king. 

We're also very near to breaking the position open with e4.

rnb2rk1/pp4pp/2pqpn2/3p1p2/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
Black castles.

And we can bring our bishop to d3.

rnb2rk1/ppp1b1pp/3ppn2/5p1q/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
Here comes the queen. 

Black usually wants stuff like ...Ng4 to target h2.

But, trusting that our king has sufficient defense thanks to our minor pieces on the kingside, we can begin a queenside initiative.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPnB2/2NBP.text:
Black jumps their knight onto e4. 

I can't stress this enough, we're not looking to capture the knight on e4. 

Bxe4 allows Black to recapture with a pawn and make their light square pawn chain longer. This loses the advantage for White.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1p3/3p1p2/2PPnBP1/2NB.text:
Instead, we have this interesting move. 

We are trying to weaken Black's Stonewall Setup, or alternatively open up the g-file for our rook. White has a nice space advantage.

It's hard to suggest what Black should do with their light-squared bishop.

rnbq1rk1/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/2N1.text:
Black castles.

We increase our pressure on e4, even though we wouldn't capture the knight if it lands on e4.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1b1pp/3ppn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2NP1/.text:
Black starts controlling the e5-square because their long-term plan is to push e5 or even to get the queen to h5.

We should fianchetto, developing before we open the position up.

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PPQNP.text: If Black castles, as was their plan when they played 4...Bb4+ ...

rnbq1rk1/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PPP3/5N2/PPQN.text: We can be slightly better after 7.e4 because we're challenging Black's control of the center and getting ready to open the position up favorably. We have more space and more pieces developed.

rnbq1rk1/ppppb1pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
Black castles.

Before playing e4, we want to develop. We'll prepare a fianchetto with g3.

rnbqk2r/pp2b1pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/4PN2.text:
Black could also develop with Be7 to simply castle and avoid trading their important dark-squared bishop.

This is a bad approach because the bishop on f4 controls important real estate on e5.

We'll develop our knight to c3. From here it'll help fight for e4.

rnbqk2r/pp4pp/2pbpn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/4PN2/P.text:
Black may attempt to trade bishops, since the f4-bishop is quite strong.

We'll accept the trade because their dark squares will be weak.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/1bPP4/5N2/PPQ1P.text:
This check is an attempt to develop quickly. It occurs 12% of the time in the database.

Like I said previously, we don't mind a trade of dark-squared bishops.

rnbqk2r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PPQbPP.text:
Black trades.

I know that I recommended taking with the queen in the 4...b6 line, but here we can go for a quick e4 by recapturing with the knight. 

In the 4...b6 line, e4 simply wasn't possible because Black controlled that square with the b7-bishop. This is not the case here.

rnbqk2r/ppppb1pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PPQ1P.text:
The most popular and natural move is for Black to enable castling. It occurs around 35% of the time, but since our move 4.Qc2 is rare, there's only 1300 games from this position. 

4...Be7 is especially common when Black is playing the Dutch as a setup-based opening.

We'll bring our knight out to c3.

We're helping fight for the control of the light squares in the center.

rnbqkb1r/p1pp2pp/1p2pn2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PPQ.text:
Developing with ...b6 is also something you may encounter. 

It occurs in around 15% of games after 4.Qc2.

We'll play g3, and prepare to place our bishop on the long diagonal.

rnbqkb1r/pp4pp/2p1pn2/3p1p2/2PP1B2/5N2/P.text:
...c6 is a good follow-up to ensure they'll hold the center down.

We should play 6.e3 to connect our pawns, especially since our bishop has been developed.

rnbqkb1r/ppp3pp/4pn2/3p1p2/2PP4/5N2/PPQ1.text:
This is Stonewall territory. 

Black wants to have a strong light-squared chain of pawns controlling the e4-square.

But the Stonewall allows us to maneuver around Black's weak dark squares. 

5.Bf4 is precisely the move to begin doing that.

rnbqkb1r/pppp2pp/4pn2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
This move 3...e6 is the prelude to the Stonewall or Gotham Dutch. 

Black can even go to e7 with their bishop or just fianchetto on the queenside. Let's see how to face these options.

c2 is a great square for our queen. This helps us remove the sting from the Gotham Dutch which would have occurred after 4.Nc3 Bb4.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2P5/5N2/PP1PPP.text:
Black develops their knight to control e4.

And we can get two pawns in the center.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black can go for the Dutch, hoping we transpose back into normal Dutch territory.

We'll play our knight out to f3 first.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, we'll come up with a creative way to face all other Dutch Variations Black may come up with. 

The early 4.Qc2 will catch many Stonewall and Gotham Dutch players off-guard. This delays committing the queenside knight and instead places the queen on a useful square. 

We'll start with 1.c4, the English.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/4p3/2P5/2N1PN2/P.text:
And we go e3, preparing a d4 push.

This position has been analyzed in the first two chapters of the course.

r1bqkb1r/pppppppp/2n2n2/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPP.text:
Black could also start with ...Nf6.

We'll develop with Nf3.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2P5/2N2N2/PP1P.text:
And we'll simply meet ...e5 with Nf3.

This position has been analyzed in the second study of the third chapter.

r1bqkbnr/pppp1ppp/2n5/4p3/2P5/2N5/PP1PPP.text: Black typically advances ...e5, taking some central space & preventing d4.

r1bqkbnr/pppppppp/2n5/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black can also play 1...Nc6, simply developing the queenside knight.

This move might look offbeat at first glance, but has no independent value as Black can hardly continue without ...e5.

Against ...Nc6, we'll also develop our queenside knight behind the c-pawn.

r2q1rk1/1bpp2pp/1p1bpn2/pNnP1p2/2P5/PP3N.text:
And we can go b3, preventing Black from pushing ...a4, supporting c4 & preparing to develop the c1-bishop.

White definitely enjoys an edge here thanks to the space advantage. We'll continue with Bb2 & should look into capturing on d6 at the right moment.

r2q1rk1/1bpp2pp/np1bpn2/p2P1p2/2P5/P1N2N.text:
Black goes ...Na6, developing their other knight and looking for ...Nc5.

We can then go Nb5, making use of the weakened b5-square and targeting Black's dark-squared bishop on d6.

rn1q1rk1/1bpp2pp/1p1bpn2/p2P1p2/2P5/P1N2.text:
Black advances their a-pawn, taking queenside space and preventing b4.

We'll simply get our king to safety.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp1ppp/1p1bpn2/3P4/2P5/P1N2NP.text:
And we can simply proceed with g3.

Once again, White is slightly better thanks to the space advantage. Our plan is to continue with Bg2 and O-O.

rn1q1rk1/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/3P1p2/2P5/P1N2N.text:
Black continues by castling

We'll fianchetto our bishop, as planned.

rn1qk2r/pbpp1ppp/1p1bpn2/3P4/2P5/P1N5/1P.text:
Black develops the f8-bishop to d6.

We should then develop our kingside knight, preventing any ...Be5 ideas.

rn1qk2r/pbpp2pp/1p1bpn2/3P1p2/2P5/P1N3P1.text:
Black develops the f8-bishop to d6.

...Be7 is also possible, but ...Bd6 is more active. The convenient thing is that our plan is the same either way.

We develop our kingside knight.

It's very slightly better to start with Nf3 in order to prevent any ...Be5 ideas.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp1ppp/1p2pn2/8/2PP4/P1N5/1P2.text:
Black's other option is to control the e4-square with ...Nf6 instead of ...f5.

Against this, I also suggest d5, with the idea to shut down Black's b7-bishop.

rn1qkb1r/pbpp2pp/1p2pn2/3P1p2/2P5/P1N5/1.text:
Black typically continues with ...Nf6.

We will then proceed with g3.

Our plan is simple - fianchetto the bishop, go Nf3, and castle short!

rn1qkbnr/pbpp1ppp/1p2p3/8/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
Black goes ...e6, controlling d5 and opening up the dark-squared bishop.

And I suggest we proceed with 4.a3!

This is a very important move - we're preventing the annoying ...Bb4 pin and preparing to take the center with e4.

rn1qkbnr/pbpp2pp/1p2p3/5p2/2PP4/P1N5/1P2.text:
Most often, Black advances ...f5.

Against this, I suggest we push d5!

I believe this approach is practically very challenging for Black since the d5-pawn kills the fianchettoed bishop.

rn1qkbnr/pbpppppp/1p6/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
Black fianchettoes their bishop.

We'll expand in the center with d4.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4p3/1PP5/2N3P1/P2.text:
And we advance our b-pawn, expanding on the queenside.

Black can continue developing in a handful of ways here, but our plan stays consistent: we'll go Rb1 to support the b-pawn and get off of the diagonal, play d3 to support the c4-pawn and e4-square, and complete our development with Nf3 and O-O.

rnbqk1nr/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP1.text: Black goes ...d6, supporting e5 and opening up the light-squared bishop.

rnbqk1nr/pppp1pbp/6p1/4p3/2P5/2N3P1/PP1P.text:
Black advances their e-pawn, taking control of the center and preventing d4.

We'll fianchetto the bishop, as planned.

rnbqk1nr/ppppppbp/6p1/8/2P5/2N5/PP1PPPPP.text:
Black fianchettoes their bishop.

We'll proceed with 3.g3, looking to fianchetto our light-squared bishop.

rnbqkbnr/p1pppppp/1p6/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black can also play 1...b6, preparing to fianchetto the light-squared bishop.

Against ...b6, we'll also develop our queenside knight behind the c-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppp1p/6p1/8/2P5/8/PP1PPPPP/R.text:
Black can play 1...g6, preparing to fianchetto.

Often this will transpose into a mainstream variation like the King's Indian or Grunfeld, but this move order holds some independent value.

Against ...g6, we'll simply develop our queenside knight.

It might be tempting to quickly take the center, but our plan here is to develop with g3 and Bg2.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/8/8/PPPPPPPP/RNBQK.text:
In this study, we will be taking a look at how to respond to unconventional first moves - 1...g6, 1...b6 & 1...Nc6.

These moves aren't considered the most critical or challenging, but it's important to know how to face them.

We'll start with 1.c4, the English.
